verdict.shared_subject: Cyber-crisis authority and market-surveillance authority handling serious incidents
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern institutional handling of cyber or serious incidents, so one might initially suspect overlapping responsibilities or procedures. However, Provision A assigns the Minister general cyber-crisis-management tasks under the national plan, while Provision B requires the market-surveillance authority to take measures within seven days after receiving a high-risk AI serious-incident notification; neither text prohibits the other authority from acting or creates incompatible duties.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, simultaneously performable functions on different authorities: the Minister has the tasks assigned by the national cyber-crisis plan, and the market-surveillance authority must act within seven days and follow Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 procedures. The texts establish no conflicting deadline, prohibition, or exclusive allocation of competence.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Onze Minister is de cybercrisisbeheerautoriteit, bedoeld in artikel 9, eerste lid, van de NIS2-richtlijn, en heeft in die hoedanigheid de taken die zijn opgenomen in het nationaal plan voor grootschalige cyberbeveiligingsincidenten en crisisrespons, genoemd in artikel 20.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De markttoezichtautoriteit neemt passende maatregelen, zoals bedoeld in artikel 19 van Verordening (EU) 2019/1020, binnen zeven dagen na de datum waarop zij de in lid 1 van dit artikel bedoelde kennisgeving heeft ontvangen, en volgt de kennisgevingsprocedures waarin die verordening voorziet.

verdict.shared_subject: Ministerial decisions concerning registration or designation of organisations/entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern ending a status by ministerial decision, so an organisation could potentially be affected by both regimes. However, Article 43 concerns a registration in the national register when the ground for registration has changed, lapsed, or is absent, while Article 2 concerns withdrawal of an organisation’s designation when it no longer provides specified electronic services; the texts do not make these decisions legally incompatible.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be obeyed together because they regulate different legal statuses and different triggers. A registration may be changed, refused, or ended under Article 43, while a designation may be withdrawn under Article 2; neither provision requires maintaining the status that the other permits or requires ending.

Provision B concerns an exemption from the obligation to maintain a register of processing activities for certain organisations with fewer than 250 employees, so one might argue that a small organisation could have an incident-reporting duty while being exempt from the processing register duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties with different triggers: A regulates incident reporting by essential or important entities, while B limits when specified organisations must maintain a processing-activities register. Neither provision requires or forbids conduct addressed by the other, and exemption from the register obligation does not affect the incident-reporting duty.

verdict.shared_subject: Administrative fines for overlapping data-protection or AI-related infringements
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits the competent authority from imposing a fine under articles 80 and 87 for the same conduct once a GDPR fine has been imposed. Provision B authorizes the European Data Protection Supervisor to impose administrative fines on EU institutions, bodies, and agencies within the AI Act’s scope, potentially for conduct that could also constitute the same infringement addressed by the GDPR fine.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions concern different authorities, addressees, and legal bases: A regulates a Dutch competent authority’s duplicate fine after a GDPR fine, while B concerns fines imposed by the European Data Protection Supervisor on EU institutions, bodies, and agencies. Nothing in B requires a second fine for the same conduct, and A does not purport to govern the EDPS’s competence under the AI Act.
verdict.evidence_span_a: legt de bevoegde autoriteit geen bestuurlijke boete op op grond van de artikelen 80 en 87 voor een inbreuk als bedoeld in het tweede lid die voortvloeit uit dezelfde gedraging
verdict.evidence_span_b: De Europese Toezichthouder voor gegevensbescherming kan administratieve geldboeten opleggen aan instellingen, organen en instanties van de Unie die binnen het toepassingsgebied van deze verordening vallen.

verdict.shared_subject: Publication of information by public bodies
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits publication of a decision before ten working days have elapsed, subject to specified exceptions. Provision B contemplates rules requiring organs to publish a current statement on their website, which could theoretically require publication during that waiting period, but it does not say that the statement must contain or publish the decision covered by A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B concerns publication of a statement about the application of an appointed standard, whereas A concerns publication of a particular decision and expressly permits earlier publication in specified circumstances. The two duties can therefore be fulfilled together without any demonstrated conflict.

verdict.shared_subject: Substantieel gewijzigde AI-systemen met een hoog risico en de verantwoordelijkheden van de oorspronkelijke aanbieder
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Artikel 25 verplicht de oorspronkelijke aanbieder tot samenwerking, informatieverstrekking en technische toegang wanneer een andere actor door de omstandigheden van lid 1 aanbieder wordt. Artikel 43 verplicht vervolgens tot een nieuwe conformiteitsbeoordeling bij een substantiële wijziging; men zou kunnen aanvoeren dat de oorspronkelijke aanbieder daardoor moet meewerken aan een beoordeling voor een systeem waarvoor hij niet langer als aanbieder geldt.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: De bepalingen leggen verschillende, naast elkaar uitvoerbare verplichtingen op: artikel 25 regelt bijstand in de AI-waardeketen, terwijl artikel 43 de conformiteitsbeoordeling van het substantieel gewijzigde systeem regelt. Niets in artikel 43 verbiedt de samenwerking of bijstand van artikel 25, en niets in artikel 25 ontslaat een betrokken actor van de nieuwe beoordeling.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Die ursprüngliche aanbieder werkt nauw samen met nieuwe aanbieders, stelt de nodige informatie beschikbaar en verstrekt de redelijkerwijs verwachte technische toegang en andere bijstand die nodig is om te voldoen aan de verplichtingen van deze verordening
verdict.evidence_span_b: AI-systemen met een hoog risico die reeds aan een conformiteitsbeoordelingsprocedure zijn onderworpen, ondergaan een nieuwe conformiteitsbeoordelingsprocedure telkens wanneer zij substantieel zijn gewijzigd

Provision B requires a digitally offered high-risk AI system's CE marking to be accessible through its interface or an accessible machine-readable code or other electronic means; an actor can comply with both without contradiction.

verdict.shared_subject: Use of a high-risk AI system and personal-data breach communications
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can concern the same organisation using a high-risk AI system and processing personal data. However, Article 34 regulates whether affected data subjects must be notified of a personal-data breach, while Article 27 regulates a fundamental-rights impact assessment before and during use of a high-risk AI system; neither requires or forbids conduct addressed by the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: An organisation can perform and update the required fundamental-rights impact assessment while also notifying data subjects of a breach, or relying on an Article 34 exception where its conditions are met. The provisions have different triggers, duties and subject matter, so compliance with one does not obstruct compliance with the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing special-category or criminal-offence personal data by a temporary commission or advisory body where the processing may rely on consent
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A creates an exception to the prohibition when obtaining explicit consent is impossible or disproportionately burdensome, provided the other safeguards are met. Provision B requires the controller to demonstrate consent whenever the processing is based on consent, so relying on A's exception could appear inconsistent with B if the processing is nevertheless characterized as consent-based.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A does not require or authorize processing on the basis of consent; it expressly addresses cases where obtaining explicit consent is impossible or disproportionately burdensome and imposes additional safeguards. Provision B applies only when the processing actually rests on consent, so both provisions can be obeyed by using A's statutory exception without claiming that the processing is consent-based, or by documenting consent where consent is used.

verdict.shared_subject: The final-incident-report duty for an essential or important entity subject to both provisions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions require a final report, but A measures its one-month deadline from the Article 27 notification, while B measures its one-month deadline from submission of the incident notification under point b). If those triggering events occur at different times, the same entity could face two different final-report deadlines.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The substantive contents of the final report are materially the same: both require a detailed incident description, the threat or root cause, mitigation measures, and cross-border consequences where applicable. The provisions can also be complied with cumulatively by submitting the report by the earlier applicable deadline; neither text forbids an earlier or additional report.
verdict.concrete_scenario: An essential entity reports a significant incident under Article 23(b) 72 hours after discovering it, but its Article 27 notification under the national provision is submitted two weeks later. Article 29 then sets the final-report deadline one month after the Article 27 notification, whereas Article 23(d) sets it one month after the Article 23(b) incident notification, creating different reference dates for the same final-report duty.

verdict.shared_subject: The handling and possible transfer of personal data by a critical third-country ICT service provider.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision B requires the critical third-country ICT service provider to provide requested information, which could entail disclosing personal data to an authority or another recipient. Provision A prohibits transferring personal data to a third country or international organisation unless the GDPR Chapter V conditions are satisfied, so an information request could appear to require a transfer that is not otherwise authorised under Chapter V.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B requires provision of requested information but does not state that the information must contain personal data or that it must be transferred to a third country or international organisation. Even if personal data are involved, B can be complied with by providing the information through a transfer that satisfies Provision A's Chapter V conditions, so the texts do not themselves establish incompatible duties.
verdict.missing_reference: The specific information request under Article 37, including its recipient, the requested contents, and the applicable GDPR Chapter V transfer mechanism or exception (for example, an adequacy decision, appropriate safeguards, or an Article 49 derogation), is needed to determine whether complying with the request would require a prohibited transfer.

Provision B exempts certain organisations with fewer than 250 employees from the register-of-processing-activities obligations, so a small provider might have no Article 30 register duty despite A requiring incident reporting that could concern processing activities.

Nothing in B forbids incident reporting, and the Article 30 exemption does not remove A's separate reporting obligation.

verdict.shared_subject: Confidential information exchanged between competent authorities under EU digital-law regulations
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A treats covered exchanges as confidential but expressly permits disclosure when the competent authority declares at the time of communication that the information may be disclosed. Provision B says confidentially exchanged information may not be disclosed without prior consultation in the specified high-risk-AI law-enforcement, border-control, immigration, or asylum context, so an A-authorised disclosure could appear to conflict with B's consultation requirement.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be satisfied together if any disclosure authorised under A is preceded by the consultation required by B, or if B's specific high-risk-AI and public/national-security conditions are not present. They also regulate different, only partly overlapping exchanges and do not establish that every disclosure covered by A falls within B's prohibition.

verdict.decisive_exception: Article 78's exceptions in paragraphs 1 and 2, together with the conditions limiting its prohibition to the specified high-risk-AI and security context.

verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be satisfied together because they may govern different designations, actors, and statutory schemes: A concerns an institution designated as an essential entity by the education minister, whereas B concerns an organisation designated under a different regime by ministers acting jointly. Provision B requires disclosure only of information necessary for demonstrating compliance, while Provision A itself allows disclosure where the law requires it or where the recipient is authorised under the referenced provisions.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A healthcare provider that offers a high-risk AI diagnostic system holds patient health records used to demonstrate compliance with the AI Act. A competent authority makes a reasoned request for those records under Article 21, but the texts shown do not establish whether that authority is legally authorised to receive and process the health data under the applicable health-data rules.
verdict.missing_reference: The specific legal provision governing whether the requesting competent authority is authorised or legally required to receive and process the health data, including the referenced first, second, or third paragraphs and any applicable disclosure exception.

verdict.shared_subject: Communicating information about cyber or personal-data incidents to affected service recipients/data subjects
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires an essential or important entity to promptly tell potentially affected service recipients what measures they can take in response to a significant cyber threat, and, if necessary, to inform them of the threat itself. Provision B states that communication to a data subject is not required in specified circumstances, which could appear to permit withholding information where the same recipient is also a data subject.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different communications and triggers: A concerns significant cyber threats affecting recipients of an entity’s services, while B concerns notification of a personal-data breach to data subjects and expressly preserves alternative public or equivalent communication where disproportionate effort applies. A can therefore be complied with by giving threat-response information without necessarily making the GDPR breach notification described in B, and B does not prohibit A’s communication.

Provision A regulates conditioning access to a public-law body's information-society service on user consent; provision B regulates confidentiality duties of notified conformity-assessment bodies and their personnel.

verdict.shared_subject: Communicating personal-data breaches to the data subject
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A states categorically that the notification to the data subject includes specified information, which could suggest that such notification is always required. Provision B, however, expressly dispenses with that notification when one of its listed conditions is met, such as effective encryption or disproportionate effort.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A can be read as prescribing the contents of a notification when one is required, while provision B identifies circumstances in which no notification to the data subject is required. Thus, A's content requirements and B's exceptions can operate together without contradiction.
verdict.decisive_exception: The exceptions in Article 34(3), especially the conditions concerning effective protective measures, elimination of high risk, or disproportionate effort, determine when the data-subject notification is not required; the text supports treating Article 11.3a as applying when notification is made.

verdict.shared_subject: Information about incidents involving electronic services and personal-data breach notifications
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires covered bodies and organisations to provide the Minister with data and information needed to prevent or end breaches of secure and reliable access to electronic services. Provision B removes the provider’s obligation to notify the affected person where appropriate technical measures make the personal data unintelligible to unauthorised persons; if the information sought under A includes such protected personal data, disclosure could appear to undermine B’s protective purpose.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different recipients and serve different functions: A concerns supplying information to the Minister for security measures, while B concerns notifying the affected data subject about a personal-data breach. A does not expressly require disclosure of intelligible personal data, and B does not prohibit supplying information to the Minister. The encryption exception in B may also mean that no notification duty arises, rather than that all disclosure is forbidden.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires security measures including policies and procedures concerning cryptography and, where appropriate, encryption, as part of protecting systems and their physical environment against incidents. Provision B provides that notification of a personal-data breach is not required when the provider has taken appropriate technical protective measures making the data encrypted or otherwise unintelligible to unauthorised persons; a broad reading could make A’s security measures relevant to avoiding B’s notification duty, while B’s exception may reduce the practical need to notify after an incident.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different rules: A is a preventive cybersecurity duty requiring specified measures, while B is an exception to a notification obligation triggered by a personal-data breach likely to adversely affect privacy. Encryption adopted under A can satisfy B’s condition, and nothing in B forbids encryption or prevents compliance with A.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: The provisions concern the same regulated entities and both impose obligations under the same Act. However, Article 24 concerns the application of governance rules to managing partners of a limited partnership, while Article 44 concerns prompt reporting of changes to register information; nothing in either text makes compliance with one prevent compliance with the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: A managing partner covered by Article 24 can comply with the applicable governance rules and also ensure that the entity reports any change in Article 44 information immediately or within two weeks. verdict.shared_subject: Acceptance and use of identification means for electronic services requiring substantial or high assurance authentication
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 6 requires access to be granted only when the identification means has at least the assurance level required for the service. Article 7 requires public authorities to accept, among other things, all EU-notified and approved schemes, without expressly stating in the excerpt that every such identification means meets the service’s required assurance level; therefore, a qualifying EU-notified means might have to be accepted even if it falls below the required level.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can operate cumulatively: Article 7 identifies the categories of means that must be accepted, while Article 6 requires that access be granted only where the means meets the required assurance level. The reference in Article 7 to EU-notified and approved schemes may in practice concern means satisfying the relevant assurance requirements, and Article 7(4) also shows that exceptions concern acceptance rules rather than an express relaxation of Article 6.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A bestuursorgaan offers an electronic service requiring a high assurance level. A natural person presents an identification means belonging to an EU-notified and approved eIDAS scheme, but the means has only a substantial assurance level. Article 7 appears to require acceptance, while Article 6 permits access only with a high-level means; deciding whether this is a real conflict requires knowing whether the relevant EU-notified means is legally required to meet the service’s required level and how the acceptance rule is qualified.
verdict.missing_reference: The omitted legal provisions governing the assurance level and legal effect of identification means belonging to an EU-notified and approved eIDAS scheme—particularly whether Article 7(1)(c) is limited to means meeting the assurance level required for the service, and any applicable eIDAS or implementing provisions.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can concern communications to natural persons, so an AI provider experiencing a personal-data breach might face both a duty to inform people that they are interacting with AI and a GDPR rule dispensing with breach notification. The strongest tension case is that the GDPR exception could permit omitting a communication while the AI Act requires disclosure, but the provisions concern different communications and triggers.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 34 concerns notifying data subjects about a high-risk personal-data breach, whereas Article 50 concerns informing persons that they are interacting with an AI system. An actor can comply with both by omitting breach notification when Article 34 permits it while still providing the separate AI-interaction disclosure required by Article 50, subject to its own exception.

verdict.shared_subject: Entities or service providers potentially subject to both an exemption from reporting obligations and recognition requirements
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits the competent minister to exempt certain essential or important entities from obligations in Articles 25–30, while Provision B requires ministerial recognition of an ontsluitende dienst or machtigingsdienst that satisfies prescribed rules. If an entity performs one of the services in B and its relevant activities fall within A, the exemption could appear to remove obligations while B still requires recognition. However, the texts do not establish that the obligations in Articles 25–30 include the recognition requirement in Article 11, or that the same actor and activity are covered.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different matters: A concerns a possible exemption from specified reporting obligations, whereas B concerns recognition of particular services upon compliance with implementing rules. An entity can receive an exemption from Articles 25–30 and still obtain recognition under Article 11; nothing in either text says that the exemption waives or conflicts with recognition.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern establishing a division of tasks, but they assign that task to different institutional mechanisms: Provision A says the members establish it, while Provision B says the committee establishes it in its rules of procedure. If the same body is subject to both, this could create an institutional question about who must validly determine the allocation.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can readily be satisfied together because they address different task allocations and potentially different bodies or relationships. Provision A concerns members involving extraordinary members in the allocation, whereas Provision B specifically concerns allocation between the chair and vice-chairs in the committee's rules of procedure; the texts do not expressly make these mechanisms mutually exclusive.

verdict.shared_subject: Handling ICT or personal-data incidents by an actor that may be both a provider under BWBR0009950 and a financial entity under Regulation (EU) 2022/2554.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A removes the obligation to notify affected data subjects when the competent authority considers the data appropriately protected and unintelligible to unauthorised persons. Provision B requires financial entities to register all ICT-related incidents and to document and follow up their underlying causes; if the incident is a personal-data breach, retaining and documenting incident details could appear to work against the confidentiality rationale underlying A, especially where those details include encrypted personal data.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties: A concerns whether notification to affected persons is required, while B concerns internal registration, monitoring, treatment, follow-up, and documentation of ICT incidents. A does not prohibit internal incident registration or documentation, and B does not require notification to data subjects, so both can be complied with simultaneously.

verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different matters: Article 15 concerns exceptions to the exclusive-acceptance duty for specified central-counter services, while Article 24 concerns the scope of transitional recognition within a private system. Nothing in the shown text requires or forbids the same conduct under both provisions, and Article 24 does not alter Article 15’s exception.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of personal data in archives of lasting public-interest value
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A excludes Articles 15, 16, 18(1)(a), and 20 GDPR from applying to certain permanently preserved archival records. Provision B nevertheless states general principles for processing personal data, including purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, and security; this could appear to create tension if the archival exemption were read as removing the need to comply with those principles.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different GDPR requirements. Provision A expressly disapplies only the listed rights and does not disapply Article 5, while Article 5(e) itself permits longer storage for archiving in the public interest under Article 89(1), subject to appropriate safeguards. Thus, qualifying archives can benefit from the exemption while still complying with Article 5’s principles.

verdict.shared_subject: Protection of personal data and ICT security by a financial entity that is also an operator subject to the Dutch notification rule.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A removes the obligation to notify affected persons when the data are rendered unintelligible through appropriate technical safeguards. Provision B requires financial entities to maintain high standards of data confidentiality and integrity, including during use and transmission; a security policy could therefore treat encryption as sufficient protection while A still leaves notification dependent on the Authority’s judgment.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties: A concerns whether a personal-data breach notification is required, while B requires financial entities to design and implement ICT-security measures. Strong encryption can satisfy B’s confidentiality objective and, where the Authority considers it appropriate, also trigger A’s notification exception; nothing in B requires notification or forbids A’s exception.

verdict.shared_subject: Coordination of vulnerability or incident-related communications involving ICT/AI products and relevant authorities or entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern communications following a problem with a digital product, and coordination under provision A could involve negotiating disclosure timelines while provision B requires the market-surveillance authority to act within seven days after receiving a serious-incident notification. If the same event is both a reported vulnerability and a serious incident involving a high-risk AI system, coordination could potentially create pressure to follow a negotiated disclosure timetable that does not align with the authority’s seven-day action deadline.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different tasks on different actors and are triggered by different communications: provision A assigns a vulnerability coordinator intermediary and coordination duties, while provision B requires a market-surveillance authority to take measures within seven days after receiving a notification from a provider of a high-risk AI system. The coordinator can negotiate disclosure schedules while the authority independently complies with its seven-day deadline, so both duties can be performed simultaneously.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulatory competence and supervision
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern public-law oversight or intervention, so one might initially suspect overlapping authority over an organisation’s conduct. However, Provision A assigns supervisory personnel to monitor compliance with the GDPR and applicable personal-data-processing law, while Provision B empowers the Minister to issue a direction when an organ’s conduct conflicts with a designated standard; neither text says that these powers are exclusive or incompatible.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can plainly operate together: the Dutch Data Protection Authority and its designated personnel supervise GDPR and personal-data compliance, while the Minister may direct an organ regarding a separately applicable designated standard. Exercising one competence does not prevent exercising the other, and the provisions impose no conflicting duty, permission, deadline, or benchmark on the same actor.

verdict.shared_subject: Handling legal requests by public authorities in data-protection matters

Provision B says a supervisory authority receiving a request for assistance may refuse it only for lack of competence or because the request violates applicable law; if the stay were treated as a refusal or non-cooperation, the provisions could appear to impose incompatible responses.

A stay is not stated to be a refusal of assistance, and nothing in B requires the Raad van State to act as the receiving supervisory authority or prevents a lawful procedural stay.

verdict.shared_subject: Cooperation and information exchange involving competent or notifying authorities and notified bodies
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires competent authorities to exchange all necessary data, including personal data, while Provision B requires each notifying authority to ensure that its notified bodies participate in a Commission-established coordination group. If participation requires sharing information that includes personal data, A's broad exchange duty could appear to press toward disclosure while B does not itself establish the legal basis or limits for that disclosure.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different institutional relationships: A governs cooperation and necessary data exchange between competent authorities, whereas B governs a notifying authority's ensuring participation by its notified bodies in a coordination group. A notifying authority can ensure participation without exchanging personal data, and nothing in B forbids the cooperation or data exchange required by A.

verdict.shared_subject: Supervision and recognition of authentication services under BWBR0048156
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern the same statutory scheme and authentication services, so one might initially suspect that the recognition decision under article 11 must be supervised by the officials designated under article 17. However, article 17 expressly identifies the provisions whose compliance is supervised and does not include article 11.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 11 imposes a substantive recognition condition on the Minister: recognition is granted only if the service meets the applicable reliability-level rules. Article 17 separately allocates supervisory competence for compliance with articles 3, 6, 7, 8(1), and 15; it neither prohibits recognition nor imposes a conflicting duty concerning article 11, so both provisions can operate together.

verdict.shared_subject: Use of a high-risk AI system for decisions significantly affecting individuals
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 22 prohibits subjecting an individual to a solely automated decision with legal or similarly significant effects, while Article 27 requires certain deployers to assess the fundamental-rights impacts of using a high-risk AI system. One might argue that the assessment obligation presupposes or facilitates deployment of such a system, including for decisions that Article 22 prohibits.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 27 requires an impact assessment before specified high-risk AI systems are put into use; it does not authorise automated decisions or require that any decision be made solely by automated processing. The assessment can be performed and the system can be used only for legally permissible purposes, including with meaningful human involvement or an applicable Article 22 exception.

verdict.shared_subject: A competent authority administering measures against an entity after an infringement
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A restricts when the competent authority may determine an end date, requiring prior measures and their failure (or a reasoned judgment that remaining measures will not work). Provision B requires competent authorities to publish final administrative-sanction decisions without delay once the affected person has been notified, which could appear to require publication even while the staged process in A has not been completed.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different acts: A concerns the authority’s power to set an end date for ending an infringement, while B concerns publication of non-appealable administrative-sanction decisions. A does not prohibit publication, and B does not require the authority to determine an end date or to bypass A’s conditions.

verdict.shared_subject: Delegated rulemaking by algemene maatregel van bestuur concerning specified procedures or information
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions authorize further rules by algemene maatregel van bestuur, and their subject matters could potentially overlap if the procedures or information under Article 11.11 are also part of the warnings, notifications, or reports covered by Article 35. In that event, separately issued implementing rules might appear to regulate related information or procedures under different statutory bases.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions confer rulemaking competence over different enumerated subject matters: Article 35 concerns implementation of specified articles, including the required contents and method of warnings and reports, while Article 11.11 concerns an investigation, information provision, cooperation obligation, and notification expressly referred to in its own paragraphs. Both can operate concurrently, and neither requires or forbids conduct by the regulated actor.

verdict.shared_subject: Cybersecurity incident policy and coordination
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A assigns a cooperation group a broad strategic and coordination role concerning cyber threats and incidents, including discussing follow-up policy after large-scale incidents. Provision B requires financial entities to establish and operate a concrete ICT-incident management process, including detection, escalation, communication, and timely recovery. One might argue that strategic coordination under A could generate policy or reporting expectations that compete with the operational process required by B, particularly during a large-scale incident.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A governs the tasks of an EU cooperation group and its reporting to EU institutions; it does not impose an operational incident-management rule on financial entities. Provision B governs the internal incident-management process of financial entities, and nothing in A forbids or limits those procedures; the two provisions operate at different institutional and functional levels and can be fully complied with simultaneously.

verdict.shared_subject: Analysis and handling of cybersecurity threats, incidents, and reports
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the Minister or another authority to conduct analyses and technical research concerning threats and incidents, but expressly excludes research into the persons or organisations responsible for them or contributing to them. Provision B permits information about voluntary reports to be provided to competent authorities, potentially including information useful for investigating the reporting entity, although it protects confidentiality and limits additional obligations.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different actors and address different functions: A governs assistance and technical analysis for certain organisations, while B governs Member States’ processing and disclosure of voluntary reports. B does not require investigation of reporting entities, and A’s exclusion concerns the object of the authority’s research rather than the receipt or confidential handling of report information.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing special categories of personal data in connection with information stored on or accessed through an end device
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A extends requirements concerning storing information on, or accessing information stored on, an end device to cases where that result is achieved by means other than an electronic communications network. Provision B permits such providers to process special categories of personal data only under narrowly defined conditions, including deletion after the bias is corrected or the retention period ends; if the end-device information is special-category data, A's extended requirements could apply while B restricts the associated processing.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different conduct and actors: A extends the applicability of requirements concerning end-device storage or access, while B governs exceptional processing of special-category personal data by providers of high-risk AI systems. Nothing in A requires processing special-category data, and B expressly permits it when all listed safeguards and conditions are met, so both can be complied with.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision B requires the provider and relevant third party to specify the information, capabilities, technical access and assistance needed for the provider to comply fully with the AI Act. Provision A prohibits the relevant personal-data transfer unless the GDPR Chapter V conditions have been met, so supplying the required assistance could involve a transfer that cannot lawfully occur under A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The contractual-assistance duty in B can be performed without transferring personal data, or by structuring any transfer so that the Chapter V conditions in A are satisfied. B does not itself require an unlawful third-country transfer and expressly operates alongside other applicable legal requirements.

verdict.shared_subject: Verstrekking en verwerking van locatie- en persoonsgegevens in noodcommunicatie en hoog-risico-AI-systemen
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a public electronic communications provider to transmit relevant location data simultaneously during an emergency call, even where the user has blocked processing of those location data. Provision B restricts processing of special categories of personal data to a narrowly necessary bias-detection purpose and imposes conditions including non-disclosure to other parties; if the emergency location data were such special-category data and the AI provider were subject to both rules, the required transmission could appear inconsistent with B.

verdict.shared_subject: Electronic access and information storage/access involving electronic communications networks
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A concerns an exception to the duty to accept only specified identification means and declarations for certain non-Dutch-established service providers using the central portal. Provision B extends unspecified requirements in its first paragraph to situations where storage or access is achieved by means other than an electronic communications network; if those requirements include the identification-acceptance duty, the exception in A could appear not to apply in such a technically different situation.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different matters: A expressly concerns acceptance of identification means for access to electronic public services, with exceptions for specified central-portal services, while B merely extends requirements from another provision to a particular technological circumstance. Nothing in the text of B says that the exception in A is withdrawn or that incompatible identification means must be accepted or rejected.

verdict.shared_subject: Organisational obligations concerning personal-data processing and ICT/cyber-threat capabilities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A exempts certain organisations with fewer than 250 employees from the referenced records-of-processing obligations, while Provision B requires financial entities to maintain capabilities and personnel to collect information about vulnerabilities, cyber threats and ICT incidents. If that information includes personal data, the financial entity might view A as removing the record-keeping obligation while B requires the underlying collection and analysis activity.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different or potentially overlapping subjects: A concerns an exemption from records-of-processing obligations, whereas B requires financial entities to have capabilities and personnel for collecting and analysing cyber-risk information. B does not require a particular GDPR record, and A does not prohibit the collection or analysis required by B; both can therefore be complied with simultaneously.

verdict.shared_subject: Administrative enforcement of overlapping data-protection and digital-resilience obligations
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits the competent authority from imposing a second administrative fine under Articles 80 and 87 for the same conduct after a GDPR fine has been imposed. Provision B requires competent authorities to have power to require corrective measures for infringements of that Regulation, which could appear to support additional enforcement for overlapping conduct.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B concerns the power to require corrective measures, not necessarily the imposition of a second administrative fine. Provision A expressly bars only a further fine for the same conduct, so an authority can comply with both by imposing no duplicate fine while still using non-fine corrective measures where appropriate.

verdict.shared_subject: Cybersecurity and personal-data breach record-keeping by entities covered by both regimes
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a public electronic communications service provider to maintain an overview of all personal-data breaches, including specified facts and data. Provision B says that relevant NIS2 provisions are not applicable to an essential or important entity where equivalent sector-specific EU requirements apply, so a provider covered by such a sector-specific regime might argue that the NIS2 record-related requirements do not apply.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B does not prohibit keeping a breach overview; it only disapplies relevant NIS2 provisions where equivalent sector-specific EU requirements exist, while preserving NIS2 application to entities not covered by those sector-specific acts. Provision A is a separate record-keeping duty and can be complied with alongside B unless a specific NIS2 provision is shown to conflict with it.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern data-protection governance, but they regulate different subjects and conduct. Provision A concerns when a prohibition on processing special-category and criminal-offence data by a commission or advisory body does not apply; provision B concerns the independence and reporting line of a data protection officer.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can readily be complied with simultaneously: a commission or advisory body may process the specified data only under the conditions in A, while any data protection officer involved must remain free from instructions, dismissal, or punishment concerning the performance of their tasks under B. Neither provision requires conduct prohibited by the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulatory requests for information or audit results from regulated ICT/electronic-communications providers
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can require a regulated provider to supply information to a supervisory authority, and the requested material could overlap, such as ICT-security audit reports. If the Dutch Minister and the lead overseer set incompatible deadlines or materially different requirements for the same report, the provider could face practical compliance pressure.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A concerns a Minister imposing an independent security-control obligation on providers of public electronic communications networks or services, while provision B concerns the lead overseer requesting information from critical third-party ICT-service providers. Neither provision forbids compliance with the other, and both can be satisfied by supplying the requested information within each authority’s applicable deadline; the texts do not establish overlapping addressees, identical requests, or incompatible deadlines.

verdict.shared_subject: ICT- en telecommunicatieregels voor entiteiten die zowel een netwerkidentificatiefaciliteit gebruiken als onder het vereenvoudigde ICT-risicokader vallen
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits using a network-identification facility to provide the called user with incorrect information about the network endpoint or individual user. Provision B requires covered entities to maintain ICT-risk controls and protect data availability, authenticity, integrity and confidentiality. One might argue that implementing B could require transmitting or presenting endpoint or user-identification information in a way that conflicts with A, but B does not require false information or any particular disclosure method.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative duties: A prohibits misleading information about network endpoints or users, while B requires specified entities to establish and maintain ICT-risk-management and security measures. Accurate endpoint and user information, and secure handling of it, can satisfy both provisions; nothing in B authorizes or requires misleading information.

verdict.shared_subject: An erkende ontsluitende dienst handling electronic means, authorisations, or attributes in connection with a high-risk AI system.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the recognised unlocking service to disclose all recognised business and organisational means, authorisation statements, and designated attributes. If those materials contain special categories of personal data and the service is an AI provider or otherwise processes them for bias detection or correction, Provision B restricts such processing and prohibits transmission, transfer, or access by other parties unless all listed safeguards and conditions are met. The texts therefore create a possible permission/obligation clash where A's required disclosure would involve B-regulated data and B's conditions are not satisfied.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different conduct: A concerns making recognised means, authorisation statements, and attributes available, while B concerns exceptional processing of special categories of personal data by providers of high-risk AI systems for detecting or correcting bias. A can be complied with by disclosing only the relevant means or attributes in a manner that does not constitute the prohibited processing or does not involve special-category data; moreover, B expressly permits such processing when its conditions and safeguards are met.

verdict.shared_subject: Personal-data breach notification and the GDPR record-of-processing exemption
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: The provisions both concern organisations handling personal data, and a small organisation may fall within the GDPR provision’s exemption from maintaining a processing register while still being an electronic-communications provider subject to the immediate breach-notification duty. One might therefore argue that the GDPR exemption reduces compliance obligations for the same organisation, potentially creating an apparent inconsistency in the data-protection regime.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties: A requires notifying the affected person promptly after a qualifying breach, while B concerns whether certain small organisations must maintain a register of processing activities. An organisation can omit the register yet still notify affected persons, so compliance with one does not prevent compliance with the other.

verdict.shared_subject: ICT incident management by entities that may be both NIS2-covered entities and financial entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can concern an entity responding to a serious ICT incident: A requires rapid external reporting, while B requires a post-incident evaluation examining response speed, analysis, escalation, and communications. The reporting workload and the retrospective evaluation could consume resources or reveal information, potentially working against rapid operational recovery, but neither text makes those duties incompatible.
