verdict.shared_subject: De Autoriteit persoonsgegevens en haar samenwerking/organisatie
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires competent authorities to cooperate with the Autoriteit persoonsgegevens and exchange all necessary data, including personal data, when handling incidents leading to personal-data breaches. Provision B requires the Minister to dismiss the chair, other members, and extraordinary members of that Authority upon their own request; one might argue that dismissal could affect the Authority’s ability to perform the cooperation duty, but the text does not make dismissal conditional on completing that duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different matters: A governs cooperation and information exchange during incidents, while B governs the Minister’s personnel decision concerning members of the Authority. A member’s dismissal on request does not prohibit the Authority or competent authorities from cooperating, and both rules can be complied with simultaneously.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De bevoegde autoriteiten werken samen met de Autoriteit persoonsgegevens bij de behandeling van incidenten die leiden tot inbreuken in verband met persoonsgegevens en wisselen in het kader van die samenwerking alle daarvoor noodzakelijke gegevens uit, waaronder persoonsgegevens.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Op eigen verzoek worden de voorzitter, de andere leden en de buitengewone leden van de Autoriteit persoonsgegevens door Onze Minister ontslagen.

verdict.shared_subject: ICT and personal-data risk management by a financial entity that is also a GDPR controller
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A financial entity may identify and assess a cyber threat or ICT vulnerability under Provision B while Provision A says that notifying affected data subjects of a personal-data breach is not required when one of its conditions is met. If the entity’s risk assessment reveals a breach involving personal data, B could be read as requiring continuing risk identification and assessment even though A removes the notification duty, creating at most a possible difference between risk-management duties and breach-notification duties.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties: A governs whether a controller must communicate a personal-data breach to data subjects, subject to specified conditions, while B requires financial entities to identify ICT-risk sources and assess threats, vulnerabilities, and risk scenarios. An entity can comply with both by conducting the required assessments and, where an Article 34 condition applies, not making the data-subject communication.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De in lid 1 bedoelde mededeling aan de betrokkene is niet vereist wanneer een van de volgende voorwaarden is vervuld:
verdict.evidence_span_b: Financiële entiteiten identificeren permanent alle bronnen van ICT-risico, met name de wederzijdse risicoblootstelling ten aanzien van andere financiële entiteiten, en beoordelen de cyberdreigingen en ICT-kwetsbaarheden die relevant zijn voor hun door ICT ondersteunde bedrijfsfuncties en informatie- en ICT-activa.

verdict.shared_subject: Communicating personal-data breaches to data subjects
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A states that the notification to the person concerned must include specified information, apparently imposing a notification duty. Provision B states that the communication referred to in Article 34(1) is not required when one of its conditions is met, so applying both without identifying their relationship could make A require a communication that B dispenses with.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A can be read as prescribing the contents of a notification when notification to the person concerned is required, while Provision B defines circumstances in which that communication is not required or may be replaced by an equally effective public measure. Thus, the provisions can operate together if A applies only where the communication obligation remains applicable.
verdict.missing_reference: The relationship between BWBR0009950 art. 11.3a and the GDPR Article 34 obligation and exceptions—particularly whether art. 11.3a is subject to Article 34(3) and whether it independently requires notification even when a GDPR exception applies—is not established by the texts shown.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De kennisgeving aan de Autoriteit persoonsgegevens en de persoon wiens persoonsgegevens het betreft, omvat in ieder geval de aard van de inbreuk in verband met persoonsgegevens, de instanties waar meer informatie over de inbreuk kan worden verkregen en de aanbevolen maatregelen om de negatieve gevolgen van de inbreuk te beperken.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De in lid 1 bedoelde mededeling aan de betrokkene is niet vereist wanneer een van de volgende voorwaarden is vervuld:

verdict.shared_subject: Information and cybersecurity requirements for organisations involved in electronic services or conformity-assessment tasks
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose security-related obligations on an organisation that could fall within both categories. However, Article 4 delegates the applicable rules to an implementing general administrative measure, while Article 31 separately requires notified bodies to meet appropriate cybersecurity requirements; the texts do not state that compliance with one benchmark satisfies or conflicts with the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: An organisation can comply with both obligations by meeting the implementing rules under Article 4 and the appropriate cybersecurity requirements under Article 31. The provisions address different aspects and potentially different organisational roles, and neither prescribes a deadline, content, or prohibition incompatible with the other.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Bestuursorganen en aangewezen organisaties voldoen aan bij of krachtens algemene maatregel van bestuur te stellen regels met betrekking tot de werking, betrouwbaarheid en beveiliging van de toegang tot elektronische diensten op verschillende betrouwbaarheidsniveaus.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Aangemelde instanties voldoen aan de eisen inzake organisatie, kwaliteitsbeheer, personeel en processen die nodig zijn voor het vervullen van hun taken, alsook aan de passende cyberbeveiligingseisen.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing activities involving special categories of personal data by a high-risk AI provider that submits its processing to certification.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision B requires deletion of the special-category data once the bias has been corrected or the retention period ends. If the certification body needs access to those same data or related processing information after that point, Provision A could require the provider to provide necessary information and access, while B prevents the data from being retained or accessed by other parties. This is only a potential tension because A does not expressly require retention of the deleted data, and B permits processing subject to its conditions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A concerns information and access necessary for a certification procedure, whereas Provision B regulates exceptional processing of special-category personal data and expressly requires safeguards, access controls, and deletion when the purpose or retention period ends. A provider can comply with both by giving the certification body the necessary information and access during the permitted period, without retaining or disclosing the special-category data contrary to B.
verdict.evidence_span_a: verstrekt aan het in artikel 43 bedoelde certificeringsorgaan, of, waar van toepassing, aan de bevoegde toezichthoudende autoriteit de voor de uitvoering van de certificeringsprocedure noodzakelijke informatie en verleent het orgaan of de autoriteit toegang tot zijn verwerkingsactiviteiten.
verdict.evidence_span_b: de bijzondere categorieën persoonsgegevens worden verwijderd zodra de vertekening is gecorrigeerd of de periode van bewaring van de persoonsgegevens ten einde is gekomen, indien dit eerder is;

verdict.shared_subject: Organisations or entities that process personal data and may experience significant incidents
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A exempts many organisations with fewer than 250 employees from the obligation to maintain a register of processing activities, while Provision B requires covered entities to report significant incidents within specified deadlines. A small organisation might therefore be exempt from the GDPR register duty yet still have to report a significant incident under NIS2, creating different compliance burdens concerning incident-related information.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties: A concerns maintaining a register of processing activities, whereas B concerns reporting significant incidents to a CSIRT or competent authority. Nothing in either text requires an organisation to omit information, destroy records, or violate the other provision; the duties can be performed simultaneously where both apply.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De in de leden 1 en 2 bedoelde verplichtingen zijn niet van toepassing op ondernemingen of organisaties die minder dan 250 personen in dienst hebben, tenzij het waarschijnlijk is dat de verwerking die zij verrichten een risico inhoudt voor de rechten en vrijheden van de betrokkenen, de verwerking niet incidenteel is, of de verwerking bijzondere categorieën van gegevens, als bedoeld in artikel 9, lid 1, of persoonsgegevens in verband met strafrechtelijke veroordelingen en strafbare feiten als bedoeld in artikel 10 betreft.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De lidstaten zorgen ervoor dat de betrokken entiteiten, voor de in lid 1 bedoelde melding, bij het CSIRT of, indien van toepassing, de bevoegde autoriteit:

verdict.shared_subject: Early warning/reporting of significant cybersecurity incidents by essential or important entities, where an EU sector-specific act may also regulate the entity.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the entity to give an early warning to its CSIRT and competent authority, immediately or within 24 hours. Provision B says that, where a sector-specific EU act imposes equivalent cybersecurity-risk or significant-incident-reporting requirements, the relevant provisions of this directive, including supervision and enforcement, do not apply; thus A could appear inapplicable to an entity covered by such an act.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B does not prohibit the early warning required by A; it allocates which regime applies when an equivalent sector-specific act exists. If no such act covers the entity, B expressly leaves the directive provisions applicable, and if the sector-specific act does apply, the entity can comply with that act instead of A.
verdict.missing_reference: The specific sector-specific EU legal act applicable to the entity, including whether it imposes requirements at least equivalent to A's early-warning obligation and whether it covers that entity.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Dit doet zij onverwijld of, indien dat niet mogelijk is, binnen 24 uur nadat zij kennis heeft gekregen van het significante incident.
verdict.evidence_span_b: zijn de relevante bepalingen van deze richtlijn, met inbegrip van de in hoofdstuk VII bedoelde toezichts- en handhavingsbepalingen, niet van toepassing op dergelijke entiteiten.

verdict.shared_subject: Handling and confidentiality of information or documentation obtained by public authorities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 55 prohibits providing information covered by professional secrecy to any other person or authority unless Union or national law provides otherwise. Article 77 contemplates national public authorities obtaining and inspecting documentation, so an authority might seek information that is protected by Article 55, creating a possible disclosure/access issue.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 77 does not itself require disclosure of information covered by professional secrecy; it requires information obtained under that article to be processed according to Article 78 confidentiality obligations. Article 55 expressly permits disclosure where Union or national law provides for it, and Article 77 is a Union-law provision that may supply such a legal basis, subject to the applicable confidentiality rules.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Onder het beroepsgeheim vallende informatie, waaronder de uitwisseling van informatie tussen de bevoegde autoriteiten uit hoofde van deze verordening en de overeenkomstig Richtlijn (EU) 2022/2555 aangewezen of ingestelde bevoegde autoriteiten, wordt aan geen enkele andere persoon of autoriteit verstrekt, tenzij op grond van Unierechtelijke of nationaalrechtelijke bepalingen;
verdict.evidence_span_b: Informatie of documentatie die op grond van dit artikel door de in lid 1 van dit artikel bedoelde overheidsinstanties of -organen wordt verkregen, wordt verwerkt overeenkomstig de in artikel 78 beschreven vertrouwelijkheidsverplichtingen.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing personal data in archives of permanent value for archiving in the public interest
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A removes Articles 15, 16, 18(1)(a), and 20 from application for specified permanently preserved archival materials, while Provision B requires personal-data processing to comply with principles including purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, and security. This could appear to create tension if the exemption from selected data-subject rights were understood to permit archival processing that would otherwise be constrained by those principles, especially indefinite retention.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A exempts only the listed GDPR provisions, not Article 5. Provision B expressly permits longer storage for archiving in the public interest when Article 89(1) safeguards are met, so permanent preservation can comply with the storage-limitation principle; the remaining Article 5 duties can also be observed alongside the exemption.
verdict.decisive_exception: None needed: Article 45 does not disapply Article 5, and Article 5(e) expressly accommodates longer storage for archiving in the public interest subject to Article 89(1).
verdict.evidence_span_a: De artikelen 15, 16, 18, eerste lid, onderdeel a, en 20 van de verordening zijn niet van toepassing
verdict.evidence_span_b: persoonsgegevens mogen voor langere perioden worden opgeslagen voor zover de persoonsgegevens louter met het oog op archivering in het algemeen belang, wetenschappelijk of historisch onderzoek of statistische doeleinden worden verwerkt overeenkomstig artikel 89, lid 1

verdict.shared_subject: Processing special categories of personal data by a non-EU-established provider of a high-risk AI system
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A exempts certain controllers or processors from the obligation to appoint an EU representative, including where the processing is not large-scale processing of special categories of personal data. Provision B expressly permits exceptional processing of special categories of personal data by providers of certain high-risk AI systems, so one might argue that the AI Act provision makes the GDPR representative obligation relevant while the GDPR exception removes it.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties: A concerns appointment of an EU representative, and B concerns conditions for processing special categories of personal data. B does not require or prohibit appointment of a representative, and A does not prohibit the processing authorised under B; the GDPR representative exception applies only if its factual conditions are met.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De verplichting vervat in lid 1 van dit artikel geldt niet voor:
verdict.evidence_span_b: mogen de aanbieders van dergelijke systemen uitzonderlijk bijzondere categorieën persoonsgegevens verwerken, mits passende waarborgen worden geboden voor de grondrechten en fundamentele vrijheden van natuurlijke personen.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires domain-name registries and registration-service entities to answer a lawful, properly motivated access request within 72 hours. Provision B requires notified bodies and their personnel to keep information obtained during conformity-assessment activities confidential, so disclosure to a requester could appear problematic if the requested domain-registration data were held in that capacity.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different actors and duties: A concerns domain-name registries or registration-service entities responding to legitimate access requests, while B concerns notified bodies and confidentiality of conformity-assessment information. Nothing in the texts establishes that a notified body is the entity receiving an Article 50 request or that the requested data were obtained during conformity assessment; moreover, B expressly permits disclosure when legally required.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De registers voor topleveldomeinnamen en de entiteiten die domeinnaamregistratiediensten verlenen beantwoorden een verzoek om toegang als bedoeld in het eerste lid onverwijld of, indien dat niet mogelijk is, binnen 72 uur na ontvangst van het verzoek.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Aangemelde instanties beschikken over gedocumenteerde procedures die waarborgen dat hun personeel, comités, dochterondernemingen, onderaannemers, geassocieerde instanties of personeel van externe instanties overeenkomstig artikel 78 de informatie die zij tijdens conformiteitsbeoordelingsactiviteiten in hun bezit krijgen vertrouwelijk houden, behalve wanneer de openbaarmaking ervan wettelijk vereist is.

verdict.shared_subject: A controller/user of a high-risk AI system processing personal data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions may apply to the same organisation using a high-risk AI system that processes personal data. Article 24 requires appropriate measures to ensure and demonstrate GDPR compliance, while Article 27 requires a fundamental-rights impact assessment on first use and updating measures when relevant elements change; the additional assessment and updating burden could work against a streamlined compliance approach, but the texts do not impose incompatible duties.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties address different but complementary requirements: Article 24 concerns ongoing, risk-based technical and organisational measures for GDPR-compliant processing, whereas Article 27 concerns a specific fundamental-rights impact assessment for certain high-risk-AI uses and updating its information when circumstances change. An organisation can perform the Article 27 assessment and updates as part of, or alongside, its Article 24 measures; neither provision permits what the other forbids or sets an incompatible standard.
verdict.evidence_span_a: treft de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke passende technische en organisatorische maatregelen om te waarborgen en te kunnen aantonen dat de verwerking in overeenstemming met deze verordening wordt uitgevoerd
verdict.evidence_span_b: De verplichting als neergelegd in lid 1 is van toepassing op het eerste gebruik van een AI-systeem met een hoog risico

verdict.shared_subject: Delegated rulemaking by algemene maatregel van bestuur
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions authorize further rules by or under an algemene maatregel van bestuur, so one might initially suspect overlapping delegated powers concerning the CSIRT or the subject matter of article 11a.3. If both delegations purported to regulate the same issue with inconsistent requirements, their interaction could require clarification.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A concerns requirements for the organization designated as the CSIRT, while provision B merely permits further rules concerning the matters already laid down in article 11a.3. Neither provision imposes a substantive obligation or prohibition, and the texts do not establish overlapping subject matter or incompatible delegated instructions.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Bij of krachtens algemene maatregel van bestuur kunnen regels worden gesteld over de functionele, financiële, technische en organisatorische vereisten ten aanzien van de organisatie die bij of krachtens algemene maatregel van bestuur als CSIRT wordt aangewezen.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Bij of krachtens algemene maatregel van bestuur kunnen nadere regels worden gesteld ten aanzien van het bepaalde in dit artikel.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern digital-risk or AI governance, so a financial entity could conceivably also provide a general-purpose AI model. In that unusual overlap, the ICT-risk-management duties in A and the documentation, copyright-policy, and training-content-summary duties in B would add compliance work, but neither text requires conduct that the other forbids or sets incompatible standards.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: A applies to specified small or exempt financial entities and requires them to maintain an ICT-risk-management framework and related controls. B applies to providers of general-purpose AI models and imposes separate documentation and disclosure duties; an entity subject to both can perform all duties simultaneously, with no conflicting deadline, content requirement, or prohibition shown.
verdict.evidence_span_a: een degelijk en gedocumenteerd kader voor ICT-risicobeheer tot stand brengen en handhaven
verdict.evidence_span_b: de technische documentatie van het model opstellen en up-to-date houden

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern information connected with ICT or digital services, so an entity might superficially encounter both in the same operational setting. However, provision A governs the transfer of stored information by an accredited service after withdrawal or transfer of its recognition, while provision B governs how a financial entity exercises audit and inspection rights over an ICT-service provider.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different actors and address different triggers: A requires the recognised service to transfer necessary stored information to the Minister, whereas B requires financial entities to plan audits risk-based and ensure auditor competence where contracts are highly complex. Compliance with one does not prevent compliance with the other.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De erkende dienst waarvan de erkenning wordt ingetrokken of overgedragen draagt er zorg voor dat alle door hem opgeslagen informatie en gegevens die noodzakelijk was voor de uitvoering van de activiteiten waarvoor hij was erkend, worden overgedragen aan Onze Minister.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Bij het uitoefenen van toegangs-, inspectie- en auditrechten ten aanzien van de derde aanbieder van ICT-diensten bepalen financiële entiteiten op basis van een risicogebaseerde benadering vooraf de frequentie van de audits en inspecties alsook de te controleren gebieden

verdict.shared_subject: Compliance and oversight functions for regulated entities or providers
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern checking compliance and interacting with authorities, so an entity or person performing both roles could face overlapping requests or reporting responsibilities. However, Article 70 assigns an independent control officer to monitor and inform authorities about an essential entity’s NIS2 compliance, while Article 54 gives an authorised representative of a general-purpose AI-model provider a separate mandate to perform AI Act tasks; neither text requires incompatible conduct.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions apply to different legally defined roles, duties and regulatory regimes. The control officer monitors and informs about NIS2-related compliance, whereas the authorised representative checks AI Act documentation, retains it for ten years, supplies information on reasoned request and cooperates with authorities; all of these duties can be performed together.
verdict.evidence_span_a: het monitoren van de naleving van het bepaalde bij of krachtens de artikelen 21 en 25 tot en met 30
verdict.evidence_span_b: een kopie van de in bijlage XI gespecificeerde technische documentatie beschikbaar houden voor het AI-bureau en de nationale autoriteiten gedurende een periode van tien jaar

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern institutional arrangements in the digital-regulation sphere, and a CSIRT coordinator could conceivably interact with entities involved in conformity assessment. However, Article 12 regulates coordinated vulnerability reporting and Article 28 regulates the internal independence of notifying authorities’ decision-makers; neither text imposes an incompatible duty on the same actor.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different actors, functions, and triggers. Article 12 requires a Member State to designate a CSIRT and ensure anonymous vulnerability reporting and follow-up, while Article 28 requires notifying authorities to use competent decision-makers who did not assess conformity-assessment bodies; both obligations can be fully performed simultaneously.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Elke lidstaat wijst een van zijn CSIRT’s aan als coördinator met het oog op een gecoördineerde bekendmaking van kwetsbaarheden.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Aanmeldende autoriteiten worden zodanig georganiseerd dat besluiten in verband met de aanmelding van conformiteitsbeoordelingsinstanties worden genomen door bekwame personen die niet de beoordeling van die instanties hebben verricht.

verdict.shared_subject: Communicating information about cyber or personal-data incidents to affected service recipients/data subjects
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A says that communication to the data subject is not required when one of its listed conditions is met, including appropriate protective measures or disproportionate effort. Provision B requires essential and important entities, where applicable, to promptly tell service recipients who may be affected by a significant cyber threat what measures they can take, and sometimes to notify them of the threat itself. If the same communication concerns the same recipients and event, A could appear to permit withholding information that B requires.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different communications, triggers, and recipients: A concerns notification of a personal-data breach to data subjects, while B concerns advice to service recipients potentially affected by a significant cyber threat. A's exemption concerns the GDPR breach-notification duty and does not expressly exempt an entity from separately communicating protective measures or the cyber threat under B; both duties can therefore be performed where their respective conditions apply.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De in lid 1 bedoelde mededeling aan de betrokkene is niet vereist wanneer een van de volgende voorwaarden is vervuld:
verdict.evidence_span_b: Indien van toepassing zorgen de lidstaten ervoor dat essentiële en belangrijke entiteiten de ontvangers van hun diensten die mogelijkerwijs door een significante cyberdreiging worden getroffen, onverwijld meedelen welke maatregelen die ontvangers kunnen nemen in reactie op die dreiging.

verdict.shared_subject: Use and management of ICT or AI-model-related third-party services
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires financial entities to remain fully responsible for compliance with applicable financial-services law and to manage third-party ICT risk proportionately. Provision B exempts certain providers of general-purpose AI models from the obligation in that article when the model is released under a qualifying free and open-source licence, unless the model presents systemic risks. If a financial entity relies on such an exempt provider, A could be read as requiring management of the associated ICT risk while B removes the provider-facing obligation.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different actors and concern different obligations: A governs financial entities and their management of third-party ICT risk, whereas B exempts qualifying providers of general-purpose AI models from an obligation concerning authorised representatives. A does not require the provider to comply with B's obligation, and B does not prohibit a financial entity from managing the risk or remaining responsible for its own legal obligations.
verdict.decisive_exception: None is needed to reconcile the provisions: the apparent exemption in B concerns a provider-facing obligation, while A imposes an independent risk-management and responsibility duty on financial entities.
verdict.evidence_span_a: financiële entiteiten die contractuele overeenkomsten voor het gebruik van ICT-diensten voor hun bedrijfsactiviteiten hebben getroffen, blijven te allen tijde volledig verantwoordelijk voor de naleving en de verantwoording van alle verplichtingen uit hoofde van deze verordening en het toepasselijke recht inzake financiële diensten;
verdict.evidence_span_b: De in dit artikel genoemde verplichting geldt niet voor aanbieders van AI-modellen die worden vrijgegeven in het kader van een vrije en opensource licentie die de raadpleging, het gebruik, de wijziging en distributie van het model mogelijk maakt en waarvan de parameters, met inbegrip van de wegingen, de informatie over de modelarchitectuur en de informatie over het gebruik van het model, openbaar worden gemaakt, tenzij de AI-modellen voor algemene doeleinden systeemrisico’s vertonen.

verdict.shared_subject: Cross-border and cross-sector cooperation among competent authorities, including the role of the central contact point.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A assigns the Minister responsibility for ensuring cross-border cooperation through the central contact point. Provision B requires competent authorities to cooperate and provide mutual assistance, and requires certain communications to occur via that contact point. One might argue that A centralises the coordinating function in the Minister, while B imposes direct cooperation and assistance duties on the competent authorities.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be satisfied together: the Minister, as central contact point, can facilitate the cooperation required by Article 37, while the competent authorities carry out the substantive supervisory or enforcement cooperation and assistance. Provision A does not prohibit direct cooperation or limit the authorities' duties under Provision B.
verdict.evidence_span_a: het zorgen voor grensoverschrijdende samenwerking van de autoriteiten van Nederland met de relevante autoriteiten van andere lidstaten van de Europese Unie, de Europese Commissie en Enisa, door middel van het vervullen van een verbindingsfunctie
verdict.evidence_span_b: de bevoegde autoriteiten die in een lidstaat toezichts- of handhavingsmaatregelen toepassen, via het centrale contactpunt de bevoegde autoriteiten in de andere betrokken lidstaten informeren en raadplegen over de genomen toezichts- en handhavingsmaatregelen

verdict.shared_subject: The provision of data and information to the Minister versus the processing of retained traffic and location data by public communications providers
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires covered organisations and recognised issuers/providers to provide information to the Minister when requested or on their own initiative if needed to prevent or end interference with secure and reliable access to electronic services. Provision B prohibits providers from processing retained traffic and location data for other purposes unless processing is permitted under Articles 11.5 and 11.5a and complies with those articles; supplying such data to the Minister could therefore be a prohibited purpose if it falls outside those exceptions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A does not expressly require the disclosure of traffic or location data, nor does it override the purpose limitation in Provision B. The requested information may consist of other data, and any processing or disclosure of traffic and location data can comply with both provisions if it is permitted under Articles 11.5 and 11.5a.
verdict.missing_reference: Articles 11.5 and 11.5a of BWBR0009950, including whether disclosure or processing of the retained traffic and location data for the Minister’s stated security purpose is permitted under those provisions.
verdict.decisive_exception: The exception in Provision B for processing permitted under Articles 11.5 and 11.5a, subject to compliance with those articles.
verdict.evidence_span_a: verstrekken aan Onze Minister desgevraagd en uit eigen beweging de gegevens en inlichtingen die hij nodig heeft om maatregelen te kunnen nemen om inbreuk op de veilige en betrouwbare toegang tot elektronische dienstverlening te voorkomen of beëindigen.
verdict.evidence_span_b: worden door de aanbieders niet voor andere doelen verwerkt, tenzij het gegevens betreft waarvan de verwerking op grond van de artikelen 11.5 en 11.5a is toegestaan en de verwerking plaatsvindt met inachtneming van die artikelen.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A concerns rules on the accuracy and reliability of data supplied under other paragraphs, while provision B requires national competent authorities to comply with confidentiality obligations. If the supplied data included sensitive information, one might speculate that accuracy-related disclosure and confidentiality could pull in different directions, but neither text creates such a conflict.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires an essential or important entity to promptly inform service recipients of significant incidents affecting service provision. verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties: A concerns notifying service recipients about significant incidents, while B concerns whether certain small organisations must maintain a register of processing activities. The Article 30 exemption does not prohibit or excuse incident notification, so both duties can be complied with simultaneously.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A financial entity may have to establish and maintain a comprehensive digital-operational-resilience testing programme under Provision B while Provision A exempts some organisations with fewer than 250 employees from the referenced record-keeping obligations. If the testing programme involves non-incidental processing of personal data or processing special-category or criminal-offence data, the GDPR record obligation may nevertheless apply, creating an apparent compliance burden alongside the DORA programme.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties with different triggers: Provision A concerns maintaining a register of processing activities, while Provision B concerns testing digital operational resilience. Nothing in either text forbids performing the other duty, and the GDPR provision itself contains exceptions that can make the record obligation applicable even to smaller organisations.

verdict.shared_subject: Restrictions on personal-data processing and solely automated decisions affecting a data subject
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 41 requires a controller applying a restriction under its first paragraph to take account of the purposes, safeguards, storage periods and risks involved. Article 22, however, gives the data subject a right not to be subjected to a qualifying solely automated decision, so a controller might view the Article 41 restriction as permitting it to limit information or other rights connected with such processing while Article 22 protects against the decision itself.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties and address different objects: Article 41 concerns how a controller must design and assess a restriction of specified GDPR rights, whereas Article 22 concerns the data subject's exposure to a solely automated decision with significant effects. Article 41 does not authorise such a decision or disapply Article 22, so both can be complied with simultaneously.

verdict.shared_subject: Openbaarmaking van besluiten tot bestuurlijke/administratieve sancties
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the Dutch supervisory authority to make a decision imposing an administrative sanction public, while Provision B requires the competent authority, where publication could have disproportionate effects or specified risks, to delay publication, anonymise it, or refrain from publication. Thus, for a sanction falling within B’s risk conditions, immediate full publication under A could conflict with B.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A expressly makes its publication duty subject to the exceptions in article 5.1 of the Wet open overheid, and Provision B does not necessarily prohibit all publication: it permits delayed or anonymised publication and only requires non-publication in narrower circumstances. The texts therefore can be complied with if A’s statutory reservation accommodates B or if the authority applies B’s alternatives.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A Dutch authority has imposed an administrative sanction on a natural person, and publishing the person’s identity and personal data would create a disproportionate risk to personal-data protection. A appears to require publication, while B requires delayed, anonymised, or possibly withheld publication; whether the authority may withhold or modify publication under A depends on the applicable exception in article 5.1 of the Wet open overheid.

verdict.shared_subject: Exchange of information, including potentially confidential information, between competent authorities under Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 and related national/EU authorities.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the competent authorities to exchange all necessary data, expressly including personal data, while Provision B prohibits disclosure of information covered by professional secrecy to any other person or authority. If the authorities receiving data under A are treated as an 'other authority' and the data is covered by professional secrecy, A appears to require disclosure that B forbids.

verdict.shared_subject: Delegated rulemaking by algemene maatregel van bestuur
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions authorize further rules by algemene maatregel van bestuur, but they concern different statutory subjects: Provision A concerns criteria for identifying significant incidents, while Provision B concerns further rules under its own article. Without the full subject matter of article 11a.3, one might argue that delegated rules could overlap or impose inconsistent criteria.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can readily be obeyed together because each is an enabling provision for delegated legislation in its own statutory context. Provision A specifically authorizes criteria distinguishing significant incidents across sectors and entities, whereas Provision B merely permits further rules concerning its own article; neither commands or forbids conduct, sets incompatible deadlines, or establishes a conflicting benchmark.

verdict.shared_subject: AI Act obligations concerning providers and third parties in the AI value chain
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern free-and-open-source AI, and Article 25 excludes certain third parties from its written-assistance obligation, while Article 54 states that an obligation does not apply to certain providers of general-purpose AI models. One might therefore suspect that a free-and-open-source provider or supplier could be treated differently under the two provisions, especially where the model presents systemic risks.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 25 concerns written agreements between providers of high-risk AI systems and third parties supplying tools, services, components or processes used in those systems; its exception concerns third parties making non-general-purpose-model items available under a free and open-source licence. Article 54 concerns the separate obligation of providers of general-purpose AI models and expressly preserves its application where those models present systemic risks, so the provisions impose no incompatible commands on the same actor in the same situation.

verdict.shared_subject: Governance obligations for board members of essential or important entities versus acceptance of recognised business and organisational means in public service delivery
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions mention organisational or corporate actors, so a natural person acting for a legal person could appear in both contexts. If a board member of an essential or important entity sought public services using a recognised business or organisational means, the acceptance rule could seem to impose an operational requirement alongside the governance rules incorporated by Provision A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A merely extends specified governance provisions to natural persons representing a legal person on the board of an essential or important entity. verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A GDPR controller may avoid notifying affected individuals when one of the listed conditions is met, while NIS2 requires administrative fines for essential entities that infringe specified cybersecurity obligations. In a concrete incident, the entity could face a fine under Provision B even though Provision A removes the individual-notification requirement, but the provisions impose different consequences rather than incompatible duties.

verdict.shared_subject: The Autoriteit Consument en Markt (ACM)
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the ACM, when recording measures, to take account as far as possible of the European Commission’s comments and recommendations. Provision B requires the ACM to implement Article 10(6) of the Data Act; if that implementation required measures inconsistent with Commission comments or recommendations, the duties could pull in different directions, but no such inconsistency is shown.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different aspects of the ACM’s work: A concerns how the ACM records measures, while B concerns implementation of a specified provision of the Data Act. The ACM can implement Article 10(6) while also taking the Commission’s comments and recommendations into account as far as possible.
verdict.missing_reference: The content of Article 10(6) of Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 (the Data Act), together with the relevant European Commission comments or recommendations, is needed to determine whether implementation could conflict with the obligation in Article 11.8a.

verdict.evidence_span_b: De Autoriteit Consument en Markt geeft uitvoering aan artikel 10, zesde lid, van de dataverordening.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern public authorities and information-handling functions, but Article 65 imposes a procedural deadline and disclosure duties on supervisory authorities, while Article 11 assigns operational cybersecurity tasks to CSIRTs. One might argue that a CSIRT’s incident monitoring or forensic work could overlap with a supervisory authority’s GDPR dispute-resolution process, creating coordination pressure.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different institutional actors and address different triggers: Article 65 governs a supervisory authority’s final decision after an EDPB binding decision, whereas Article 11 governs CSIRTs’ cybersecurity monitoring, assistance, scanning, and information-sharing tasks. Nothing in either text prohibits the other authority’s activity or makes compliance with one deadline or task incompatible with compliance with the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Information and records concerning processing by organisations involved in electronic public services
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires covered organisations to provide the Minister, on request or spontaneously, with data and information needed to prevent or end breaches affecting secure and reliable electronic access. Provision B states that the Article 30(1) and (2) obligations do not apply to certain organisations with fewer than 250 employees, which could appear to remove a record-keeping obligation relevant to supplying such information.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B concerns whether specified small organisations must maintain a register of processing activities; it does not prohibit them from providing information to the Minister. Provision A imposes an information-supply duty on a defined set of bodies and organisations, while B creates an exception to a separate register-keeping duty, so both can be complied with.

verdict.shared_subject: Cross-border cooperation and mutual assistance between supervisory or competent authorities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions require authorities in different Member States to cooperate and provide mutual assistance, including information requests and supervisory measures. A possible tension is that Provision A states a broad obligation to provide assistance, while Provision B expressly permits refusal in specified circumstances, so an authority might face different apparent instructions when a request implicates national security or exceeds its competence.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be satisfied together because they concern different regulatory regimes and actors: Article 61 GDPR governs supervisory authorities implementing the GDPR, while Article 37 NIS2 governs competent authorities concerning covered entities and cybersecurity supervision. Even where both apply, Article 37's refusal grounds qualify its own assistance duty, and nothing in Article 61 expressly forbids refusal where another applicable legal regime supplies such limits.

verdict.shared_subject: Electronic storage/access of information and data-subject information rights
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A conditions storage of or access to information in a user's terminal equipment on clear information and consent. Provision B gives the data subject a right to be informed about appropriate safeguards when personal data are transferred to a third country or international organisation, which could require disclosure in a situation where A's consent condition is not met.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties concerning different acts: A regulates storing or accessing information in terminal equipment, while B regulates informing a data subject about safeguards for an international transfer. B does not require such storage or access, and A does not prohibit informing the data subject about a transfer.

verdict.shared_subject: ICT security and personal-data protection
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can concern the same financial entity and the same ICT environment: testing may uncover a personal-data breach, while Article 34 governs whether affected individuals must be notified. One might argue that testing or its results could trigger notification-related handling obligations, creating operational tension.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 34 concerns notification to data subjects after a personal-data breach and expressly permits non-notification only under stated conditions. Article 25 requires an ICT-resilience testing programme, including vulnerability assessments and penetration tests; it neither requires nor forbids notifying data subjects, so both duties can be performed together.

verdict.shared_subject: Technical or organizational continuity and security measures imposed on entities/providers
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A authorizes rules and requirements concerning measures for entities, while provision B allows the Minister to impose a technical or organizational measure on a qualifying provider within a specified period. If both mechanisms imposed incompatible measures or deadlines, the provider might face conflicting requirements, but neither text shown actually creates such an incompatibility.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A is a competence provision under which further rules may be made by general administrative order, whereas provision B independently empowers the Minister to require a qualifying provider to take a measure supporting continuity. The duties can readily be complied with cumulatively, and no concrete requirement, prohibition, deadline, or exception in A conflicts with B.

verdict.shared_subject: A small financial entity processing personal data in connection with its ICT-activity
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A can exempt an organisation with fewer than 250 employees from the Article 30 register obligation, while Provision B requires financial entities to maintain and test mechanisms for detecting anomalous activities. If those detection mechanisms involve processing personal data, the entity might view the GDPR register obligation as inapplicable while still having to document or operate the DORA mechanisms.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties: A concerns whether certain controllers must keep a register of processing activities, whereas B requires financial entities to have and regularly test ICT-detection mechanisms. A does not prohibit detection mechanisms, and B does not require or forbid a GDPR Article 30 register; moreover, the Article 30 exemption itself is conditional and may not apply where the processing is risky, non-incidental, or involves special-category or criminal-offence data.

verdict.shared_subject: Use of special-category personal data in high-risk AI systems and solely automated decisions affecting individuals
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 10 permits providers of high-risk AI systems, in narrowly defined circumstances, to process special-category personal data to detect and correct bias. Such processing could involve profiling or automated evaluation of individuals, and Article 22 prohibits decisions based solely on automated processing that have legal or similarly significant effects. If the bias-correction processing itself produces such a decision, the permission in Article 10 might appear to conflict with Article 22’s prohibition.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 10 regulates exceptional processing of special-category data for bias detection and correction; it does not require or authorize making solely automated decisions affecting individuals. Article 22 regulates a different act—the imposition of a significant solely automated decision—and both provisions can be complied with by using the data for bias testing while ensuring that any significant decision is not solely automated or falls within Article 22’s stated exceptions.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De betrokkene heeft het recht niet te worden onderworpen aan een uitsluitend op geautomatiseerde verwerking, waaronder profilering, gebaseerd besluit waaraan voor hem rechtsgevolgen zijn verbonden of dat hem anderszins in aanmerkelijke mate treft.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Voor zover dit strikt noodzakelijk is om de opsporing en correctie van vertekeningen te waarborgen in verband met de AI-systemen met een hoog risico overeenkomstig lid 2, punten f) en g), van dit artikel, mogen de aanbieders van dergelijke systemen uitzonderlijk bijzondere categorieën persoonsgegevens verwerken, mits passende waarborgen worden geboden voor de grondrechten en fundamentele vrijheden van natuurlijke personen.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of personal data by providers of trust services, including processing for direct marketing.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits processing by a trust-service provider when the data were obtained from the data subject or with explicit consent and the processing is required for providing the trust service. Provision B prohibits further processing for direct-marketing purposes once the data subject objects, so a provider might otherwise regard such processing as permitted under A but be barred by B.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different purposes: A permits only processing required to provide the trust service, while B prohibits processing for direct marketing after an objection. Direct marketing is not shown to be required for providing the trust service, so both rules can normally be complied with. The supplied exception in A concerns fraud detection or processing required by law and does not establish a direct-marketing exception.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Verleners van vertrouwensdiensten verwerken alleen persoonsgegevens die van de betrokkene zelf of met diens uitdrukkelijke toestemming zijn verkregen, en voor zover de verwerking van deze persoonsgegevens voor het verlenen van de vertrouwensdienst is vereist.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Wanneer de betrokkene bezwaar maakt tegen verwerking ten behoeve van direct marketing, worden de persoonsgegevens niet meer voor deze doeleinden verwerkt.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: The provisions both mention competent authorities and impose obligations connected with regulated digital activity, so one might initially suspect overlapping compliance duties. However, Provision A concerns certification bodies notifying supervisory authorities about certification decisions, while Provision B concerns financial entities conducting post-incident ICT evaluations and, in some cases, reporting implemented changes.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different actors and are triggered by different events: certification issuance or withdrawal under Provision A, versus serious ICT incidents affecting financial entities under Provision B. A certification body can notify authorities while a financial entity conducts its evaluation and communicates subsequent changes; neither provision restricts or makes impossible compliance with the other.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De in lid 1 bedoelde certificeringsorganen stellen de bevoegde toezichthoudende autoriteiten op de hoogte van de redenen voor het afgeven of het intrekken van het aangevraagde certificaat.

verdict.shared_subject: Information to data subjects about the transfer of healthcare records and safeguards for transfers to third countries or international organisations
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions require information connected with a transfer of personal data. If a healthcare-record transfer is to a third country or international organisation, Article 30a may permit general public notice where individual information is impossible, disproportionately burdensome, or confidential under professional secrecy, while Article 15 gives the data subject a right to be informed of the appropriate Article 46 safeguards.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different informational content and can be fulfilled together: Article 30a requires information about the transfer and applicable rights, or general notice in specified circumstances, whereas Article 15 requires notice of the appropriate safeguards for a third-country or international-organisation transfer. Nothing shown expressly makes general notice under Article 30a incompatible with also providing the Article 15 information or otherwise exercising the access right.

verdict.evidence_span_b: Wanneer persoonsgegevens worden doorgegeven aan een derde land of een internationale organisatie, heeft de betrokkene het recht in kennis te worden gesteld van de passende waarborgen overeenkomstig artikel 46 inzake de doorgifte.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: The provisions concern different duties and apparently different actors: A requires the ETAs to submit a confidential joint report every five years, while B requires importers to provide information and documentation to competent authorities on request. Nothing in either text requires an actor to withhold information or makes the reporting duties incompatible.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties can readily coexist: an ETA can submit its periodic confidential report, while an importer can separately provide the requested AI-system documentation in an understandable language and make the technical documentation available. The provisions have different actors, triggers, recipients, and subject matter, with no conflicting deadline, content requirement, or prohibition.

verdict.shared_subject: ICT-risk management and transfers of personal data by financial entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A financial entity subject to DORA may need to conduct internal ICT-risk audits, potentially involving auditors or audit materials in a third country. GDPR Article 44 prohibits transferring personal data to that third country unless the Chapter V conditions are satisfied, so the audit obligation could create practical pressure to transfer data that Article 44 restricts.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 6 imposes an internal-audit duty but does not require transferring personal data outside the EU or disclosing any particular personal data to auditors. The entity can conduct the audit using anonymised data, EU-based auditors, or otherwise compliant transfer mechanisms, so both provisions can be satisfied.

verdict.shared_subject: Sanctions for non-compliance by entities potentially subject to both Dutch financial-supervision obligations and DORA oversight
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A authorizes the Dutch Data Protection Authority to impose an administrative fine of up to €20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover for violations of obligations under the Dutch Financial Supervision Act. Provision B sets a maximum daily coercive fine of 1% of the critical ICT third-party provider’s average worldwide daily turnover for non-compliance with specified measures, so the same conduct could potentially attract materially different sanction regimes.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions concern different authorities, legal bases, and sanction types: A concerns an administrative fine for violating obligations under Article 3.17(7) of the Financial Supervision Act, while B concerns a coercive fine imposed by the DORA lead overseer for non-compliance with measures referred to in Article 35(6). Nothing in the texts says that either sanction excludes or limits the other, so both could be imposed or complied with independently.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing special-category and criminal-offence personal data by a temporary commission or advisory body, and facilitating data-subject rights
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits the prohibition on processing special-category and criminal-offence data not to apply when its listed conditions are met. Provision B requires the controller to facilitate the data subject’s rights under Articles 15–22, which could require access to or other handling of such data; if that exercise were treated as processing prohibited by another applicable rule, the duties could appear to pull in opposite directions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A concerns the conditions under which a specific processing prohibition does not apply, while Provision B concerns facilitating data-subject rights and expressly preserves an inability-to-identify exception. Nothing in either text forbids facilitating those rights, and the provisions can be complied with simultaneously, including by applying the safeguards in A while handling rights requests under B.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits using a network-number facility to provide a called user with incorrect information about the network endpoint or individual user. Provision B requires notified bodies and their personnel to keep information confidential, subject to specified exceptions. One might argue that confidentiality could require withholding or misstating such information, but B does not require disclosure or misstatement.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different conduct and, on the texts shown, different actors: A concerns use of a network-number facility and inaccurate information to a called user, while B concerns confidentiality procedures and professional secrecy for notified bodies. A notified body can comply with B by withholding confidential information rather than providing incorrect information, so both provisions can be satisfied without conflict.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern institutional responses to regulatory or cybersecurity-related risks, so one might initially suspect that a national cyber-crisis plan could affect supervision of GDPR-approved codes. However, neither provision imposes a duty or prohibition on the same actor concerning the same conduct, and no incompatibility is stated.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A requires the Minister to establish a national plan for large-scale cybersecurity incidents and crisis response. Provision B requires the competent supervisory authority to withdraw an accredited code-monitoring body's accreditation when accreditation conditions fail or its measures breach the GDPR; these duties can operate independently and can both be fulfilled.

verdict.shared_subject: Information supplied by entities and telecommunications facilities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires covered entities to provide the central contact point with current contact details and IP ranges. Provision B prohibits using a facility to provide a called user with incorrect information about the network termination point or individual user; supplying accurate registry information under A does not itself involve providing such incorrect information.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different conduct and purposes: A concerns administrative registration information supplied by specified digital-service entities to a central contact point, while B concerns misleading information supplied through a network-connection identification facility to a called user. An entity can comply with A while also complying with B by providing accurate registry data and not misleading users.

verdict.shared_subject: Information handled by CSIRTs and notifying authorities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: CSIRTs must collect and analyse forensic data and disseminate information about cyber threats, vulnerabilities and incidents to relevant stakeholders, while notifying authorities must keep information obtained under Article 78 confidential. If a CSIRT’s dissemination involved information obtained under Article 78, disclosure could conflict with that confidentiality duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different actors: Article 11 governs CSIRTs, whereas Article 45 governs notifying authorities. Article 11 does not require disclosure of Article 78 information, and Article 45 does not prohibit CSIRTs from performing their monitoring, analysis or assistance tasks, so both can ordinarily be complied with.
verdict.missing_reference: The text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Article 78, including what information is obtained under it and any confidentiality exceptions or permitted disclosures, is needed to determine whether Article 11 dissemination by a CSIRT can include information covered by Article 45.

verdict.shared_subject: A significant incident affecting personal data at an essential or important entity in the medical-device manufacturing sector.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the entity to give an early warning about a significant incident to its CSIRT and competent authority within 24 hours at the latest. Provision B exempts communication to the data subject when, for example, appropriate protective measures were applied or communication would require disproportionate effort, so the same incident may trigger an authority/CSIRT warning but no individual notification.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different recipients: A concerns an early warning to a CSIRT and competent authority, while B concerns communication to the data subject. Nothing in B prohibits the warning required by A, and the exemption in B can coexist with that warning.

No actor, trigger, duty, permission, or prohibition is shared in the texts.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can both be complied with because they regulate wholly different matters: A excludes certain assistance and advice services from its scope, whereas B imposes a publication-suspension rule following a request for voorlopige voorziening. Nothing in either provision requires or prevents compliance with the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Handling requests under the GDPR by the Dutch administrative courts and administrative bodies
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits the Raad van State to stay a request when a related preliminary question is pending before the Court of Justice. Provision B requires a written decision on requests under Articles 15–22 within the GDPR’s Article 12(3) time limits, so a stay under A could appear to prevent a timely decision under B.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different actors and procedural stages: A concerns the Raad van State’s competence to stay judicial proceedings, while B concerns written decisions by bestuursorganen. Moreover, A says the court “can” stay the request, not that it must, so the court can avoid a stay where it would conflict with an applicable decision deadline.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De Afdeling bestuursrechtspraak van de Raad van State kan besluiten het verzoek aan te houden als er bij het Hof van Justitie van de Europese Unie al een prejudiciële vraag omtrent de geldigheid van het desbetreffende besluit aanhangig is.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Een schriftelijke beslissing op een verzoek als bedoeld in de artikelen 15 tot en met 22 van de verordening wordt genomen binnen de in artikel 12, derde lid, van de verordening genoemde termijnen en geldt, voor zover deze is genomen door een bestuursorgaan, als een besluit in de zin van de Algemene wet bestuursrecht.

verdict.shared_subject: An entity/provider handling a personal-data breach that may trigger both the notification rule and NIS2 administrative fines.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A exempts a provider from notifying affected persons when the data were rendered unintelligible through appropriate technical safeguards. Provision B requires Member States to impose substantial fines on essential entities that infringe Articles 21 or 23, so an entity might face a fine-related consequence for conduct connected with a breach even though A removes the notification duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different consequences and have different triggers: A concerns whether notification of affected persons is required, while B concerns administrative fines for infringement of Articles 21 or 23. Nothing in the shown text makes failure to notify under A an infringement of Articles 21 or 23, and B does not require notification or prohibit A's exemption.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De kennisgeving, bedoeld in het tweede lid, is niet vereist indien de aanbieder naar het oordeel van de Autoriteit persoonsgegevens gepaste technische beschermingsmaatregelen heeft genomen waardoor de persoonsgegevens die het betreft, versleuteld of anderszins onbegrijpelijk zijn voor een ieder die geen recht heeft op toegang tot die gegevens.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De lidstaten zorgen ervoor dat essentiële entiteiten die inbreuk maken op artikel 21 of 23 overeenkomstig de leden 2 en 3 van dit artikel onderworpen worden aan administratieve geldboeten met een maximumbedrag van ten minste 10 000 000 EUR of ten minste 2 % van de totale wereldwijde jaaromzet in het voorgaande boekjaar van de onderneming waartoe de essentiële entiteit behoort, afhankelijk van welk bedrag hoger is.

verdict.shared_subject: Use of ICT technologies and processes by financial entities, including access to users’ terminal equipment for a public-law service
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits making a user’s access to a public-law information-society service conditional on consent under paragraph 1. Provision B requires financial entities to use ICT technologies and processes that protect data and prevent unauthorised access, loss, and technical defects; one might argue that obtaining consent for terminal-equipment access could be part of secure or compliant processing. However, B does not require consent or address access conditions for a public-law service.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different duties and triggers: A concerns a public-law legal person’s service-access condition, while B concerns financial entities’ ICT security and data-protection measures. A financial entity can comply with B by using suitable security processes without conditioning service access on consent, so both provisions can be satisfied simultaneously.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De toegang van de gebruiker tot een dienst van de informatiemaatschappij die wordt geleverd door of namens een krachtens publiekrecht ingestelde rechtspersoon wordt niet afhankelijk gemaakt van het verlenen van toestemming als bedoeld in het eerste lid.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Om de in lid 2 bedoelde doelstellingen te verwezenlijken, maken financiële entiteiten gebruik van ICT-technologieën en -processen die geschikt zijn overeenkomstig artikel 4.

verdict.shared_subject: Administrative sanctions for statutory violations
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern imposing administrative fines, so an entity could theoretically be exposed to sanctioning under both regimes. However, Provision A concerns a competent authority sanctioning a violation of Article 5:20(1) Awb, while Provision B assigns the AP sanctioning powers for a separately enumerated set of provisions; the texts do not prescribe incompatible sanctions or prohibit concurrent competence.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be satisfied simultaneously because they confer powers on authorities for different legal bases and do not require mutually exclusive outcomes. Provision A permits a competent authority to fine a significant entity for violating Article 5:20(1) Awb, whereas Provision B authorizes the AP to impose sanctions for the listed provisions, with no shown rule making one sanction unlawful or displacing the other.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De bevoegde autoriteit kan tevens aan een belangrijke entiteit een bestuurlijke boete opleggen in geval van overtreding van artikel 5:20, eerste lid, van de Algemene wet bestuursrecht.
