verdict.shared_subject: National competent authorities’ duties concerning regulatory AI sandboxes
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose reporting or information-related duties concerning the same regulatory AI sandbox. One could argue that the public list under Provision A and the publicly available annual reports or summaries under Provision B create overlapping publication obligations, potentially requiring authorities to publish similar information in different formats or at different times.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose distinct, cumulative duties: Provision A requires notifying the AI Office and AI Board of the sandbox’s establishment, while Provision B requires annual and final substantive reports and public availability of those reports or summaries. Nothing in either text forbids performing the other duty, and the obligations can readily be fulfilled together.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De nationale bevoegde autoriteiten stellen het AI-bureau en de AI-board in kennis van de oprichting van een testomgeving
verdict.evidence_span_b: De nationale bevoegde autoriteiten dienen vanaf één jaar na de oprichting van de AI-testomgeving voor regelgeving en vervolgens elk jaar tot de beëindiging ervan, bij het AI-bureau en de AI-board jaarverslagen in, alsook een afsluitend verslag.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of personal data in high-risk AI systems, including special categories of personal data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a controller to conduct a data-protection impact assessment before processing where the processing is likely to create a high risk to individuals’ rights and freedoms. Provision B permits providers of high-risk AI systems to exceptionally process special-category personal data only when strict necessity and several safeguards are satisfied; conducting the assessment required by A could itself involve processing personal data, potentially including the sensitive data governed by B.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties at different stages: A requires a prior assessment, while B regulates the exceptional processing of special-category data for bias detection and correction. An assessment can be designed and documented without processing special-category data, and B expressly operates alongside Regulation 2016/679 rather than prohibiting impact assessments.
verdict.evidence_span_a: voert de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke vóór de verwerking een beoordeling uit van het effect van de beoogde verwerkingsactiviteiten op de bescherming van persoonsgegevens
verdict.evidence_span_b: mogen de aanbieders van dergelijke systemen uitzonderlijk bijzondere categorieën persoonsgegevens verwerken, mits passende waarborgen worden geboden

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: The provisions both concern enforcement measures, so one might initially suspect that the prohibition on imposing a second administrative fine could constrain enforcement against a critical ICT provider. However, provision A concerns a competent authority imposing a fine for the same conduct after an AVG fine, while provision B requires the lead overseer to impose a coercive penalty for non-compliance with measures after at least 30 days; the texts do not establish that these are the same authority, actor, conduct, or type of sanction.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be obeyed simultaneously because A prohibits duplicative administrative fines for the same conduct, whereas B requires a coercive penalty to compel compliance with supervisory measures. Nothing in A prohibits such a coercive penalty, and nothing in B requires a second administrative fine for the conduct covered by A.
verdict.evidence_span_a: legt de bevoegde autoriteit geen bestuurlijke boete op op grond van de artikelen 80 en 87 voor een inbreuk als bedoeld in het tweede lid die voortvloeit uit dezelfde gedraging
verdict.evidence_span_b: neemt de lead overseer een besluit aan waarmee een dwangsom wordt opgelegd om de kritieke derde aanbieder van ICT-diensten tot nakoming van die maatregelen te dwingen

verdict.shared_subject: Delegated rulemaking by general administrative order (algemene maatregel van bestuur)
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions authorize further rules by or under an algemene maatregel van bestuur, but they refer to different underlying provisions: Article 62 concerns implementation of Article 29(3) of the NIS2 Directive, while Article 11a.3 concerns the provision containing Article 11a.3 itself. If the delegated rules addressed the same subject, their scopes or requirements could theoretically diverge.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The texts establish separate competences rather than conflicting commands. Each permits supplementary rules concerning a different legal basis, and neither provision requires or forbids anything that would make compliance with the other impossible.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Bij of krachtens algemene maatregel van bestuur kunnen regels worden gesteld ter uitvoering van het bepaalde in artikel 29, derde lid, van de NIS2-richtlijn.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Bij of krachtens algemene maatregel van bestuur kunnen nadere regels worden gesteld ten aanzien van het bepaalde in dit artikel.

verdict.shared_subject: Communicating significant cyber threats and personal-data breaches to affected service recipients or data subjects
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires an essential or important entity to promptly tell service recipients what measures they can take in response to a significant cyber threat, and, if necessary, to inform them of the threat itself. If that threat involves a personal-data breach, Provision B says the notification referred to in its second paragraph is not required when the provider has taken appropriate technical protective measures making the data encrypted or otherwise unintelligible to unauthorised persons. This could appear to create an exception to notification in a fact pattern where A would otherwise require communication.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B expressly concerns the notification described in its second paragraph: notification by a provider to the person whose personal data are concerned when a personal-data breach is likely to adversely affect privacy. Provision A instead concerns an essential or important entity informing recipients of its services about measures responding to a significant cyber threat and, if necessary, the threat itself; the texts do not establish that B’s exception applies to A’s distinct communication duty.
verdict.decisive_exception: None established as necessary: the shown text does not make Provision B’s exception applicable to Provision A’s distinct cyber-threat communication duty.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit deelt de ontvangers van haar diensten, die mogelijkerwijs door een significante cyberdreiging in relatie tot het ontvangen van die diensten worden getroffen, onverwijld mee welke maatregelen die ontvangers kunnen nemen in reactie op die dreiging.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De kennisgeving, bedoeld in het tweede lid, is niet vereist indien de aanbieder naar het oordeel van de Autoriteit persoonsgegevens gepaste technische beschermingsmaatregelen heeft genomen waardoor de persoonsgegevens die het betreft, versleuteld of anderszins onbegrijpelijk zijn voor een ieder die geen recht heeft op toegang tot die gegevens.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A concerns an exemption from an information-provision obligation for certain trust-service providers, while provision B prohibits making access to a public-law service conditional on consent under article 11.7a(1). If a public-law service provider also fell within A and used user-device information, the exemption might appear relevant to the information and consent framework, but the texts do not establish that overlap or that A authorises conditioning access on consent.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different matters: A limits when an information-provision obligation applies to a trust-service provider, whereas B prohibits conditioning access to a specified public-law information-society service on consent. Nothing in A requires such conditioning, and nothing in B removes or modifies A's exemption.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Het eerste lid is niet van toepassing wanneer en voor zover een entiteit optreedt als verlener van vertrouwensdiensten die niet uitsluitend worden gebruikt binnen systemen die gesloten zijn als gevolg van een wettelijke regeling of een overeenkomst tussen een bepaalde groep deelnemers.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De toegang van de gebruiker tot een dienst van de informatiemaatschappij die wordt geleverd door of namens een krachtens publiekrecht ingestelde rechtspersoon wordt niet afhankelijk gemaakt van het verlenen van toestemming als bedoeld in het eerste lid.

verdict.shared_subject: Disclosure of personal information by notified conformity-assessment bodies in response to third-country legal demands
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 48 restricts recognition or enforceability of a third-country judgment or administrative decision requiring a controller or processor to disclose personal data unless based on an international agreement. Article 31 requires notified bodies to keep information confidential but makes an exception where disclosure is legally required, which could appear to require disclosure in response to such a third-country decision.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different things: Article 48 limits when a third-country demand for personal-data disclosure may be recognised or enforced, while Article 31 requires confidentiality by notified bodies and expressly permits disclosure when legally required. A third-country demand that is not recognised or enforceable under Article 48 need not be treated as legally requiring disclosure, so both provisions can be obeyed.
verdict.decisive_exception: The Article 31 exception for disclosure that is legally required, read together with Article 48's rule that a third-country judgment or administrative decision may be recognised or enforced only when based on an applicable international agreement.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Elke rechterlijke uitspraak en elk besluit van een administratieve autoriteit van een derde land op grond waarvan een verwerkingsverantwoordelijke of een verwerker persoonsgegevens moet doorgeven of verstrekken, mag alleen op enigerlei wijze worden erkend of afdwingbaar zijn indien zij gebaseerd zijn op een internationale overeenkomst, zoals een verdrag inzake wederzijdse rechtsbijstand, tussen het verzoekende derde landen en de Unie of een lidstaat, onverminderd andere gronden voor doorgifte uit hoofde van dit hoofdstuk.
verdict.evidence_span_b: behalve wanneer de openbaarmaking ervan wettelijk vereist is.

verdict.shared_subject: Public disclosure of administrative sanctions or coercive fines by supervisory authorities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose publication duties on supervisory authorities, but they attach different exceptions to disclosure. In a case where a sanction or coercive fine is covered by both regimes, one provision may require publication while the other permits withholding it to protect financial markets or avoid disproportionate harm.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions may govern different authorities, sanctions, and legal regimes: provision A concerns an AP decision imposing an administrative sanction, while provision B concerns all coercive fines imposed by the lead overseer. If their scopes do not overlap, both duties can be complied with independently; even if they overlap, the exceptions might be capable of cumulative application.
verdict.missing_reference: The provisions establishing whether the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens is a “lead overseer” under Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 and whether the same measure is both a bestuurlijke sanctie under art. 21b and an opgelegde dwangsom under art. 35; also the applicable rule resolving which disclosure exception prevails in an overlap.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens maakt een door haar genomen beschikking tot het opleggen van een bestuurlijke sanctie openbaar, behoudens voor zover artikel 5.1, eerste, tweede en vijfde lid van de Wet open overheid, aan openbaarmaking in de weg staan.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De lead overseer maakt alle opgelegde dwangsommen openbaar, tenzij die openbaarmaking de financiële markten ernstig in gevaar zou brengen of onevenredige schade zou toebrengen aan de betrokken partijen.

verdict.shared_subject: Governance and allocation of tasks within an organisation or committee
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the members to establish a division of tasks and, as far as possible, involve extraordinary members. Provision B requires the secretariat to perform its tasks exclusively according to the chair's instructions; tension might arise if the members' task division assigns the secretariat tasks or requires involvement that conflicts with the chair's instructions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different actors and functions: A governs the members' establishment of a task division, while B governs how the secretariat performs its tasks. Members can allocate tasks while the secretariat follows the chair's instructions, and nothing in A expressly directs the secretariat or overrides the chair.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De leden stellen een verdeling van taken vast en betrekken hierbij zoveel mogelijk de buitengewone leden.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Het secretariaat verricht zijn taken uitsluitend volgens de instructies van de voorzitter van het Comité.

verdict.shared_subject: Use and disclosure of personal/contact data in unsolicited communications and spiritual care
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits providing personal data revealing religious or philosophical beliefs to third parties without the data subject’s consent. Provision B requires the sender, when sending unsolicited communications with consent through certain means, to give the recipient an easy, cost-free opportunity to object; that opt-out duty could be relevant where the communication involves such sensitive data, but B does not itself authorize disclosure without consent.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties in different regulatory settings: A governs disclosure of sensitive belief-related personal data to third parties, while B governs unsolicited communications and objection mechanisms. A sender can comply with both by obtaining consent before disclosure and also providing the opt-out opportunity required by B; B’s obligation does not require disclosure without consent.
verdict.evidence_span_a: worden geen persoonsgegevens aan derden verstrekt zonder toestemming van de betrokkene.
verdict.evidence_span_b: geeft de verzender de desbetreffende natuurlijke persoon bij iedere boodschap duidelijk en expliciet de gelegenheid om kosteloos en op gemakkelijke wijze verzet aan te tekenen tegen het gebruik van zijn contactgegevens.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A assigns a CSIRT operational and analytical tasks involving cyber threats, incidents, and network and information systems. Provision B requires a supervisory authority to withdraw accreditation from a code-monitoring body when that body's measures infringe the GDPR; if the same body were both the CSIRT and an accredited code-monitoring body, some CSIRT measures might potentially be viewed as GDPR-infringing.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different functions and actors: A defines CSIRT tasks, while B governs withdrawal of accreditation of an accredited code-monitoring body. Nothing in A requires a GDPR-infringing measure, and B does not prohibit CSIRT monitoring, assistance, scanning, or analysis as such.
verdict.evidence_span_a: het monitoren en analyseren van cyberdreigingen, kwetsbaarheden en incidenten op nationaal niveau
verdict.evidence_span_b: De bevoegde toezichthoudende autoriteit trekt de accreditatie van een in lid 1 bedoeld orgaan in indien de voorwaarden voor accreditatie niet of niet meer worden vervuld of indien de door het orgaan genomen maatregelen inbreuk maken op deze verordening.

verdict.shared_subject: BWBR0048156: erkende diensten versus bestuursorganen of aangewezen organisaties
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Artikel 13 imposes a delivery obligation on an erkende dienst, while article 29 delays the acceptance obligations in articles 7 and 15 until connection under an official schedule. If the delivery obligation were understood to require delivery to an unconnected bestuursorgaan or aangewezen organisatie before that schedule permits acceptance, the service could be required to deliver where the recipient is not yet required or able to accept.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different duties and actors: article 13 governs an erkende dienst and its rules of service, whereas article 29 limits when acceptance duties apply to a bestuursorgaan or aangewezen organisatie. A delivery obligation can therefore coexist with a staged commencement of the recipient's acceptance obligation, and nothing in the shown text says that delivery must occur before infrastructure connection or that acceptance must be simultaneous.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Een krachtens artikel 11 erkende dienst voldoet aan de voor de betrokken dienst bij of krachtens algemene maatregel van bestuur gestelde regels en aan de aan de erkenning of aanwijzing verbonden voorschriften en beperkingen.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De in de artikelen 7 en 15 opgenomen acceptatieplichten zijn voor een bestuursorgaan of aangewezen organisatie niet eerder van toepassing dan nadat dat bestuursorgaan of die aangewezen organisatie kan worden aangesloten op de in artikel 5, eerste lid, onderdelen a tot en met e, en tweede lid bedoelde infrastructuur en voorzieningen overeenkomstig het bij regeling van Onze Minister, gehoord Onze Ministers die het mede aangaat, op te stellen aansluitschema.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern public disclosure by an authority, so one might initially suspect overlapping publication duties. If a ministerial decision under Provision A were also an administrative penalty decision under Provision B, the provisions could appear to impose different publication channels or timing requirements.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A requires the Minister to announce a decision designating attributes in the Staatscourant. Provision B requires competent authorities to publish final administrative penalty decisions on their official website after notifying the affected person; the provisions address different decision types and do not impose incompatible duties.

verdict.shared_subject: ICT-diensten and entities subject to NIS2/DORA oversight
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires cooperation and notification between authorities when exercising supervisory and enforcement powers concerning an entity designated as a critical ICT third-party provider. Provision B requires financial entities, before contracting for ICT services, to perform specified assessments and due diligence; if the same organisation is both the relevant financial entity and an authority exercising powers, the provisions address different actions but could create coordination or timing burdens.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different actors and at different stages: A governs cooperation and notification by competent authorities during supervision or enforcement, while B governs pre-contract assessments by financial entities. Nothing in A forbids or limits the assessments required by B, and nothing in B prevents the authorities from cooperating or notifying the oversight forum.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De lidstaten zorgen ervoor dat hun uit hoofde van deze richtlijn bevoegde autoriteiten samenwerken met de relevante uit hoofde van Verordening (EU) 2022/2554 bevoegde autoriteiten van de betrokken lidstaat.

verdict.shared_subject: Small enterprises or organisations that are also essential or important entities under NIS2 and experience a significant incident involving personal-data processing.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A exempts enterprises with fewer than 250 employees from the Article 30 record-keeping obligations unless one of its listed exceptions applies. Provision B nevertheless requires every essential or important entity to report significant incidents, potentially including information about incidents involving personal data, so a small entity might face substantial reporting duties despite being exempt from the GDPR register duty. This is, however, a difference in subject matter rather than an incompatibility: reporting an incident does not necessarily require maintaining the Article 30 register.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties: A concerns whether certain small organisations must keep a register of processing activities, while B concerns prompt reporting of significant incidents by essential and important entities. An entity can comply with both by reporting the incident under B and, where A's exemption applies, not keeping the Article 30 register; neither provision requires or forbids the conduct required by the other.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De in de leden 1 en 2 bedoelde verplichtingen zijn niet van toepassing op ondernemingen of organisaties die minder dan 250 personen in dienst hebben, tenzij het waarschijnlijk is dat de verwerking die zij verrichten een risico inhoudt voor de rechten en vrijheden van de betrokkenen, de verwerking niet incidenteel is, of de verwerking bijzondere categorieën van gegevens, als bedoeld in artikel 9, lid 1, of persoonsgegevens in verband met strafrechtelijke veroordelingen en strafbare feiten als bedoeld in artikel 10 betreft.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Elke lidstaat zorgt ervoor dat essentiële en belangrijke entiteiten elk incident dat aanzienlijke gevolgen heeft voor de verlening van hun diensten als bedoeld in lid 3 (significant incident) onverwijld meldt bij zijn CSIRT of, indien van toepassing, zijn bevoegde autoriteit overeenkomstig lid 4.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern procedures under the same legislative instrument, so one might initially suspect that a ministerial regulation setting requirements for a termination plan could interact with parliamentary procedures for delegated regulation. However, neither provision regulates the same act, actor, trigger, or legal instrument in a way that creates an incompatibility.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 14 governs a recognised service's request to withdraw its recognition and the accompanying termination plan. Article 25 governs the parliamentary submission and possible delayed entry into force or withdrawal of a general administrative measure adopted under Article 5(6); the provisions can operate independently without either preventing compliance with the other.

verdict.evidence_span_b: Een krachtens artikel 5, zesde lid, vastgestelde algemene maatregel van bestuur wordt aan beide Kamers der Staten-Generaal overgelegd.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing biometric and criminal-law personal data in real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits a commission or advisory body to process special-category or criminal-law personal data without the prohibition applying, provided the listed safeguards are met. Provision B separately makes real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law-enforcement purposes dependent on prior judicial or independent administrative authorisation, so an A-covered body might regard its statutory task and safeguards as sufficient while B still withholds permission absent that authorisation.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different conditions that can be satisfied cumulatively: A concerns an exception to the data-processing prohibition for a commission or advisory body, whereas B regulates the use of a particular biometric-identification system in public spaces for law enforcement. Compliance with A does not purport to replace B's separate authorisation requirement, so both can be obeyed by obtaining the required authorisation and meeting A's safeguards.

verdict.evidence_span_b: wordt elk gebruik van systemen voor biometrische identificatie op afstand in real time in openbare ruimten met het oog op de rechtshandhaving afhankelijk gesteld van een voorafgaande toestemming

verdict.shared_subject: Processing personal data by a temporary commission or advisory body and the data subject’s right to object
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A removes the prohibition on processing special-category or criminal-offence data when its stated conditions are met, while provision B gives the data subject a right to object to processing based on Article 6(1)(e) or (f) and requires cessation unless overriding grounds exist. Thus, if the commission relies on Article 6(1)(e) or (f), an objection could require stopping processing even though A permits it.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different legal questions: A concerns when processing otherwise prohibited categories of data is permitted, whereas B governs objections to processing based on Article 6(1)(e) or (f). The texts can both be satisfied because A’s permission does not displace B’s separate objection right, and B itself allows continued processing where overriding grounds exist.

verdict.shared_subject: Cybersecurity incidents involving financial entities that may also involve personal-data breaches

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions authorize further rules by general administrative order, so one might initially suspect overlapping delegated regulation concerning digital-service operation. verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A extends the referenced governance rules to every member of a maatschap when the essential or important entity is a maatschap. Provision B removes the relevant Directive provisions, including supervision and enforcement, where equivalent sector-specific EU requirements apply, so the same members could appear both subject to and excluded from those provisions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions operate at different levels: A determines who within a maatschap is covered by the governance rules, while B allocates precedence between the Directive and equivalent sector-specific EU legislation. B also preserves the Directive for entities not covered by the sector-specific act, so the rules can be applied without contradiction once the entity's sector-specific coverage and equivalence are established.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A can disapply relevant NIS2 provisions, including supervision and enforcement, for entities covered by an equivalent sector-specific Union act. verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions concern different notifications to different recipients and are triggered by different conditions: A concerns a significant incident affecting provision of a trust service, while B concerns notifying affected individuals of a personal-data breach likely to adversely affect their privacy. B also expressly permits disclosure where the authority declares it may be disclosed or where disclosure is necessary for judicial proceedings, so the texts do not establish an unavoidable incompatibility.

verdict.shared_subject: A high-risk AI system involving personal-data processing and changes in the AI value chain
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the controller to conduct a data-protection impact assessment before processing where the processing is likely to create a high risk to individuals’ rights and freedoms. Provision B requires the original provider to cooperate and provide information, technical access, and assistance for compliance with high-risk AI obligations, which could create additional operational demands before or during deployment.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different actors and address different regulatory objects: A concerns the controller’s personal-data processing, while B concerns the original AI provider’s cooperation after another actor becomes a provider under the AI Act. The provider can supply the required assistance while the controller separately performs the impact assessment; neither provision requires conduct prohibited by the other.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires covered entities to provide information to the Minister through a designated mechanism. Provision B restricts the use of a public identification means and a specified facility to access to electronic services provided by administrative bodies and designated organisations. If the mechanism in A required such a public identification means for access by an entity that is not an administrative body or designated organisation, B could appear to prohibit that access.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different conduct and actors: A concerns information that covered entities must supply to the Minister, while B concerns the permitted use of a particular public identification means and facility for access to electronic services. A does not require use of the means or facility covered by B, and it does not establish that the reporting mechanism is an electronic service or that covered entities must access it using that means.

verdict.shared_subject: ICT-risk management and instructions for high-risk AI systems used by certain exempt financial entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires certain exempt financial entities to maintain ICT-risk controls, including protection of data confidentiality and integrity. Provision B requires high-risk AI systems to come with instructions containing information that is relevant, complete, correct, clear, accessible and understandable; detailed security or operational information could potentially make those instructions harder to keep concise and understandable, creating a possible goal tension.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties: A concerns the entity’s ICT-risk-management framework and operational resilience, while B concerns information supplied by an AI provider to an AI-system user. An entity can maintain the required ICT controls while receiving or using instructions that satisfy B; neither provision requires conduct prohibited by the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Use of a high-risk AI system to make solely automated decisions producing legal or similarly significant effects on individuals.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 22 prohibits subjecting an individual to such a solely automated decision, while Article 27 requires certain deployers to assess the fundamental-rights impacts before putting a high-risk AI system into use. A deployer might therefore view the assessment obligation as permitting or facilitating deployment of a system whose actual decision-making use is prohibited by Article 22.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 27 imposes only a prior assessment and notification duty; it does not authorise the use of the system or require the deployer to make prohibited solely automated decisions. A deployer can comply with Article 27 by assessing the system and then refraining from the prohibited use, or by using it only in circumstances permitted by Article 22’s exceptions.

verdict.shared_subject: Providers of public electronic communications networks or services
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A is framed as an exception to a prohibition on procuring products or services from certain suppliers, and it removes that prohibition for essential and important entities that are communications providers. Provision B imposes a separate duty on those same providers to remove or anonymise traffic data once it is no longer needed for transmitting communications; procuring a supplier does not itself excuse compliance with that data-retention duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different conduct: A concerns whether specified entities are subject to a prohibition on using certain suppliers, while B concerns deletion or anonymisation of traffic data. A provider can both benefit from A's exception and comply with B, including any applicable exceptions in B's second, third, or fifth paragraphs.

Nothing in A exempts an entity from, or conflicts with, the conditions for recognition in B.

verdict.shared_subject: Protection and security of personal/data systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits omitting notification of a personal-data breach when the data are rendered unintelligible through appropriate technical measures. Provision B requires covered entities to maintain ICT-risk controls protecting data confidentiality and handling ICT incidents, which could be argued to create an operational duty that includes responding to breaches that A allows not to notify.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties: A concerns whether a provider must notify affected individuals after a personal-data breach, while B requires a simplified ICT-risk-management framework for specified financial entities. Nothing in B requires notifying individuals, and nothing in A prevents the security, monitoring, detection, and incident-response measures required by B.

verdict.shared_subject: Governance and oversight of ICT third-party risk involving financial entities and critical ICT providers
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A possible tension is that Provision A requires competent authorities under NIS2 to notify the DORA oversight forum when exercising supervisory and enforcement powers concerning an important entity designated as a critical ICT third-party provider, while Provision B places continuing responsibility for compliance and accountability on financial entities using ICT providers. One might therefore ask whether regulatory oversight of the provider could displace or conflict with the financial entity’s own responsibility.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different actors and operate at different levels: Provision A governs cooperation and notification by public authorities, whereas Provision B governs how financial entities manage third-party ICT risk and retain responsibility for their own obligations. An authority’s notification and supervision can coexist with the financial entity’s continuing responsibility; neither provision requires or forbids conduct incompatible with the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Information handling by public authorities in digital-law supervision
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the competent authority to notify the Dutch Data Protection Authority or other competent supervisory authorities without delay when it learns of a possible personal-data breach. Provision B requires notifying authorities to ensure that information obtained under Article 78 is treated confidentially; disclosure to another authority could therefore appear to conflict with confidentiality if the notification information falls within Article 78.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different authorities and address different information flows: A concerns notifying data-protection authorities about a possible GDPR breach, while B concerns confidentiality of information obtained by notifying authorities under Article 78. Notification can be made through confidential channels and therefore can satisfy both provisions; the texts do not establish that Article 78 information includes the information required by A or that confidentiality forbids the notification.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing controllers subject to both the Dutch restrictions on data-subject rights and the GDPR representative requirement
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern a controller and processing of personal data, but they regulate different matters: Article 41 requires the controller to take specified factors into account when applying a restriction, while Article 27(2) states that the representative obligation in Article 27(1) does not apply in listed cases. The strongest tension case is that a controller might treat Article 41's restriction framework as permitting non-compliance with the representative obligation, although Article 27(2) separately removes that obligation only in its own circumstances.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can plainly be obeyed together because Article 41 concerns safeguards and proportionality when restricting data-subject rights, whereas Article 27(2) concerns exceptions to appointing an EU representative. Nothing in Article 41 requires appointment of a representative, and nothing in Article 27(2) prohibits considering the listed safeguards when a lawful restriction is applied.

verdict.shared_subject: National competent authorities acting as lead overseers when inspecting critical third-party ICT service providers
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A lead overseer must normally notify the inspected provider within a reasonable period before a planned on-site inspection, while national competent authorities must comply with confidentiality obligations. If advance notice of the inspection would disclose protected confidential information, the provisions could appear to pull in opposite directions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The inspection provision expressly permits withholding notice where notification would make the inspection ineffective, and the confidentiality provision does not itself prohibit all advance notice. The authority can therefore comply with both by protecting confidential information and applying the inspection rule's stated exception where necessary.

Provision A concerns responding to information requests by critical third-party ICT service providers, while Provision B creates a narrowly conditioned permission and safeguards for high-risk AI providers processing special-category personal data; A does not require disclosure of that data or override B's conditions.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern governmental competence to issue rules or prescriptions, so one might argue that their delegated powers could overlap if the same continuity-plan matter were also governed by NIS2 implementation measures. However, neither text states that the powers are exclusive or that an exercise of one power would prohibit or displace the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A authorizes rules by or under a general administrative measure implementing NIS2 acts and guidance, while Provision B authorizes the Minister to prescribe how a joint continuity plan is established when designated providers cannot agree. verdict.shared_subject: Use of identification by public-service organisations and high-risk AI systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires designated organisations and courts to accept specified identification means when substantial or high authentication is required. Provision B generally prohibits the responsible deployer of certain high-risk AI systems from taking measures or decisions based on the system's identification unless at least two qualified natural persons separately verify and confirm it, so an AI-based identification accepted under A might not by itself support a decision.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different conduct: A concerns which electronic identification means must be accepted for authentication, while B concerns safeguards for measures or decisions based on identification by a high-risk AI system. An organisation can accept an identification means under A and still obtain the separate human verification required by B; A does not require reliance on an AI identification without that verification.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern governmental action in the broad area of cybersecurity and digital regulation, so one might initially suspect overlapping administrative responsibilities. However, provision A requires a national plan for large-scale cyber incidents and crisis response, while provision B requires notifying qualifying conformity-assessment bodies to the Commission and other Member States; the texts impose different duties on different subject matters.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties can plainly be performed together: the Minister can establish the national cyber-incident and crisis-response plan, while notifying authorities separately notify eligible conformity-assessment bodies through the Commission’s electronic system. verdict.shared_subject: Potentially overlapping public bodies or designated organisations that process personal data and transfer it to a third country or international organisation
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the relevant bodies or organisations to obtain and submit an auditor’s statement concerning compliance with specified electronic-services security rules. Provision B prohibits international transfers unless the controller and processor have satisfied the GDPR Chapter V conditions; obtaining an auditor’s statement under A does not itself establish those transfer conditions, so treating A compliance as sufficient could permit a transfer that B forbids.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties with different subject matter: A concerns an audit statement about the operation, reliability and security of access to electronic services, while B independently regulates transfers of personal data to third countries or international organisations. An actor can obtain and submit the audit statement and separately comply with all applicable Chapter V transfer conditions, so both provisions can be satisfied without contradiction.

verdict.shared_subject: Handling information about voluntary vulnerability reports by a coordinator and a competent authority’s investigative powers
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: The coordinator must safeguard the anonymity of the person or entity reporting a vulnerability, while the competent authority may demand access to documents and data relevant to its tasks and obtain copies. If the authority’s requested material identifies the reporter, disclosure could appear to undermine the coordinator’s anonymity duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different actors and address different functions: the coordinator follows up vulnerability reports and protects reporter anonymity, whereas the authority’s power concerns documents and data relevant to its regulatory tasks. The authority’s power does not expressly require disclosure of the reporter’s identity, so both provisions can be complied with by withholding or redacting identifying information where appropriate.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions may be triggered by the same incident: Article 34 permits omitting communication to data subjects in specified circumstances, while Article 13 requires a post-incident evaluation and, for non-micro financial entities, communication to competent authorities of changes made after that evaluation. If the post-incident evaluation or resulting changes contain personal-data breach information, disclosure to the authority could appear to undermine Article 34’s non-communication choice, although Article 13 does not expressly require communication to data subjects.

Provision B independently requires the provider to supply clear, complete and accessible instructions to the deployer, which may entail explaining such information use and any relevant user-consent mechanism.

verdict.shared_subject: Obligations concerning information, documents, and possible reporting by organs or data controllers
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the verwerkingsverantwoordelijke and belanghebbende to comply with a court’s request for written information and documents within the court-set period. verdict.shared_subject: Recognition of an ontsluitende dienst or machtigingsdienst under BWBR0048156
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern ministerial recognition and require compliance with statutory or regulatory conditions. A possible tension is that art. 9 requires refusal where serious danger to cybersecurity, state security, or the reliability and safety of the Dutch electronic-services system exists, while art. 11 says the Minister recognizes the specified service if it satisfies the rules set by or under a general administrative measure; if those rules were satisfied despite such danger, the provisions might appear to point in different directions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Art. 11's recognition condition is expressly tied to compliance with applicable rules, while art. 9 separately makes refusal mandatory for serious overriding reasons. Compliance with the art. 11 rules does not negate art. 9's independent refusal grounds, so both can be satisfied by recognizing only services that meet the rules and do not present the stated serious dangers.

verdict.shared_subject: Acceptance of authentication/identification means for electronic services provided by a bestuursorgaan or aangewezen organisatie.

Article 15, introduced by “Onverminderd het bepaalde in artikel 7,” requires acceptance of all and only recognised business and organisation means and related authorisation statements for access to services to an enterprise or legal person; if one means falls into both categories, the “uitsluitend” wording could appear to impose incompatible acceptance sets.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different service users and authentication contexts: Article 7 concerns natural persons and substantial/high assurance, while Article 15 concerns access on behalf of an enterprise or legal person using business/organisation means. Article 15 expressly preserves Article 7, and the texts do not establish that a single access transaction must simultaneously satisfy both provisions or that the categories overlap incompatibly.

verdict.shared_subject: Cross-border mutual assistance between competent authorities concerning certain digital-service entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A says a competent authority may make a reasoned assistance request to another Member State’s authority for listed entities whose main establishment is there. Provision B says that, in the specified cross-border circumstances, authorities must cooperate and provide assistance when necessary, and that a recipient may not refuse except on stated grounds; this could appear to make A’s discretionary request power part of a broader mandatory assistance regime.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate complementary aspects of the same cooperation mechanism: A authorizes a Dutch authority to request assistance for listed entities, while B requires cooperation and governs when the requested authority must provide assistance. A’s “may request” concerns initiation of a request, not permission to refuse assistance, and B expressly allows refusal where the requested authority lacks competence or another listed exception applies.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A central securities depository must maintain a secondary processing site that is immediately accessible to its personnel and capable of continuing critical functions. If that site contains high-risk AI training, validation, or testing datasets, giving market-surveillance authorities full access to those datasets could expose or disrupt the resilience arrangements, creating a possible tension with maintaining secure, continuously available operations.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different subjects and address different matters: Article 12 governs central securities depositories’ backup and recovery facilities, while Article 74 governs providers of high-risk AI systems and their disclosure to market-surveillance authorities. Even where one entity is subject to both, Article 74 requires access only insofar as relevant and necessary and expressly contemplates security safeguards, so both duties can ordinarily be satisfied.

verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A authorises the competent authority to direct a domain-registration provider to comply with specified statutory provisions, while provision B authorises the Minister to direct an erkende dienst when necessary for reliable access to electronic services. They have different triggers, authorities, and apparent scopes, and both directions can be obeyed unless their concrete contents conflict.

Nothing in B prohibits or alters A’s reporting deadlines, and sanctions for a DORA infringement can coexist with compliance with A.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A exempts certain organisations with fewer than 250 employees from the Article 30 record-of-processing obligations, while provision B requires an immediate, and at latest two-day, notification of a widespread breach or serious incident. If the notification duty required retaining or maintaining records that A exempts, the provisions could pull in different directions, but B itself only imposes a reporting deadline and does not state such a recordkeeping requirement.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different duties: A concerns whether specified organisations must keep a register of processing activities, whereas B concerns when a high-risk AI-system provider or deployer must notify authorities of a serious incident. An organisation can be exempt from the register duty and still make the required incident notification, so both provisions can be satisfied without conflict.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the entity, when giving an early warning about a significant incident, to state specified facts and provide the responsible officer’s contact details. Een entiteit kan haar ICT-risico’s en systemen overeenkomstig artikel 16 beheren en tegelijk de AI-verordening uiterlijk op 31 december 2030 naleven; artikel 111 verbiedt naleving vóór die datum niet.

They address different authorities, duties, and triggers, and nothing in the texts makes the duties mutually exclusive.

Provision B requires a financial entity’s governing body to establish and oversee ICT-risk-management arrangements, including policies for data integrity and confidentiality. One might argue that a governance arrangement could involve such a facility, but B does not require or authorise providing incorrect information.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A imposes a specific prohibition on misleading information about network-identification details, while provision B assigns governance and ICT-risk responsibilities to the governing body of a financial entity. The governing body can satisfy B by adopting and overseeing arrangements that comply with A, including truthful use of the facility.

Provision B nevertheless makes the AP and ACM obliged, when requested, to provide each other data necessary to execute the relevant law, potentially creating an apparent conflict if an excluded provision would have limited that disclosure.

verdict.shared_subject: Cooperation and exchange of information between supervisory authorities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern supervisory cooperation and assistance, and Article 19 imposes a duty to provide necessary personal-data-processing information to the specified authorities. If assistance under Article 68 required withholding such information, the duties could point in opposite directions, but no such withholding rule appears in the texts shown.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 68 assigns officials the task of assisting a competent authority of another EU Member State, while Article 19 authorizes and, when requested, requires the AP and other supervisors to exchange necessary information with each other. The provisions can operate cumulatively: information sharing under Article 19 can support the assistance required by Article 68, subject to any applicable legal limits not shown here.

verdict.shared_subject: Cybersecurity incidents and vulnerabilities involving cooperation or information exchange by public authorities/CSIRTs
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can involve the same underlying cybersecurity event: a vulnerability may cause an incident involving a personal-data breach. In that situation, cooperation and information exchange under Article 58 could potentially disclose personal data while the coordinating CSIRT must preserve the reporting person’s anonymity under Article 12, creating a possible tension if the reporter’s identity is among the necessary data exchanged.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose complementary duties on different institutional mechanisms: Article 58 concerns cooperation with the Dutch data-protection authority when incidents lead to personal-data breaches, while Article 12 concerns coordinated vulnerability disclosure and protection of the vulnerability reporter’s anonymity. Article 58 requires only data that are necessary for handling the incident, so both duties can ordinarily be satisfied by sharing necessary incident information while withholding or anonymising the reporter’s identity.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A person anonymously reports a vulnerability to the designated CSIRT; exploitation of that vulnerability later causes a personal-data breach, and the CSIRT and another competent authority must cooperate with the Dutch data-protection authority. The issue would arise if the reporter’s identity were considered necessary data for handling the breach and Article 58 therefore required its exchange, while Article 12 required the CSIRT to preserve the reporter’s anonymity.
verdict.missing_reference: The provision governing whether, and under what conditions, the reporter’s identity may be disclosed despite Article 12’s anonymity guarantee—such as an applicable exception to that guarantee or a rule defining the scope of “all necessary data” under Article 58—is not shown.
verdict.decisive_exception: Any exception in the applicable vulnerability-reporting or data-protection rules permitting disclosure of an anonymous reporter’s identity to the data-protection authority for incident handling would resolve the apparent conflict.

verdict.shared_subject: Bevoegde autoriteiten en maatregelen tegen niet-naleving of ICT-risico’s
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Beide bepalingen geven bevoegde autoriteiten ingrijpende bevoegdheden tegenover entiteiten: A kan bestuurders laten schorsen zolang een besluit niet wordt nageleefd, terwijl B een financiële entiteit kan verplichten een kritieke ICT-dienst tijdelijk te staken of het contract te beëindigen. In een concreet geval kunnen zulke maatregelen de continuïteit van dezelfde entiteit of haar bestuur beïnvloeden, maar geen van beide bepalingen verbiedt of verhindert de andere maatregel.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: De bepalingen hebben verschillende adressaten, triggers en maatregelen: A betreft schorsing van bestuursleden van een essentiële entiteit wegens niet-uitvoering van een besluit, terwijl B ziet op een financiële entiteit en het staken of beëindigen van diensten van een kritieke ICT-aanbieder wegens niet-verholpen ICT-risico’s. Beide bevoegdheden kunnen naast elkaar worden uitgeoefend; de teksten stellen geen onverenigbare verplichtingen of exclusiviteit vast.

verdict.shared_subject: Notification of a personal-data breach to data subjects versus reporting a significant incident to cybersecurity authorities or, where applicable, service recipients
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A significant incident may also be a personal-data breach, and Article 34 says communication to data subjects is not required when one of its conditions is met, including that the data were rendered unintelligible or that communication would require disproportionate effort. Article 23 nevertheless requires affected entities, where applicable, to inform service recipients of significant incidents, so the same event could appear to require recipient notification despite Article 34 dispensing with data-subject communication.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different communications with different triggers and recipients: Article 34 concerns communication to data subjects about a personal-data breach, while Article 23 primarily requires reporting significant incidents to a CSIRT or competent authority and only conditionally concerns recipients of services. Article 23 does not require disclosure of personal data or necessarily require communication to every data subject, so both duties can be performed without contradiction.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing and transparency obligations concerning personal data, potentially including special-category or criminal-offence data.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits the prohibition on processing special-category and criminal-offence data by a commission or advisory body to be inapplicable when its stated conditions are met. Provision B separately requires the controller to provide extensive information when personal data were not obtained from the data subject, so processing permitted under A may entail disclosure and transparency duties under B. However, B does not prohibit the processing permitted by A, and A does not exempt the controller from B.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative rules: A concerns when a processing prohibition does not apply, while B concerns information that must be supplied when data were obtained indirectly. A commission can satisfy A's safeguards and still provide the information required by B; the more specific permission in A does not displace B's independent transparency obligation.

verdict.shared_subject: Protection and handling of personal data in the event of a personal-data breach
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires measures protecting personal data against unauthorized access and other forms of unauthorized processing, while Provision B permits withholding notice of a high-risk breach when appropriate protective measures were applied, especially measures making the data unintelligible to unauthorized persons. One might argue that A's security obligation and B's non-notification rule pull in opposite directions by treating the same protective measures differently, but B does not prohibit any measure required by A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can both be satisfied: an organisation can implement A's access controls, protection measures, and security policy, and B can then exempt it from notifying affected persons if the specific conditions in B are met. B regulates whether notification is required after a breach; A regulates baseline security measures, so the duties are complementary rather than incompatible.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulatory information and reporting involving EU financial-sector authorities and providers of general-purpose AI models
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern the production of information in an EU regulatory context, so an entity involved in both regimes might need to coordinate confidential reporting with responses to information requests. If the requested information overlapped, disclosure could potentially raise confidentiality or timing concerns.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A imposes a periodic reporting duty on the ESAs concerning discussions with third-country authorities, while provision B requires providers of general-purpose AI models or their representatives to supply requested information. They impose duties on different actors, with no prohibition, incompatible deadline, confidentiality rule, or other conflicting requirement shown.

verdict.shared_subject: Legal proceedings and cooperation involving authorities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A bars any legal remedy against the Council of State’s handling of the request, while provision B requires a requested supervisory authority to inform the requesting authority about results or progress. One might argue that the bar on remedies prevents the requesting authority from challenging inadequate handling of the request.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different matters: A concerns the availability of a legal remedy against a specific judicial handling of a request, whereas B governs administrative mutual assistance between supervisory authorities. The duty to provide information can be fulfilled without any legal proceeding, so both provisions can be obeyed simultaneously.

verdict.shared_subject: Recognition and acceptance of a bedrijfs- or organisatiemiddel at a specified betrouwbaarheidsniveau
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 11 requires the Minister to recognize a means issuer when the service and means satisfy the rules set by or under a general administrative measure. Article 15 prohibits an acceptance decision for a means that fails the security and reliability requirements for the substantial or high assurance level, so a possible tension would arise if Article 11's recognition rules permitted recognition despite failure of those Article 15 requirements.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different decisions: Article 11 concerns recognition of an issuer and its service/means, while Article 15 concerns a later acceptance decision concerning the means itself. Recognition under Article 11 can comply with Article 15 by ensuring that any subsequent acceptance decision is not made unless the substantial or high-level security and reliability requirements are met; the texts do not require acceptance of a non-compliant means.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Onze Minister erkent een middelenuitgever met betrekking tot een door die dienst uit te geven bedrijfs- en organisatiemiddel en het bijbehorende betrouwbaarheidsniveau, indien de dienst en het middel voldoen aan de daartoe bij of krachtens algemene maatregel van bestuur gestelde regels.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Een besluit als bedoeld in het vijfde lid wordt niet genomen ten aanzien van een bedrijfs- of organisatiemiddel dat niet voldoet aan de voor het betrouwbaarheidsniveau substantieel of hoog gestelde eisen ten aanzien van veiligheid en betrouwbaarheid.

verdict.shared_subject: The bodies’ performance of their respective tasks
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions regulate how an institutional body performs its tasks: Provision A requires the secretariat to act exclusively on the chair’s instructions, while Provision B requires the Cooperation Group to act on biennial work programmes. If the secretariat were responsible for carrying out Cooperation Group tasks, a work programme could require action not instructed by the chair, creating a possible conflict in operational direction.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions concern different bodies and different sources of direction: the secretariat follows the Committee chair’s instructions, whereas the Cooperation Group performs its tasks on the basis of its work programmes. Nothing shown states that the secretariat performs the Cooperation Group’s tasks or that a work programme can contradict the chair’s instructions, so both rules can be complied with independently.

verdict.evidence_span_b: De samenwerkingsgroep voert zijn taken uit op basis van de in lid 7 bedoelde tweejaarlijkse werkprogramma’s.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern regulated digital-service institutions and could superficially be associated with institutional governance. However, Article 14 regulates transfer of an accreditation, while Article 54 regulates professional secrecy by supervisory-authority members and staff; neither imposes a duty or prohibition that conflicts with the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: An accredited service may be transferred only subject to the conditions and ministerial refusal grounds in Article 14, while supervisory-authority personnel must keep confidential information secret under Article 54. A transfer decision can comply with Article 14 without disclosing confidential information, and Article 54 does not prohibit or require any transfer.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits using a network-connection or user-identification facility to provide the called user with incorrect information about the connection point or individual user. Provision B requires informing a data subject about appropriate safeguards when personal data are transferred to a third country or international organisation. The provisions concern different conduct and do not establish that complying with the information right requires providing incorrect information.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: An actor could comply with both by providing accurate information about the network connection point or user while separately informing the data subject of the Article 46 safeguards for any relevant international transfer. Nothing in Provision B authorises or requires inaccurate information, and Provision A does not prohibit accurate information about safeguards.

verdict.shared_subject: Electronic-service providers and regulatory requirements
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern rules that may be imposed on service providers, and an erkende dienst could potentially also be an aanbieder of openbare elektronische communicatienetwerken or diensten. In that overlap, a ministerial exemption from rules under article 13 might appear to weaken or conflict with requirements imposed by an order in council under article 11a.1.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A authorizes an exemption from rules under its own article 13 when those rules obstruct technological developments concerning reliable access to electronic services. Provision B separately authorizes additional rules and requirements concerning measures for ensuring service availability during network outages or force majeure; nothing shown makes those requirements subject to, or displaced by, the exemption in A.

verdict.evidence_span_b: Bij of krachtens algemene maatregel van bestuur kunnen nadere regels worden gegeven met betrekking tot de in het eerste en derde lid bedoelde maatregelen en kunnen eisen worden gesteld aan aanbieders van openbare elektronische communicatienetwerken en openbare elektronische communicatiediensten.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern institutional arrangements around recognition or assessment, so one might argue that an authority recognizing an authentication service could also be subject to the AI Act’s impartiality requirements. However, the texts do not establish that the Dutch Minister is an “aanmeldende autoriteit” or that the authentication service is a conformity-assessment body.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A governs when the Minister recognizes an authentication service based on compliance with reliability-level rules. Provision B governs the establishment and functioning of notifying authorities, specifically requiring avoidance of conflicts with conformity-assessment bodies; the provisions impose no incompatible duty or permission on the same actor.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Onze Minister erkent een authenticatiedienst op het betrouwbaarheidsniveau van het bedrijfs- en organisatiemiddel waarvoor hij erkend wenst te worden, indien de dienst voldoet aan de daartoe voor dat betrouwbaarheidsniveau bij of krachtens algemene maatregel van bestuur gestelde regels.

verdict.shared_subject: The provision and disclosure of subscriber or location data in emergency communications
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a communications provider to transmit the caller’s number and available subscriber or public-payphone address data to designated emergency-number managers. Under the GDPR definition, that transmission is processing of personal data, and Provision B requires the controller to provide specified information and communications to the data subject in a transparent and accessible form; one might therefore argue that emergency disclosure creates a GDPR transparency issue, especially where immediate disclosure occurs without prior notice.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B governs how information and communications concerning processing are given to the data subject, whereas Provision A governs the provider’s substantive duty to transmit emergency-call identification and address data to designated emergency-number managers. The texts impose no incompatible act, deadline, or content requirement: a provider can transmit the emergency data and separately provide GDPR information in the required form, subject to the GDPR provisions governing when that information is required or may be limited.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern legal or institutional arrangements, but they regulate different matters: provision A governs a court’s handling of a request, while provision B concerns adding categories of organisations by governmental order. No actor is placed under incompatible duties by the texts.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: A court can decide a request and, where necessary, hear interested parties under provision A, while the competent ministers can propose adding categories of organisations providing certain electronic services under provision B. These obligations and powers operate independently and can both be exercised without conflict.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose obligations involving institutional oversight: Article 46 requires a supervisory authority to apply the consistency mechanism in specified cases, while Article 34 requires notified bodies to check high-risk AI systems under Article 43 procedures. One might argue that an institution could face competing procedural demands, but the texts identify different actors, subject matters, and triggers.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can plainly be obeyed together because Article 46 concerns a supervisory authority handling appropriate safeguards for transfers of personal data, whereas Article 34 concerns notified bodies assessing conformity of high-risk AI systems. Nothing in either provision requires or prohibits conduct that conflicts with the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Entities and governmental bodies involved in the respective statutory schemes
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A allows the competent minister to exempt certain essential or important entities from obligations under article 21, while provision B requires costs related to articles 5 and 9 to be charged to specified bodies. If the costs under provision B are themselves an obligation under article 21, an exemption under A might appear to remove the basis for charging them.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different matters: A concerns a ministerial power to grant exemptions from obligations under article 21 of BWBR0052872, whereas B concerns charging costs incurred in implementing articles 5 and 9 of BWBR0048156. Nothing in the texts establishes that B's cost-charging rule is an obligation covered by A's exemption or that the same actor must both be exempted and charged.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Onze Minister die het aangaat kan bij regeling of besluit, in overeenstemming met Onze Minister, een essentiële entiteit respectievelijk een belangrijke entiteit die activiteiten uitvoert op het gebied van nationale veiligheid, openbare veiligheid, defensie of rechtshandhaving of die uitsluitend diensten verleent aan een overheidsinstantie als bedoeld in artikel 5, eerste lid, met betrekking tot die activiteiten of diensten ontheffen van de verplichtingen, bedoeld in artikel 21.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De kosten die het Rijk maakt samenhangend met de uitvoering van de artikelen 5 en 9 worden door Onze Minister ten laste gebracht van de bestuursorganen, aangewezen organisaties en andere organen die het betreft.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A extends certain requirements concerning information stored on, or access to information on, an end device to situations where that result is achieved by means other than an electronic communications network. Provision B imposes confidentiality and professional-secrecy duties on notified bodies and their personnel, so disclosure of information obtained during conformity-assessment activities could appear to conflict if the information is also covered by A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different subject matters and actors: A extends requirements concerning storage or access to information on an end device, while B governs confidentiality by notified bodies during conformity-assessment activities. Nothing in A requires disclosure, and B itself permits disclosure where legally required, so both can be complied with without any identified conflict.

verdict.shared_subject: Use of a public identification means in connection with electronic services and GDPR transparency communications
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 8 restricts use of the public identification means and related facility to access to electronic services provided by public authorities and designated organisations. Article 12 GDPR may require a controller to provide information or communications electronically, but it does not require use of that particular public identification means, so the texts do not create an actual incompatibility.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: A controller can comply with Article 12 by providing the required information or communication in writing or by other appropriate means, including electronic means, without using the public identification means for any purpose outside Article 8. If the communication concerns access to a qualifying public electronic service, use of the means for that access is also permitted by Article 8.
