verdict.shared_subject: Processing of special-category personal data by providers of high-risk AI systems established outside the EU
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A exempts certain non-EU controllers or processors from the obligation to appoint an EU representative when the processing is not large-scale processing of special-category data. Provision B exceptionally permits providers of certain high-risk AI systems to process special-category data for bias detection, so the same activity may fall within B while appearing to qualify for A’s exemption.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different duties: A concerns appointment of an EU representative, while B regulates the conditions for processing special-category data. B expressly requires compliance with Regulation 2016/679, and its processing may be large-scale or otherwise high-risk, in which case A’s exemption would not apply; the texts do not require or forbid the same conduct.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulatory obligations concerning ICT/AI-related entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose governance and documentation-related obligations in technology contexts, so an entity involved in both financial ICT risk management and general-purpose AI could face overlapping compliance work. However, the duties concern different subject matters and are addressed to different categories of entities, without any incompatible requirement.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 16 requires certain exempt financial entities to maintain an ICT-risk-management framework and related operational controls, while Article 53 requires providers of general-purpose AI models to prepare model documentation, downstream-provider information, copyright policies, and training-content summaries. An entity subject to both can perform all of these duties simultaneously; neither provision requires conduct that the other prohibits.

verdict.shared_subject: The powers and duties of public authorities under the Data Act and the GDPR
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A assigns the ACM responsibility for implementing Article 10(6) of the Data Act, while provision B gives every supervisory authority GDPR corrective powers. If the ACM is also acting as a GDPR supervisory authority, the instruments could appear to allocate overlapping enforcement functions. However, neither text requires or forbids a particular action, and A does not specify the content of Article 10(6).
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can readily be satisfied together: A is an institutional implementation obligation concerning the Data Act, whereas B is a list of GDPR corrective powers for supervisory authorities. They concern different legal instruments and do not prescribe incompatible conduct, deadlines, or limits.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions use confidentiality or access-related language, but they regulate different actors and duties. A domain-name registry or registrar must answer a justified access request within 72 hours, while a notified conformity-assessment body must keep information confidential subject to stated exceptions; the texts do not make the registry or registrar a notified body, nor do they establish that the requested information is information held during conformity-assessment activities.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can plainly be obeyed together because they apply to different institutional roles and regulate different subject matters. Provision A concerns access to domain-registration data by registries and registrars; Provision B concerns confidentiality procedures and professional secrecy for notified conformity-assessment bodies.

verdict.shared_subject: Use of ICT or AI-model services by financial entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires financial entities to manage third-party ICT risk proportionately, while provision B states that a particular obligation does not apply to certain open-source general-purpose AI-model providers unless the models present systemic risks. A financial entity might therefore rely on a provider benefiting from B's non-application while still having to manage the resulting third-party ICT risk under A. However, B concerns the provider's obligation, not the financial entity's risk-management duty, so the texts do not establish an actual incompatibility.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different subjects and regulate different matters: A governs a financial entity's management of third-party ICT risk, whereas B creates an exception from an obligation applicable to providers of general-purpose AI models. A financial entity can comply with A regardless of whether the provider's obligation under B applies.

verdict.shared_subject: An organisation using a high-risk AI system that processes personal data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose accountability-related obligations on an overlapping operator, but they require different assessments or measures: GDPR Article 24 requires risk-based technical and organisational measures ensuring and demonstrating compliance, while Article 27 requires updating a fundamental-rights impact assessment when listed elements change. It is arguable that the operator faces two potentially overlapping, differently framed compliance duties, although neither text says that satisfying one substitutes for the other or sets incompatible benchmarks.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties address different objects and can readily be performed together. Article 24 concerns general GDPR-compliance measures for personal-data processing, whereas Article 27 concerns updating a specific fundamental-rights impact assessment for a high-risk AI system; updating that assessment can itself form part of the Article 24 measures without conflicting with them.

verdict.shared_subject: Communication to service recipients or data subjects following a significant cyber threat or personal-data breach
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A significant cyber threat may involve a personal-data breach, while Article 34 permits withholding communication to the data subject in specified circumstances. Article 23 nevertheless requires an essential or important entity to promptly communicate measures, and if necessary the threat itself, to potentially affected service recipients; this could create an apparent overlap where the same person is both a data subject and service recipient.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different triggers, recipients, and purposes: Article 34 concerns notification of a personal-data breach to data subjects, whereas Article 23 concerns communicating protective measures or the cyber threat to service recipients. Article 34's exceptions do not prohibit separate cybersecurity communications under Article 23, and Article 23 does not expressly require disclosure of the personal-data-breach information covered by Article 34.

verdict.shared_subject: Automated or AI-assisted decisions affecting natural persons
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 22 gives the affected person a right not to be subjected to a solely automated decision with legal or similarly significant effects. Article 14 instead requires proportionate human-oversight measures for high-risk AI systems, but those measures may be designed or implemented without necessarily providing that particular person with a human decision-maker or review.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can operate cumulatively: an operator can design and use human oversight under Article 14 while also ensuring that decisions covered by Article 22 are not solely automated. Article 14 does not expressly authorise solely automated significant decisions or purport to replace Article 22's individual right.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A provider deploys a high-risk AI system used by a bank to automatically reject a person's loan application, with legal or similarly significant effects. The provider documents proportionate oversight measures and makes them available for the deployer, but the rejected person is still subjected to the decision without an actual human decision-maker reviewing that person's case.

verdict.shared_subject: Automated decision-making and human oversight
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 22 gives the data subject a right not to be subjected to a solely automated decision with legal or similarly significant effects. Article 26 requires a high-risk AI operator to assign human oversight to qualified persons, but that system-level assignment may not itself prevent a particular significant decision from being made solely automatically or give the affected person a usable route to invoke human intervention.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be satisfied together: an operator can assign qualified, authorised human overseers and ensure that significant decisions are not solely automated, thereby respecting Article 22. Article 26 is a preventive organisational safeguard, while Article 22 is an individual protection, and the texts do not expressly require incompatible conduct.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A company uses a high-risk AI system to automatically reject a person's loan application, producing a legally or similarly significant effect, while it has formally assigned qualified and authorised human overseers under Article 26 but provides no mechanism for that person to obtain human review before or after the rejection. The person is subjected to the solely automated decision despite the operator's compliance with the system-level oversight assignment.
verdict.decisive_exception: Article 22(2)'s exceptions could permit the automated decision if their conditions are met, but those exceptions are not part of the compared provision text and Article 26 does not establish that any of them applies.

verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different conduct: Article 22 concerns the individual's exposure to a qualifying solely automated decision, whereas Article 10 concerns the provider's exceptional processing of special-category data for bias detection and correction. verdict.shared_subject: Information and cybersecurity assistance concerning electronic services
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern information connected with cybersecurity or secure electronic services. A CSIRT may monitor, analyse, and assist an essential or important entity, while B requires the Minister to provide data and information to specified bodies or service providers when necessary for their tasks; in a concrete case, the information handled by the CSIRT could overlap with information the Minister must disclose.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different actors and do not prescribe incompatible treatment of the same information. A assigns CSIRT monitoring, analysis, assistance, and information-sharing tasks, while B authorises or requires ministerial information provision only insofar as necessary for specified statutory tasks or services; both can be performed with appropriate lawful information-sharing and confidentiality safeguards.

verdict.shared_subject: An entity that is both subject to NIS2 registration/reporting duties and an AI Act provider of a high-risk AI system
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the entity to provide identifying and contact information and promptly report changes to competent authorities. Provision B restricts exceptional processing of special-category personal data and permits it only for narrowly necessary bias detection and correction under multiple safeguards; an entity’s reporting duty could involve contact details relating to individuals, but A does not require or authorize processing of special-category data.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different subject matter: A concerns registration information about an entity and its services, while B concerns exceptional processing of special-category personal data by providers of certain high-risk AI systems. The entity can comply with A using ordinary organizational and contact information without processing special-category data, while separately complying with B’s conditions if such processing is undertaken.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern regulatory information flows involving authorities, so one might initially suspect overlapping reporting or documentation burdens. However, Article 44 concerns the ESAs’ periodic confidential report on discussions with third-country authorities, while Article 23 concerns importers’ responses and technical documentation for competent authorities regarding high-risk AI systems.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties have different actors, triggers, recipients, purposes, and subject matter: ESAs must submit a joint report every five years, whereas importers must provide information and make technical documentation available upon a reasoned request. An importer can comply with Article 23 without affecting the ESAs’ Article 44 report, and vice versa.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing biometric data in real-time remote biometric identification for law-enforcement purposes in public spaces
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 9 prohibits processing biometric data for uniquely identifying a person, while Article 5(h) permits real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law-enforcement purposes when strictly necessary for specified objectives. Thus, the same deployment may appear permitted under Article 5(h) but prohibited under Article 9 unless an Article 9(2) exception independently applies.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 5(h) expressly states that it does not affect Article 9 GDPR for processing biometric data for purposes other than law enforcement, and its permission is limited to strictly necessary law-enforcement uses. The provisions can therefore operate cumulatively: an Article 5(h) exception does not itself displace the Article 9 prohibition, and the operator must also satisfy an applicable Article 9(2) condition.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A police authority deploys real-time facial-recognition cameras in a public square to identify a person suspected of a qualifying serious offence. The use is strictly necessary, proportionate, and judicially authorised under Article 5(h), but it processes biometric data for unique identification and no fact establishes that an Article 9(2) exception applies; the authority therefore faces Article 5 permission alongside Article 9's prohibition.
verdict.decisive_exception: An applicable exception to Article 9(1), such as Article 9(2)(g) (substantial public interest under Union or Member State law with appropriate safeguards), is not established by the provisions shown. Article 5(h)'s strict-necessity conditions and authorisation do not themselves establish that Article 9(2) exception.

verdict.shared_subject: Cross-border mutual assistance and cooperation between supervisory authorities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions regulate cooperation and mutual assistance between authorities, but they impose different formulations and procedural conditions. A possible tension is that Provision A broadly requires authorities to provide relevant information and assistance, while Provision B permits refusal of a requested assistance in specified circumstances and requires proportionality to the requested authority’s resources.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be satisfied together because they concern different regulatory regimes and authorities, and Provision A’s general cooperation duty can operate subject to applicable limits such as competence, proportionality, and essential national-security interests. Provision B’s more detailed refusal grounds do not expressly require an authority to violate Provision A; they can define when assistance is not required under that regime.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing special-category personal data in high-risk AI systems, particularly biometric data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 5 prohibits certain biometric categorisation practices, including categorisation intended to infer sensitive characteristics, while Article 10 exceptionally permits providers of certain high-risk systems to process special-category personal data for bias detection and correction. A system could therefore process biometric or other special-category data for bias-related purposes while its use also falls within one of Article 5’s biometric prohibitions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 10 is narrowly limited to processing strictly necessary for detecting and correcting bias in specified high-risk systems, requires that other data cannot achieve that purpose, and imposes extensive safeguards. Article 5 does not generally prohibit all processing of special-category data; its prohibitions target specified AI practices, so Article 10 may operate without conflict where the system’s conduct does not fall within one of those practices.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A provider operates a high-risk biometric categorisation system and processes users’ biometric data revealing racial or religious characteristics to test and correct bias. The processing may be permitted under Article 10 if its conditions are met, but the system’s biometric categorisation for inferring those characteristics is prohibited by Article 5(g), leaving the relationship between the Article 10 permission and the Article 5 prohibition unresolved.
verdict.decisive_exception: The text does not establish whether Article 10’s exceptional permission to process special-category data for bias detection and correction constitutes an applicable exception to Article 5(g)’s prohibition on biometric categorisation intended to infer race, political opinions, trade-union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life, or sexual orientation; nor does it establish whether the processing can be separated from the prohibited categorisation use.

verdict.shared_subject: The Autoriteit Consument en Markt (ACM) and its implementation of EU Data Act obligations
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern the ACM, but they impose different-looking obligations: Article 11.8a requires the ACM, when recording measures, to take the European Commission’s comments and recommendations into account as much as possible, while Article 2 requires it to implement Article 10(6) of the Data Act. If Article 10(6) required implementation inconsistent with those Commission comments or recommendations, the ACM might face competing instructions. The texts shown, however, do not establish any such inconsistency.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can readily be satisfied together: the ACM can implement Article 10(6) of the Data Act while taking relevant Commission comments and recommendations into account when recording its measures. Article 2 merely identifies an implementation duty and does not prescribe conduct incompatible with Article 11.8a.
verdict.missing_reference: The content of Article 10(6) of Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 and the relevant European Commission comments or recommendations would be needed to assess any concrete inconsistency.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Bij het vastleggen van de maatregelen houdt de Autoriteit Consument en Markt zoveel mogelijk rekening met de door de Europese Commissie gemaakte opmerkingen en aanbevelingen.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De Autoriteit Consument en Markt geeft uitvoering aan artikel 10, zesde lid, van de dataverordening.

verdict.shared_subject: Organisations processing personal data while providing electronic public services
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires certain organisations to provide the Minister with data and information needed to prevent or end breaches affecting secure and reliable electronic access. Provision B exempts some organisations with fewer than 250 employees from the register-of-processing-activities obligation, potentially leaving them without the Article 30 register that would document relevant processing information. The strongest tension case is therefore that a small covered organisation may have to disclose information to the Minister while not having to maintain the GDPR register from which that information might be drawn.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties with different triggers and purposes: A concerns supplying information to the Minister when needed for secure electronic access, whereas B concerns whether a controller must maintain a processing-activities register. Article 30's exemption does not prohibit collecting or supplying information, and A does not require that the information come from an Article 30 register, so both duties can be satisfied independently.

verdict.shared_subject: ICT security and personal-data breach management
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern security controls, so one might argue that the testing duty in Article 25 could affect whether the protective measures relevant to Article 34 are adequate. However, Article 34 regulates communication to data subjects after a personal-data breach, while Article 25 requires a testing programme; neither text sets a conflicting standard, deadline, or consequence for the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can plainly be satisfied together: an entity can perform the listed ICT tests and, if a personal-data breach occurs, apply Article 34's communication rule or one of its stated exceptions. Testing does not itself require disclosure, prevent disclosure, or establish that disclosure is unnecessary.

verdict.shared_subject: Notification to individuals after a personal-data breach by a provider of a public electronic communications service
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the provider to notify the affected person immediately when the breach is likely to have adverse consequences for that person's privacy. Provision B says notification is not required in several circumstances, including effective protective measures, remedial measures eliminating the high risk, or disproportionate effort, so the same breach could appear to require notification under A but permit non-notification under B.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be read as operating with different thresholds and scopes: A concerns likely adverse effects on privacy and a provider covered by the Dutch provision, while B concerns a controller's high risk to rights and freedoms and expressly supplies exceptions. The contextual Dutch paragraph also contains an encryption-based exception, suggesting that the regimes may be reconciled through applicable exceptions rather than imposing an unavoidable contradiction.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A public electronic communications provider suffers a breach exposing customers' personal data, with likely adverse consequences for their privacy but without a high risk to their broader rights and freedoms; the provider invokes Article 34(3)'s exception for protective measures or disproportionate effort and does not notify, while Article 11.3a independently requires immediate notification. The shown texts do not establish that Article 34's exceptions displace the Dutch obligation.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the GDPR Article 34(3) exceptions, or the Dutch provision's own encryption exception in lid 5, legally displace or qualify the immediate-notification duty in Article 11.3a; that relationship is not established by the provisions shown.

verdict.shared_subject: Electronic storage or access to information in a user's terminal equipment and the data subject's GDPR access right
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can concern the same online activity involving personal data: A conditions terminal-equipment storage or access on information and consent, while B gives the data subject a right to be informed about appropriate safeguards when personal data are transferred to a third country or international organisation. A's consent condition and information requirement do not expressly ensure that the individual receives the specific transfer-safeguards information required by B.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulatively satisfiable requirements. A regulates when terminal-equipment storage or access is permitted; B applies when personal data are transferred to a third country or international organisation and requires information about Article 46 safeguards, so compliance with A does not prevent compliance with B.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of personal data, including possible special-category personal data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A states that the prohibition on processing special-category personal data does not apply only in the listed circumstances, while Provision B requires information to be provided when personal data were obtained from someone other than the data subject. If the data covered by B are special-category data and none of A’s listed exceptions applies, informing the data subject under B could appear to presuppose or accompany prohibited processing.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B does not authorize processing special-category data; it only sets information deadlines for a controller where personal data were not obtained from the data subject. Provision A permits processing in the listed cases, and the texts do not require a controller to process data merely to provide the information, so both provisions can generally be complied with without conflict.

verdict.shared_subject: Who bears the costs of a security scan or safety inspection
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern a security-related examination, but they assign its costs to different actors: provision A assigns the security-scan costs to the competent authority, while provision B allows the Minister to impose an independent safety inspection whose costs are borne by the provider. If the same provider and examination fall under both provisions, the cost allocation appears incompatible.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions may concern different examinations and different statutory regimes: A concerns a 'beveiligingsscan' paid for by the competent authority, whereas B concerns an independently performed 'veiligheidscontrole' that the Minister may impose on a specified provider. They can therefore both operate if A's scan and B's inspection are separate measures, or if their scopes do not overlap.
verdict.missing_reference: The provision defining the scope and cost rule for the competent authority's 'beveiligingsscan'—in particular whether it applies to the same provider and the same independent 'veiligheidscontrole' imposed under art. 11a.3—is needed to determine whether the cost obligations overlap.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of personal data by providers of trust services, including direct-marketing processing
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A restricts trust-service providers to processing personal data obtained from the data subject or with explicit consent, and only when required for the trust service. Provision B requires cessation of processing for direct-marketing purposes when the data subject objects; if a trust-service provider otherwise processes such data for direct marketing, A's source/necessity limits and B's objection prohibition could both affect the same processing.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, sequential conditions rather than incompatible commands: A limits when the provider may process personal data, while B adds that direct-marketing processing must stop after an objection. A provider can comply with both by not conducting non-required direct marketing and, in any event, stopping it upon objection.

verdict.shared_subject: Information to the data subject about a transfer of health records and the recipient’s safeguards when data are transferred to a third country or international organisation.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions address informing the data subject about a transfer, but they require different information: provision A requires information about the transfer and applicable rights, while provision B requires information about the appropriate safeguards under Article 46. In a transfer of health records to a third country, an operator might be uncertain whether the general information required by A must also include the Article 46 safeguards required by B.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties are cumulative and can readily be performed together: the operator can inform the person about the transfer and applicable rights and also provide information about the appropriate Article 46 safeguards. Neither provision forbids the additional information required by the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Whether a small organisation must maintain a GDPR record of processing while operating ICT-activity detection mechanisms
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A exempts organisations with fewer than 250 employees from the referenced record-keeping obligations unless specified conditions apply. Provision B requires financial entities to have and regularly test mechanisms for detecting anomalous activities and ICT-related incidents, which may involve processing personal data and could therefore make one of A's exceptions applicable. However, B does not itself require or forbid a GDPR record, so the strongest case is only a possible overlap in compliance burdens, not an actual contradiction.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties: A defines when the GDPR register obligations do not apply, while B requires ICT-detection mechanisms for financial entities. A financial entity can operate and test those mechanisms while also keeping a register if an exception to the small-organisation exemption applies, or without that register if no exception applies; nothing in B prohibits the register or makes compliance with A impossible.

verdict.shared_subject: Technical and organizational continuity/security measures for regulated entities or providers
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern technical or organizational measures, and an entity that is also a covered provider might face measures specified under the general care-duty framework as well as a ministerial order under the continuity-plan regime. The texts, however, do not prescribe incompatible measures, benchmarks, deadlines, or outcomes.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A authorizes further rules and requirements concerning measures under a care duty, while Provision B permits the Minister to impose a measure when a provider's continuity plan is insufficient. A provider can comply with both: additional continuity measures can coexist with requirements made under the other framework, and neither provision forbids compliance with the other.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions mention duties involving competent authorities and organizational processes, but they regulate different actors and different subject matters. Provision A concerns certification bodies notifying supervisory authorities about certification decisions; provision B concerns financial entities evaluating serious ICT incidents and, on request, reporting resulting changes.

A certification body can notify authorities under Provision A while a financial entity performs post-incident evaluations and communicates implemented changes under Provision B.

verdict.shared_subject: High-risk AI systems that process special-category personal data and make solely automated decisions significantly affecting individuals
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 22 GDPR gives the affected person a right not to be subjected to a solely automated decision with legal or similarly significant effects. Article 10 AI Act permits exceptional processing of special-category data for bias detection in high-risk AI systems, but that permission does not itself establish that an affected person can avoid or obtain protection from such an automated decision.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different conduct: Article 22 concerns the individual's exposure to a qualifying solely automated decision, while Article 10 concerns exceptional processing of special-category data for bias detection and correction. Article 10's safeguards, together with the GDPR provisions it expressly preserves, could allow the provider to detect bias without necessarily making a prohibited decision or could support compliance with Article 22.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A provider operates a high-risk hiring AI system that uses health or biometric data solely to test and correct bias, while the system makes solely automated hiring decisions that significantly affect applicants. The provider may satisfy Article 10's necessity, security, access-control, deletion, and documentation requirements, yet an applicant may still be subjected to the automated decision without the individual being able to invoke Article 22's protection; whether a GDPR exception permits that decision is not established by the provisions shown.
verdict.decisive_exception: The decisive issue is whether an exception to GDPR Article 22(1), particularly Article 22(2)(b) (an applicable Union or Member State legal provision with appropriate safeguards), applies; the supplied Article 22(2) context is not part of the compared provision and Article 10 does not establish that exception.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulatory enforcement powers and monetary sanctions
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern monetary enforcement measures, and their maximum amounts are calculated differently: Provision A permits up to €20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, while Provision B caps a coercive fine at 1% of average worldwide daily turnover. If the same actor and non-compliance were subject to both regimes, the applicable monetary limits could diverge substantially.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions confer different powers on different authorities for different regulated subjects and violations: Provision A concerns the Dutch data-protection authority and obligations under the Financial Supervision Act, whereas Provision B concerns the lead overseer and critical ICT third-party providers. Nothing in the texts requires the same proceeding or sanction to be imposed under both provisions, so both can operate independently.

verdict.shared_subject: Public authorities and information handled in cybersecurity and AI conformity-assessment contexts
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: CSIRTs must collect and analyse forensic data and monitor incidents, while the AI Act provision requires notifying authorities to keep information obtained under Article 78 confidential. If a CSIRT were also an authority receiving Article 78 information, its monitoring, analysis, or dissemination functions could appear to conflict with confidentiality obligations.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different actors and concern different information flows: Article 11 governs CSIRTs’ cybersecurity tasks, whereas Article 45 governs notifying authorities’ treatment of information obtained under Article 78. Nothing in the texts says that Article 11 information is Article 78 information or that confidentiality prevents the CSIRT from performing its tasks; the duties can therefore coexist.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits processing of special-category and criminal-offence data only under specified public-interest, consent-impossibility, and safeguards conditions. Provision B requires the controller to facilitate the data subject’s rights under Articles 15–22, which may require handling requests concerning that sensitive processing; this creates a possible interaction between the permission conditions and individual-rights handling, but the texts do not make the duties incompatible.

Provision B separately requires the controller to facilitate data-subject rights, and both can be complied with: the body may lawfully process the data under A while still facilitating the rights under B, subject to the GDPR’s applicable rules and exceptions.

verdict.shared_subject: A non-micro financial entity that processes personal data and transfers it to a third country or international organisation.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A restricts international transfers of personal data unless the GDPR Chapter V conditions are met, while provision B requires regular internal audits of the entity’s ICT-risk-management framework. An audit could involve examining or transmitting personal-data-related material to auditors outside the EU, potentially creating a transfer-compliance issue.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident and personal-data breach notification duties
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A significant incident affecting personal data could require the entity to warn its CSIRT and competent authority within 24 hours, while GDPR Article 34 may exempt communication to affected individuals where encryption, remedial measures, or disproportionate effort applies. This creates different notification recipients and conditions, but not an incompatibility: the provisions do not require or forbid the same communication.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties address different recipients and purposes: Article 26 requires an early warning to cybersecurity authorities, whereas Article 34 governs communication to data subjects and expressly permits non-communication in specified circumstances. An entity can comply with both by making the Article 26 warning and separately assessing whether Article 34 requires communication to individuals.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern regulatory oversight and compliance, so one might initially suspect that the national cyber-crisis plan could affect how GDPR-approved code-of-conduct bodies are supervised. verdict.shared_subject: Biometrische gegevens and prohibited AI practices
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits processing biometric data used for unique identification, while provision B permits a narrow law-enforcement use of real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces when strictly necessary for specified objectives. Thus, the same biometric-identification operation may appear permitted under B but prohibited under A unless an exception to A applies.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can operate cumulatively: B regulates whether the AI practice may be used, while A independently regulates the underlying processing of biometric data. B expressly preserves A for other purposes, and A's shown text is only its prohibition paragraph, not its exceptions; therefore B does not itself establish that the processing is lawful under A.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A police authority uses a real-time remote facial-recognition system in a public space to locate a person suspected of a qualifying serious offence. The use is strictly necessary and satisfies one of Article 5(1)(h)'s objectives, but it processes biometric data for unique identification, which Article 9 prohibits unless an Article 9(2) exception applies; the provisions shown do not establish that exception.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether an exception to Article 9(1), particularly one under Article 9(2) such as a sufficiently specific substantial-public-interest legal basis, applies to this law-enforcement processing; Article 5(1)(h)'s necessity exception does not itself establish that Article 9 exception.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions mention communications-related information and could involve an entity operating network infrastructure. However, Article 47 requires supplying specified entity and network information to a central contact point, while Article 11.10a regulates misleading information given to a called user; the provisions impose different duties on different recipients and do not require incompatible conduct.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of personal data in connection with prohibited or conditionally permitted AI practices
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a controller assessing further processing for a new purpose to consider purpose compatibility, the collection context, the nature of the data, consequences, and safeguards. Provision B prohibits or conditionally permits specified AI uses, including biometric identification and categorisation, so a controller might view a compatible-purpose assessment and safeguards as supporting continued processing while B independently prohibits the AI practice.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different kinds of rules: A governs the lawfulness and compatibility assessment for further processing of personal data, whereas B directly prohibits specified AI practices, subject to its own expressly stated exceptions. Compliance with A does not authorise conduct prohibited by B, and B does not prevent a controller from performing A's assessment for AI processing that is not prohibited.
verdict.decisive_exception: Not applicable: the texts do not establish an actual permission-versus-prohibition conflict. Any apparent overlap would be resolved by applying the AI Act prohibition in addition to the GDPR processing-lawfulness requirements.

verdict.shared_subject: Administrative handling of requests under the GDPR, including possible judicial proceedings concerning a third-country transfer decision
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits the Council of State to stay a request when a related validity question is pending before the CJEU. Provision B requires a written decision on requests under Articles 15–22 within the GDPR deadlines. If the stayed matter is such a request, the court’s stay could delay the decision beyond those deadlines.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A concerns the Council of State’s judicial handling of a request and gives it a discretionary power to stay proceedings. Provision B concerns written decisions by administrative bodies; it does not expressly govern the Council of State or state that a judicial stay suspends or overrides the applicable decision deadline. The provisions therefore do not clearly impose incompatible commands on the same actor.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing special-category personal data in connection with a code of conduct for transfers to third countries or international organisations
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A states that processing special-category personal data is prohibited unless one of the listed Article 9 exceptions applies. Provision B permits controllers or processors to join an approved code of conduct involving safeguards for transfers and requires binding commitments concerning data-subject rights, but it does not itself establish that any Article 9 exception authorises the underlying special-category processing.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B concerns safeguards and enforceable commitments for international transfers, not a general authorisation to process special-category data. A controller can comply with both by processing such data only where an applicable Article 9 exception under Provision A exists and then applying the transfer safeguards required by Provision B.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A controller processes employees’ health data and joins an approved code of conduct under Article 40 to transfer that data to an organisation in a third country, making binding commitments concerning data-subject rights. The transfer safeguards may satisfy Provision B, but the texts shown do not establish that the health-data processing is covered by any of Provision A’s listed exceptions, so the controller may still face the prohibition in Provision A.
verdict.decisive_exception: The missing link is an applicable Article 9(2) exception authorising the specific processing of special-category data for the transfer/code-of-conduct purpose; Article 40’s transfer safeguards and commitments do not, on the text shown, establish that exception.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits making a user's access to a qualifying information-society service dependent on consent, while Provision B requires financial entities to use ICT processes that protect data and prevent unauthorised access. In a service involving both regimes, one might argue that refusing access without consent could be a security or data-protection measure, creating friction between access and security controls.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties with different triggers: A regulates conditioning user access on consent, whereas B requires financial entities to implement suitable ICT security and data-protection measures. Financial entities can comply with B through technical and organisational safeguards that do not make service access dependent on the consent described in A.

verdict.shared_subject: Administrative enforcement and fines for violations of different digital-law obligations
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern the power to impose administrative fines, so an entity potentially subject to both regimes could face overlapping enforcement. verdict.shared_subject: High-risk AI systems involving processing of personal data, potentially including special-category data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a controller to conduct a data-protection impact assessment before processing where the processing is likely to create a high risk to natural persons’ rights and freedoms. Provision B exceptionally permits providers of certain high-risk AI systems to process special-category personal data for bias detection and correction, but only under strict necessity and safeguard conditions; this permission operates alongside, rather than obviously replacing, the DPIA duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulatively satisfiable requirements: A is a prior assessment obligation, while B regulates whether and under what safeguards special-category data may actually be processed. A controller/provider can perform the required assessment and, if the processing is justified and safeguarded under B, comply with both.

verdict.shared_subject: Notification duties concerning cyber threats or personal-data breaches
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires an essential or important entity to promptly inform service recipients about measures they can take in response to a significant cyber threat, and, if necessary, about the threat itself. Provision B removes a personal-data-breach notification requirement where the provider has taken appropriate protective measures making the data unintelligible to unauthorised persons; if the same incident is both a significant cyber threat affecting recipients and a breach involving encrypted data, the provisions could point toward notification versus no notification.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different notifications, recipients, triggers, and legal duties. A concerns informing service recipients about significant cyber threats and protective measures, while B concerns notification to affected data subjects under the referenced breach-notification rule; B's exemption does not expressly prohibit a separate cyber-threat communication required by A.

The texts do not establish a common actor, activity, or obligation that would make compliance with one prevent compliance with the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: An entity could comply with both: it could fall within or outside A’s information-supply exemption while separately ensuring that access to its service is not conditioned on the consent described in B. Neither provision requires conduct that the other forbids.

verdict.shared_subject: Confidentiality and disclosure of information held during conformity-assessment activities, where the information may include personal data.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A restricts recognition or enforcement of a third-country judicial or administrative demand for disclosure of personal data unless based on an international agreement. Provision B requires notified bodies to disclose information when disclosure is legally required, which could appear to require compliance with such a third-country demand even where Article 48 would not permit recognition or enforcement.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different legal situations: Article 48 governs recognition or enforcement of third-country demands for disclosure of personal data, while Article 31 governs confidentiality procedures of notified bodies and preserves disclosure where legally required. Article 31 does not itself say that a third-country demand must be treated as legally requiring disclosure, so the duties can be satisfied by refusing or not recognizing an impermissible demand.

verdict.shared_subject: Delegated rulemaking authority by general administrative order
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions authorize further rules by or under a general administrative order, so a superficial reading might suggest overlapping delegated powers. However, Provision A implements Article 29(3) of the NIS2 Directive, while Provision B concerns the separate subject matter of its own Article 11a; neither text requires or forbids the same substantive rule.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can plainly coexist: each grants rulemaking authority concerning a different underlying provision and legal framework. Exercising either authority does not prevent exercising the other, and no incompatible duty, deadline, permission, classification, or benchmark appears in the texts.

verdict.shared_subject: Enforcement measures and penalties involving ICT/data-protection compliance
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits the competent authority from imposing a second administrative fine for the same conduct after a GDPR fine has been imposed. Provision B requires the lead overseer to impose a coercive penalty for non-compliance with measures after the specified period, which could appear to create a second financial sanction for overlapping conduct.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different enforcement mechanisms and potentially different authorities: A concerns an administrative fine for the same conduct, while B concerns a coercive penalty intended to compel compliance with oversight measures. A therefore does not clearly prohibit B, particularly where the coercive penalty concerns subsequent non-compliance rather than the original infringement.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the coercive penalty under Article 35 is legally classified as a bestuurlijke boete under the national provisions, and whether it concerns the same conduct as the GDPR fine, is not established by the texts shown.

verdict.shared_subject: Use of real-time remote biometric identification by a committee or advisory body performing a law-enforcement task
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A creates an exception to the prohibition on processing special-category and criminal-offence personal data by a qualifying committee or advisory body, provided its cumulative conditions are met. Provision B separately requires prior judicial or independent administrative authorisation for real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement, with only a narrowly defined emergency route; A does not establish that its public-interest task and safeguards replace or satisfy B’s authorisation requirement.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can operate cumulatively: a committee or advisory body may process the relevant sensitive data only under A’s conditions and may use real-time remote biometric identification only after obtaining B’s required authorisation and satisfying B’s necessity, proportionality, purpose, and scope limits. Nothing in A expressly permits bypassing an independent authorisation requirement, and nothing in B expressly removes A’s data-processing conditions.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A Dutch advisory committee established to perform a law-enforcement task uses real-time remote facial identification in a public space to locate a specifically sought suspect, processing biometric and criminal-offence personal data. Its establishment instrument contains the public-interest task and safeguards and consent is impossible, so it invokes A’s exception, but it begins the operation without the prior judicial or independent administrative authorisation required by B, or relies on A’s exception as the legal basis for that processing without showing that the applicable special-category-data exception covers this specific biometric-identification use.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the exception permitting the committee’s processing under article 9(2)(g) and article 10 of the GDPR, as reflected in A, also constitutes a sufficient legal basis for the specific real-time remote biometric-identification processing governed by B, including B’s separate prior-authorisation requirement; the texts shown do not establish that link.

verdict.shared_subject: Use of personal/contact data for communications and spiritual care
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A restricts disclosure of personal data revealing religious or philosophical beliefs to third parties without the person's consent. Provision B requires a sender using certain means for unsolicited communications to give a natural person an easy, free opportunity to object, which could involve using contact data connected with such beliefs without obtaining consent for the disclosure.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different conduct and triggers: A concerns disclosure of special-category belief data in the context of spiritual care, while B concerns unsolicited communications and an objection mechanism. B does not expressly authorize disclosure of belief data, and its consent/objection rules can be complied with without disclosing such data to third parties.

verdict.shared_subject: Public disclosure of administrative sanctions or coercive fines by regulatory authorities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions require a supervisory authority to publish an imposed monetary enforcement measure, but they state different exceptions. Provision A incorporates the exceptions in article 5.1(1), (2), and (5) of the Wet open overheid, while Provision B uses the distinct thresholds of seriously endangering financial markets or causing disproportionate harm to the parties concerned. For an authority subject to both, the provisions could therefore point to different publication outcomes for the same measure.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions may apply to different authorities, enforcement measures, and legal regimes: A concerns a decision by the Dutch data-protection authority imposing an administrative sanction, whereas B concerns fines imposed by a lead overseer under the DORA framework. Even if both apply, publication could be required only where neither provision's exception applies, and the texts do not expressly make the exceptions mutually exclusive or prescribe incompatible publication deadlines or content.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A Dutch data-protection authority acting as a DORA lead overseer imposes a coercive fine that is also an administrative sanction. Publication would be required under one provision but withheld under the other because, for example, the Wet open overheid exception applies while the financial-markets or disproportionate-harm exception in Article 35 does not, or vice versa.
verdict.decisive_exception: The decisive exceptions are the Wet open overheid article 5.1(1), (2), and (5) exceptions in Provision A and Article 35's exceptions for serious danger to financial markets or disproportionate harm to the parties concerned in Provision B; the texts do not establish how these exceptions interact.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing personal data by a temporary commission or advisory body and the data subject’s right to object
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits processing of special-category and criminal-offence data when its listed conditions are met. Provision B gives a data subject a right to object to processing based on Article 6(1)(e) or (f), and requires cessation unless overriding legitimate grounds or litigation-related grounds exist; thus, a commission’s reliance on a public-interest task could raise a question whether it must stop processing after an objection.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different legal requirements that can operate cumulatively. A’s permission is expressly subject to necessity and safeguards, while B’s objection right applies only where the processing is based on Article 6(1)(e) or (f), and B itself allows continued processing where overriding grounds or legal-claim grounds exist; the texts do not establish that A’s permitted processing necessarily uses one of those bases or that an objection defeats A’s conditions.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A temporary advisory commission lawfully processes a person’s health data and criminal-offence data to perform a recorded task of substantial public interest, after obtaining consent is shown impossible and adopting specific safeguards. The person objects to that processing because of reasons relating to their specific situation, and the commission must determine whether it may continue under Article 21 while relying on the permission in Article 47a.
verdict.decisive_exception: The text does not establish whether the Article 47a permission satisfies the GDPR legal-basis and exception requirements relevant to Article 9 and Article 10, nor whether the commission has overriding legitimate grounds under Article 21 that permit continuation after the objection. In particular, Article 47a refers to Article 9(a) and (g) and Article 10 but does not itself establish how those grounds interact with the Article 21 objection mechanism.

verdict.shared_subject: Governance and allocation of tasks within an organizational committee
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the members to establish a division of tasks, while Provision B requires the secretariat to perform its tasks exclusively according to the chair's instructions. If the secretariat is also a member whose assigned tasks require independent action or consultation of extraordinary members, the chair's exclusive-instruction rule could constrain performance of that allocation.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different actors and duties: members establish a division of tasks, whereas the secretariat performs its tasks under the chair's instructions. Nothing in Provision A requires the secretariat to disregard the chair, and the texts do not establish that the secretariat is a member or that the task allocation conflicts with the chair's instructions.

verdict.shared_subject: BWBR0048156's obligations concerning recognized services and acceptance duties
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern obligations under the same statute and could appear to affect when a service-related duty must be performed. If an erkende dienst were also an aangewezen organisatie or bestuursorgaan subject to the acceptance duties, one might ask whether its general delivery obligation applies before the infrastructure connection schedule permits the acceptance duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 13 requires a recognized service to comply with rules and recognition conditions, including a delivery obligation. Article 29 instead postpones the acceptance duties in Articles 7 and 15 for a bestuursorgaan or aangewezen organisatie until connection is possible under the published schedule; it does not suspend or prohibit Article 13's delivery obligation. The provisions therefore address different duties and triggers and can both be obeyed.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern institutional oversight in the digital sphere, so one might initially suspect that the CSIRT’s monitoring, incident-response, or information-sharing tasks could overlap with supervision of GDPR codes of conduct. However, neither provision imposes an incompatible duty on the same actor or regulates the same operational conduct.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A assigns cybersecurity-support and threat-monitoring tasks to a CSIRT, while provision B requires a supervisory authority to withdraw accreditation from a code-of-conduct monitoring body when accreditation conditions fail or its measures breach the GDPR. These duties can be performed simultaneously and do not prescribe conflicting actions, deadlines, or standards.

verdict.shared_subject: A small essential or important entity that processes personal data and experiences a significant incident
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A concerns whether the GDPR register-of-processing-activities obligation applies to an organisation with fewer than 250 employees, while provision B independently requires essential and important entities to report significant incidents. A small entity may therefore have to comply with the NIS2 reporting duty even though the quoted GDPR provision exempts it from the register duty, but that is a difference in scope and subject matter rather than an incompatibility.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties with different triggers: A concerns maintaining a register of processing activities, whereas B concerns reporting significant incidents affecting services. An entity can comply with both by reporting the incident under B and, where A's exceptions apply, maintaining the GDPR register; neither provision requires conduct that the other forbids.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De in de leden 1 en 2 bedoelde verplichtingen zijn niet van toepassing op ondernemingen of organisaties die minder dan 250 personen in dienst hebben, tenzij het waarschijnlijk is dat de verwerking die zij verrichten een risico inhoudt voor de rechten en vrijheden van de betrokkenen, de verwerking niet incidenteel is, of de verwerking bijzondere categorieën van gegevens, als bedoeld in artikel 9, lid 1, of persoonsgegevens in verband met strafrechtelijke veroordelingen en strafbare feiten als bedoeld in artikel 10 betreft.

verdict.shared_subject: Public disclosure of official decisions
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions require publication of official decisions, but they concern different decision types and impose different publication channels and timing. A possible tension would arise only if the same decision were both an aanwijzing besluit and a non-appealable administrative penalty decision, because A refers to the Staatscourant while B requires the competent authority’s official website and immediate publication.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can readily be satisfied together because A concerns a decision to designate attributes by the Minister, whereas B concerns final administrative penalty decisions by competent authorities. Even if one decision somehow fell within both descriptions, publication in the Staatscourant and on the official website are not inherently incompatible, and B’s immediacy does not contradict A’s unspecified timing.

verdict.evidence_span_b: De bevoegde autoriteiten maken op hun officiële website onverwijld alle niet voor beroep vatbare besluiten tot het nemen van administratieve strafmaatregelen bekend, nadat de natuurlijke of rechtspersoon op wie een dergelijke maatregel van toepassing is, van deze maatregel in kennis is gesteld.

verdict.shared_subject: Public notice of official decisions
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions require publication of an official decision, so an authority might need to determine whether publication under one rule also satisfies the other. However, they concern different decisions and different publication mechanisms, and neither text prohibits compliance with the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A requires the Dutch Data Protection Authority to make a sanction decision public, subject to specified Wet open overheid exceptions. Provision B requires notice of a designation or withdrawal decision by publication in the Staatscourant; both duties can be fulfilled independently without contradiction.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens maakt een door haar genomen beschikking tot het opleggen van een bestuurlijke sanctie openbaar, behoudens voor zover artikel 5.1, eerste, tweede en vijfde lid van de Wet open overheid, aan openbaarmaking in de weg staan.

verdict.shared_subject: ICT-diensten en financiële entiteiten/aanbieders onder NIS2 en DORA
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Beide bepalingen concerneren toezicht en ICT-diensten, maar zij leggen verschillende institutionele verplichtingen op: A vereist samenwerking en kennisgeving door bevoegde autoriteiten, terwijl B voorafgaande beoordelingen door financiële entiteiten vereist. In een concreet geval kan die samenwerking plaatsvinden zonder dat de financiële entiteit alle in B genoemde due-diligence- en risicobeoordelingen uitvoert, maar dat is geen onverenigbaarheid tussen de normen.

Beide verplichtingen kunnen gelijktijdig worden nageleefd; geen van beide verbiedt of vervangt de andere.

verdict.shared_subject: Telecommunications-law provisions concerning provider cooperation and exemptions
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions appear in the same statutory chapter and concern regulatory treatment of providers, so one might initially suspect that an exemption under Article 11.12 could affect the cooperation duty in Article 11.11. However, Article 11.12 merely states that an exemption may have limitations or conditions; it does not say that it exempts anyone from Article 11.11 or conflicts with the cooperation and data-disclosure duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 11.11 requires the relevant provider, upon request, to cooperate with an investigation and provide available caller-identification details when warranted. Article 11.12 permits exemptions to be granted subject to limitations or conditions, which can coexist with that duty unless a specific exemption expressly removes it; no such exemption or conflict is shown.

verdict.shared_subject: Access to personal-data files in proceedings and GDPR principles for processing personal data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision B gives parties access to the EDPS file, which may require disclosure or continued availability of personal data. Provision A requires processing to be limited to what is necessary, purpose-compatible, accurate, and appropriately secured, so unrestricted or excessive file access could create compliance pressure.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, compatible duties: B requires respecting parties’ defence rights and granting file access subject to protecting others’ personal data and trade secrets, while A governs how personal data are processed. Access can therefore be provided with appropriate redaction, limitation, accuracy, retention, and security measures; B itself expressly recognises privacy interests.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern the same legislative instrument, but they regulate entirely different matters: Provision A governs withdrawal of an accreditation and a termination plan, while Provision B governs parliamentary involvement and entry into force of a general administrative measure. No actor is required by one provision to do something that conflicts with the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can operate simultaneously without contradiction. An accredited service may request withdrawal and submit a termination plan under Article 14, while any general administrative measure adopted under Article 5(6) follows the parliamentary-submission, waiting-period, and possible-withdrawal procedure in Article 25.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing and publication of subscriber personal data in publicly available directories
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A restricts processing of special-category personal data unless one of its listed exceptions applies. Provision B requires consent before ordinary subscriber personal data may be included in a directory, but that consent rule could be read as permitting inclusion even where the data are special-category data. The texts do not establish whether B's subscriber consent satisfies the specific exception framework in A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B can be complied with by obtaining the subscriber's consent and limiting the entry to the indicated data, while Provision A independently governs any special-category data and permits processing where the data subject has given explicit consent for specified purposes. If the directory consent is explicit and sufficiently specific, both provisions can be satisfied.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A telecommunications provider seeks to publish a subscriber's name and telephone number in a publicly available directory, but the number or associated entry reveals a special category of personal data, such as a health-related service or political affiliation. The provider has the subscriber's consent under Article 11.6, yet the texts do not establish whether that consent is the explicit, purpose-specific consent required by Article 22(a) or otherwise falls within one of Article 22's exceptions.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the consent required by Article 11.6 is 'uitdrukkelijke toestemming' for one or more specifically defined purposes under Article 22(a), and whether the directory-publication purpose is sufficiently specific; the provision shown does not establish that link.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing special-category personal data while facilitating data-subject rights
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A concerns the prohibition on processing special-category personal data and lists circumstances in which that prohibition does not apply. Provision B requires the controller to facilitate the exercise of data-subject rights, which may in practice require handling personal data, potentially including special-category data; the text shown does not establish that this processing falls within one of A’s exceptions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B does not itself require processing special-category data, and facilitating rights can generally be done without such processing or under an applicable Article 9(2) exception. The provisions therefore impose duties that can ordinarily be satisfied together, with A governing any special-category processing and B governing rights facilitation.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A controller receives an access or rectification request concerning a person’s health data and must process and verify that special-category data to facilitate the request under Provision B, while Provision A prohibits that processing unless one of its listed exceptions applies; the text shown does not establish that facilitating the request is covered by one of those exceptions.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether facilitating the exercise of the rights under Articles 15–22 constitutes a processing purpose covered by one of the Article 9(2) exceptions listed in Provision A, particularly the necessity exception for establishing, exercising or defending legal claims, is not established by the text shown.

verdict.shared_subject: Cross-border mutual assistance between competent authorities under the NIS2 framework
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A says a competent authority may make a reasoned assistance request to another Member State concerning listed entities whose main establishment is there. Provision B requires competent authorities to cooperate and provide assistance when an entity operates across Member States, so A's discretionary wording could appear narrower than B's mandatory cooperation duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate compatible aspects of the same cooperation mechanism: A identifies a national authority's power to request assistance for specified entities based on their main establishment, while B sets out mandatory cooperation duties and procedures where cross-border services or systems are involved. A does not prohibit assistance or purport to exhaust the circumstances in which it may be requested, and B expressly permits refusal where the requested authority lacks competence or another listed exception applies.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing and informing individuals about personal data, potentially including special-category data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits processing special-category personal data unless one of its listed exceptions applies. Provision B requires information to be supplied to the data subject when personal data were not obtained from them, including information about the source, rights, consent withdrawal, and automated decision-making. If the data are special-category data, complying with B may require communicating information about processing that A prohibits unless an A exception applies.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B is an information duty, not an independent authorization to process special-category data, and it applies only when its own trigger is met. A can be obeyed by refraining from prohibited processing, while B can be satisfied for lawful processing covered by one of A’s exceptions; the texts do not establish that B requires any processing forbidden by A.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A controller obtains health data about an individual from a third party and processes those data in an automated decision system. Because the data were not obtained from the individual, Article 14 requires the controller to inform the individual about the source, applicable rights, and the existence and logic of automated decision-making, while Article 22 prohibits processing the health data unless one of its listed exceptions applies. The provisions shown do not establish that the Article 14 information duty itself supplies an Article 22 exception.

verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be read together: A itself limits exchange to necessary, relevant and proportionate information and requires confidentiality, while B expressly preserves disclosures authorised by Union or national law. Thus, an exchange under A may constitute the required legal basis under B, or may be limited to disclosures that B does not prohibit; the text does not establish otherwise.

A points toward the exchange, while B prohibits providing the information unless such a basis exists.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the exchange under Provision A itself qualifies as the Union- or national-law provision authorising disclosure under Provision B; the excerpts do not resolve that issue.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions address a personal-data security breach, but they impose duties toward different recipients: A requires notification to the Dutch data-protection authority, while B concerns when notification to the affected data subject is not required. An operator could therefore have to notify the authority while being exempt from notifying individuals, but that is not an incompatibility because the obligations can operate simultaneously.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose distinct, cumulatively satisfiable obligations: A requires prompt notification to the authority, whereas B permits omitting notification to the data subject when one of its listed conditions applies. Compliance with one does not prevent compliance with the other, and the texts do not require the same notification to be made to both recipients.

verdict.shared_subject: Dutch electronic communications regulation
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern the regulatory framework for electronic communications providers and permissions or obligations under that framework. One might speculate that conditions attached to an exemption could affect how the provider handles subscriber requests, but neither text says that an exemption may waive or alter the duties in Article 11.4.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 11.4 imposes specific duties on a provider of a public electronic communications service when requested by a subscriber. Article 11.12 merely authorizes an exemption to be granted subject to limitations or conditions; it does not require conduct incompatible with either duty, and the provisions can operate together.
