verdict.evidence_span_b: De verwerker en eenieder die onder het gezag van de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke of van de verwerker handelt en toegang heeft tot persoonsgegevens, verwerkt deze uitsluitend in opdracht van de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern public authorities and regulatory administration, but they assign different functions: Provision A makes the Minister the cyber-crisis-management authority, while Provision B requires a notifying authority to report changes concerning a notified conformity-assessment body. Nothing in the texts makes the Minister's crisis-management role incompatible with, or a substitute for, the notifying authority's reporting duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different authorities, subject matters, and triggers. Provision A assigns national cyber-crisis-management tasks under the NIS2 framework; Provision B imposes an administrative notification-update duty under the AI Act, and both can be performed independently if the same institution happens to hold both roles.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Onze Minister is de cybercrisisbeheerautoriteit, bedoeld in artikel 9, eerste lid, van de NIS2-richtlijn, en heeft in die hoedanigheid de taken die zijn opgenomen in het nationaal plan voor grootschalige cyberbeveiligingsincidenten en crisisrespons, genoemd in artikel 20.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De aanmeldende autoriteit stelt de Commissie en de andere lidstaten via het in artikel 30, lid 2, bedoelde elektronische aanmeldingssysteem in kennis van alle relevante wijzigingen in de aanmelding van een aangemelde instantie.

verdict.shared_subject: Digital/ICT operations and information handling
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions regulate conduct involving communications or ICT operations, but Provision A prohibits using caller-identification facilities to provide false information, while Provision B requires financial entities to maintain accessible activity registers during activated continuity or recovery plans. Nothing in the texts requires those registers to contain or communicate false information, so the strongest tension case is only a superficial topical overlap.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: A financial entity can maintain the required registers while ensuring that any use of network-access-point or individual-user identification facilities does not provide the called user with incorrect information. The provisions impose different duties on different subject matter and can be complied with simultaneously.
verdict.evidence_span_a: wordt niet gebruikt om de opgeroepen gebruiker onjuiste informatie te verstrekken
verdict.evidence_span_b: houden gemakkelijk toegankelijke registers bij van hun activiteiten vóór en tijdens storingen

verdict.shared_subject: Processing special-category personal data in automated individual decision-making
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits processing special-category personal data unless one of its listed exceptions applies. Provision B requires safeguards, including human intervention and the right to challenge, when an automated individual decision falls within the referenced exceptions; those safeguards may presuppose processing such data, but B does not itself establish that A's exceptions cover the processing.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can operate cumulatively: an automated decision-maker may process special-category data only where an exception under A applies, and, if the decision falls within B's scope, it must additionally provide the listed safeguards. Provision B regulates safeguards for automated decisions; it does not expressly authorise processing prohibited by A.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A controller uses a person's health or biometric data in an automated decision about that person, relying on one of the situations referenced in B, but none of the exceptions listed in A is clearly established as a legal basis for that processing. The controller must provide the safeguards in B while the underlying processing remains prohibited under A unless the missing exception is satisfied.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the automated processing of the special-category data is covered by an applicable exception to the prohibition under Article 9(2) of the GDPR, beyond the safeguards and Article 22(2) situations shown in Provision B.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Overeenkomstig artikel 9, tweede lid, onderdelen a, c, d, e en f, van de verordening is het verbod om bijzondere categorieën van persoonsgegevens te verwerken niet van toepassing, indien:
verdict.evidence_span_b: In de in lid 2, punten a) en c), bedoelde gevallen treft de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke passende maatregelen ter bescherming van de rechten en vrijheden en gerechtvaardigde belangen van de betrokkene, waaronder ten minste het recht op menselijke tussenkomst van de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke, het recht om zijn standpunt kenbaar te maken en het recht om het besluit aan te vechten.

verdict.shared_subject: Automated high-risk AI systems used to make decisions about natural persons
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 22 GDPR gives the person a right not to be subjected to a solely automated decision with legal or similarly significant effects. Article 13 AI Act requires instructions for high-risk systems to describe, among other things, human-oversight measures and, where applicable, mechanisms enabling users to interpret outputs, but it does not itself require that such a decision be subjected to human review or prohibit the decision.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulatively satisfiable obligations on different actors: Article 22 governs the controller's use of solely automated significant decisions, while Article 13 governs the provider's instructions for a high-risk AI system. A provider can supply the required information and oversight instructions, while the controller separately complies with Article 22 by avoiding the prohibited decision or applying an applicable Article 22(2) exception and safeguards.
verdict.decisive_exception: Article 22(2) GDPR contains exceptions to the prohibition, but their applicability is not needed to establish compatibility: Article 13 does not authorize the prohibited decision or purport to substitute for the controller's Article 22 duties.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De betrokkene heeft het recht niet te worden onderworpen aan een uitsluitend op geautomatiseerde verwerking, waaronder profilering, gebaseerd besluit waaraan voor hem rechtsgevolgen zijn verbonden of dat hem anderszins in aanmerkelijke mate treft.
verdict.evidence_span_b: d) de in artikel 14 bedoelde maatregelen voor menselijk toezicht, met inbegrip van de technische maatregelen die zijn getroffen om de interpretatie van de output van de AI-systemen met een hoog risico door gebruiksverantwoordelijken te vergemakkelijken;

verdict.shared_subject: Besluiten concerning recognition and acceptance of business or organisational means under BWBR0048156
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern ministerial decisions within the same statutory scheme, so one might initially suspect that the duty to publish a decision could interact with the prohibition on taking a decision for a non-compliant means. However, Article 14 merely prescribes publicity after a decision, while Article 15 restricts whether a particular decision may be taken; they regulate different legal consequences and do not require incompatible conduct.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The Minister can comply with both by refusing to take the Article 15 decision for a means that fails the applicable security and reliability requirements, and publishing any decision that is nevertheless made under Article 14. Publication does not authorise, validate, or require taking a prohibited decision.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Van een besluit als bedoeld in dit artikel doet Onze Minister mededeling in de Staatscourant.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Een besluit als bedoeld in het vijfde lid wordt niet genomen ten aanzien van een bedrijfs- of organisatiemiddel dat niet voldoet aan de voor het betrouwbaarheidsniveau substantieel of hoog gestelde eisen ten aanzien van veiligheid en betrouwbaarheid.

verdict.shared_subject: Potentially an entity involved in ICT services and/or an AI model for general purposes
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: The provisions concern different obligations and triggers: A concerns contract negotiations by financial entities and ICT-service providers, while B concerns an exception from documentation and information duties for certain providers of general-purpose AI models. One might argue that an ICT provider negotiating a contract could be both encouraged to use public-sector model clauses and exempt from some AI-model obligations, creating regulatory inconsistency.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose no incompatible commands. A requires parties in specified contract negotiations to take account of model contractual clauses; B merely removes obligations under Article 53(1)(a) and (b) for qualifying open-source general-purpose AI-model providers, except where the model has systemic risks. The same actor can comply with A while benefiting from B's separate exception, because neither provision requires or forbids the conduct addressed by the other.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Bij onderhandelingen over contractuele overeenkomsten houden financiële entiteiten en derde aanbieders van ICT-diensten rekening met het gebruik van modelcontractbepalingen die door overheidsinstanties zijn ontwikkeld voor specifieke diensten.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Deze uitzondering is niet van toepassing op AI-modellen voor algemene doeleinden met systeemrisico's.

verdict.shared_subject: Een verwerkingsverantwoordelijke die voorgenomen persoonsgegevensverwerking uitvoert.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Artikel 35 verplicht vooraf een gegevensbeschermingseffectbeoordeling wanneer de verwerking waarschijnlijk een hoog risico inhoudt. Artikel 36 voegt daaraan voorafgaande raadpleging toe wanneer uit die beoordeling blijkt dat het risico zonder risicobeperkende maatregelen hoog zou blijven; dat kan worden gelezen als een extra procedurele last, maar niet als een onverenigbare verplichting.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: De bepalingen vormen een opeenvolgende procedure: eerst wordt de effectbeoordeling uitgevoerd en vervolgens, alleen bij de in artikel 36 omschreven uitkomst, wordt de toezichthoudende autoriteit geraadpleegd. Beide verplichtingen kunnen volledig worden nageleefd en artikel 36 veronderstelt juist de beoordeling uit artikel 35.
verdict.evidence_span_a: voert de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke vóór de verwerking een beoordeling uit van het effect van de beoogde verwerkingsactiviteiten op de bescherming van persoonsgegevens.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Wanneer uit een gegevensbeschermingseffectbeoordeling krachtens artikel 35 blijkt dat de verwerking een hoog risico zou opleveren indien de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke geen maatregelen neemt om het risico te beperken, raadpleegt de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke voorafgaand aan de verwerking de toezichthoudende autoriteit.

verdict.shared_subject: Withdrawal of an organisation’s designation by a minister
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern withdrawing a designation, but they attach that power or duty to different factual conditions and decision-makers. One appears mandatory when the basis for designation no longer exists, while the other makes withdrawal discretionary when the organisation no longer provides specified electronic services.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can operate cumulatively and in different legal contexts: Article 11 concerns an institution of higher education designated as an essential entity, whereas Article 2 concerns an organisation providing electronic services requiring substantial or high authentication. Even if both apply, the minister can withdraw under Article 11 when its condition is met and may withdraw under Article 2 when its separate condition is met; the texts do not require mutually incompatible action.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Onze Minister van Onderwijs, Cultuur en Wetenschap trekt de aanwijzing, bedoeld in het eerste lid, in, indien er voor die aanwijzing geen grond meer aanwezig is.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Bij besluit van Onze Minister in overeenstemming met Onze Minister die het mede aangaat kan de aanwijzing van een organisatie worden ingetrokken indien die organisatie niet langer elektronische diensten verleent waarvoor authenticatie op betrouwbaarheidsniveau substantieel of hoog vereist is.

verdict.shared_subject: Ministerial regulations concerning electronic identification or numbering-related communications
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions delegate rulemaking to a ministerial regulation, and both concern aspects of electronic identification or access-related communications. One could therefore argue that implementing regulations might address overlapping technical or procedural matters.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 6 concerns authentication assurance levels and designated identification means for access to electronic services. Article 11.9 concerns telephone-number identification, blocking or refusal, prevention of caller-number identification, international implementation, and information duties for providers, users, and subscribers; the provisions impose no incompatible requirement on the same actor or subject.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Voor een identificatiemiddel op betrouwbaarheidsniveau laag geldt dat sprake moet zijn van ten minste twee authenticatiefactoren zoals bedoeld in de eIDAS-verordening.
verdict.evidence_span_b: de voorwaarden waaronder de abonnee de identificatie van het nummer van oproepende netwerkaansluitpunten dan wel een nummer waarmee een individuele gebruiker kan worden geïdentificeerd kan doen verhinderen

verdict.shared_subject: CE-markering and conformity-assessment obligations for imported high-risk AI systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions regulate CE marking and conformity assessment for high-risk AI systems. One might argue that Article 23 requires the importer to verify the CE marking before placing the system on the market, while Article 48 adds a condition concerning the notified body's identification number, potentially creating an additional compliance requirement.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 23 expressly requires the importer to check that the required CE marking is affixed, while Article 48 specifies what the marking must contain where applicable and who may affix the notified body's identification number. The importer can comply with both by verifying the complete marking and related conformity documentation; Article 48 does not prohibit or contradict Article 23.
verdict.evidence_span_a: c) de vereiste CE-markering op het systeem is aangebracht en het systeem vergezeld gaat van de in artikel 47 bedoelde EU-conformiteitsverklaring en gebruiksaanwijzingen;
verdict.evidence_span_b: Indien van toepassing, wordt de CE-markering gevolgd door het identificatienummer van de aangemelde instantie die verantwoordelijk is voor de in artikel 43 beschreven conformiteitsbeoordelingsprocedures.

verdict.shared_subject: Entities and organisational means in Dutch digital-law regulation
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern regulated entities or organisations, but they govern different matters: Provision A authorises criteria for identifying significant incidents, while Provision B prohibits acceptance of an organisational means that fails specified security and reliability requirements. Nothing in A requires accepting such a means, and nothing in B prevents setting incident criteria.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose no incompatible commands. An entity can comply with the security and reliability requirements for acceptance under B while also applying incident-significance criteria established under A; the incident-reporting classification and acceptance decision operate independently.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Bij of krachtens algemene maatregel van bestuur kunnen de criteria worden vastgesteld op basis waarvan wordt bepaald of sprake is van een significant incident als bedoeld in het tweede lid
verdict.evidence_span_b: Een besluit als bedoeld in het vijfde lid wordt niet genomen ten aanzien van een bedrijfs- of organisatiemiddel dat niet voldoet aan de voor het betrouwbaarheidsniveau substantieel of hoog gestelde eisen ten aanzien van veiligheid en betrouwbaarheid.

verdict.shared_subject: Continuity planning obligations for entities/providers
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A excludes an essential or important entity from its governance article when Article 21 does not apply. Provision B requires designated antenna-site providers to prepare and implement a joint continuity plan, so an entity might appear exempt from one governance regime while still being subject to a continuity obligation under another.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose no incompatible commands. Article 24 is merely a scope exclusion from its own article, while Article 11a.3 independently requires designated providers to maintain a joint continuity plan; an entity can comply with B regardless of whether A applies.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Dit artikel is niet van toepassing op een essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit indien artikel 21 niet van toepassing is op die entiteit.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Voor een aangewezen antenne-opstelpunt dragen de in het eerste lid bedoelde aanbieder of aanbieders zorg voor de opstelling en de uitvoering van een gezamenlijk continuïteitsplan dat voorziet in onderlinge afstemming van de maatregelen, bedoeld in het eerste lid.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of special-category or criminal-offence personal data by a temporary commission or advisory body, and the controller’s information duties when collecting personal data directly from the data subject.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A removes the prohibition on processing special-category and criminal-offence data when its stated conditions are met, while Provision B requires information to be supplied when personal data are collected directly from the data subject. If a commission is the controller and collects such sensitive data directly, the processing permission in A does not itself eliminate B’s disclosure duty. The only plausible tension is that A permits the processing while B imposes additional transparency obligations, but those obligations regulate information provision rather than prohibit the processing.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose cumulative, independently satisfiable requirements: A concerns when the prohibition on processing sensitive or criminal-offence data does not apply, whereas B concerns information that a controller must provide at collection. A commission can satisfy A’s safeguards and public-interest conditions and also provide the information required by B; neither provision says that the processing permission substitutes for or overrides the transparency duty.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing health data in connection with information access by providers of general-purpose AI models
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A imposes confidentiality conditions when health data are processed under the referenced exceptions. Provision B requires a general-purpose AI-model provider to provide requested information and grant access, which could in a concrete evaluation involve health data; disclosure to evaluators might then appear to conflict with A's confidentiality duty unless the recipients are authorised or another disclosure basis applies.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B does not itself require processing or disclosure of health data, and Provision A permits disclosure where the law requires it or where the controller's task necessitates disclosure to persons otherwise authorised to process the data. The provider can therefore supply non-sensitive information, redact health data, or disclose such data only through an applicable confidentiality or legal-authorisation route; the provisions do not expressly require incompatible conduct.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A provider of a general-purpose AI model is subject to an evaluation request under Article 92 and the requested information or access necessarily exposes identifiable health data processed under Article 30's exceptions. The provider must provide the requested access, but Article 30 requires that the data be handled only by persons bound by confidentiality and permits disclosure only where legally required or necessary to the provider's task to persons authorised to process them; Article 92 alone does not establish that the evaluators satisfy those conditions or that the requested disclosure falls within the permitted exception.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the Article 92 information/access request itself legally requires disclosure of the health data, or whether the evaluators are persons authorised under Article 30's referenced exceptions and bound by the required confidentiality obligation.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Indien toepassing wordt gegeven aan het eerste, tweede of derde lid, worden de gegevens alleen verwerkt door personen die uit hoofde van ambt, beroep of wettelijk voorschrift dan wel krachtens een overeenkomst tot geheimhouding zijn verplicht.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De aanbieders van AI-modellen voor algemene doeleinden of hun vertegenwoordiger verstrekken de gevraagde informatie.

verdict.shared_subject: Duties of authorised representatives or services acting for another entity
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern an intermediary acting on behalf of another party, but they impose different operational duties: Provision A requires an accredited unlocking service to make specified credentials and attributes available, while Provision B requires an AI provider to enable its authorised representative to perform the tasks in its mandate. If the same entity and activity fell under both regimes, the duties could overlap without the texts specifying how to reconcile them.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different actors and functions. Provision A concerns an erkende ontsluitende dienst providing access to recognised business or organisational means, authorisations and attributes for electronic public services; Provision B concerns an AI-model provider enabling its authorised representative to perform delegated obligations under the AI Regulation. Nothing in either text requires withholding, disabling or otherwise preventing compliance with the other duty.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Een erkende ontsluitende dienst ontsluit alle erkende bedrijfs- en organisatiemiddelen, alle door erkende machtigingsdiensten afgegeven elektronische verklaringen waaruit blijkt dat een natuurlijke persoon, onderneming of rechtspersoon gemachtigd is namens de onderneming of rechtspersoon, bedoeld in artikel 15, eerste lid, op te treden bij de toegang tot elektronische dienstverlening en alle op grond van artikel 12 aangewezen attributen.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De aanbieder stelt zijn gemachtigde in staat de taken uit te voeren die staan gespecificeerd in het mandaat dat hij van de aanbieder heeft ontvangen.

verdict.shared_subject: High-risk processing or AI-system data governance
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can apply to a high-risk activity involving personal-data processing, but they impose different obligations: Article 36 requires prior consultation where a DPIA identifies an unmitigated high risk, while Article 10 requires data-governance practices for high-risk AI training, validation and test datasets. One might argue that the AI Act’s detailed governance process could address the risks identified in the DPIA, leaving uncertainty about whether separate consultation remains necessary.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties have different triggers and can be performed cumulatively. Article 36 is a conditional prior-consultation duty for a controller whose DPIA identifies high risk absent mitigation; Article 10 is a data-management duty for high-risk AI datasets, and nothing in Article 10 deems compliance with its practices to replace or override GDPR consultation.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Wanneer uit een gegevensbeschermingseffectbeoordeling krachtens artikel 35 blijkt dat de verwerking een hoog risico zou opleveren indien de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke geen maatregelen neemt om het risico te beperken, raadpleegt de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke voorafgaand aan de verwerking de toezichthoudende autoriteit.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Datasets voor training, validatie en tests worden onderworpen aan praktijken op het gebied van databeheer die stroken met het beoogde doel van het AI-systeem met een hoog risico.

verdict.shared_subject: Disclosure of information and documentation by an AI-system provider where the information may include health data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A imposes confidentiality on health data and permits disclosure only where the law requires it or disclosure is necessary to the controller’s task to other persons authorised to process it. Provision B requires a high-risk AI provider to give a competent authority all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate compliance, which could in a concrete case include health data; the shown texts do not establish that the authority is authorised under A’s conditions to receive those data.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B requires disclosure only of information and documentation necessary for the stated compliance demonstration, while Provision A expressly allows disclosure where the law requires it. A reasoned request under B may therefore constitute a legal obligation, and the provisions can be complied with by disclosing only necessary information to an appropriately authorised authority, subject to confidentiality safeguards.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A provider of a high-risk AI system used in healthcare holds patient health data in its technical documentation or compliance records. A competent authority makes a reasoned request under Article 21 for all information necessary to demonstrate compliance, including those patient-level health data; the provider must disclose them under B but must keep them confidential under A unless the request is a legally sufficient obligation and the authority is authorised to process the data under A’s conditions.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the Article 21 request itself is a legal obligation that falls within A’s disclosure exception, and whether the requesting competent authority is a person authorised to process the health data under the applicable health-data provisions, is not established by the texts shown.

verdict.shared_subject: Organisational security and data-processing record obligations
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions may apply to a small communications provider processing personal data: Provision A requires technical, operational and organisational security measures, while Provision B removes the Article 30 register obligation only subject to specified exceptions. One might argue that the security-management duty could require documenting processing or security activities in a register even where Article 30 says the register obligation does not apply.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A concerns measures to control risks to public electronic communications networks or services and limit effects on national security or public order; Provision B concerns whether certain small organisations must maintain a GDPR record of processing activities. The provider can comply with A's security measures without maintaining the Article 30 register, and if an Article 30 exception applies, both duties can simply be performed cumulatively.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulation and operation of electronic-service and cybersecurity entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can concern the security and reliability of entities involved in electronic services. One might argue that a private service admitted to support continuity could later be subject to a competent authority’s deadline to remedy a cybersecurity-related infringement, creating regulatory pressure on the same operational activity.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A merely gives the competent authority a power to set an end date after an essential entity has committed an infringement; it does not require or prohibit any particular conduct that conflicts with Provision B. Provision B requires the Minister to admit a private unlocking service only when continuity is necessary and the service meets applicable requirements, so both powers and duties can operate cumulatively without contradiction.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions occur in the same instrument and involve governmental actors and delegated regulation. One could argue that the auditor statement under Article 4 might concern compliance with rules established by an order in council, while Article 25 imposes procedural conditions on such an order in council, creating a possible dependency between the security obligation and the delegated-rule procedure.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 4 requires administrative bodies and designated organisations to provide the Minister with an auditor’s statement about compliance with information-security rules. Article 25 governs parliamentary presentation and entry into force of a specific order in council under Article 5(6); it neither alters the audit duty nor conflicts with its content, timing, or addressees.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions use mandatory language, but they regulate different actors and actions: Provision A concerns an essential or important entity informing service recipients about significant incidents, while Provision B concerns conformity-assessment bodies submitting a notification application. No fact pattern makes the same actor unable to perform both duties.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can plainly coexist because they impose separate obligations on different actors, with different triggers and recipients. A conformity-assessment body could submit its application under Provision B and, if it is also an essential or important entity experiencing a significant incident affecting service provision, separately inform its service recipients under Provision A.

verdict.shared_subject: Annual reporting and accountability by public data-protection authorities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose annual obligations on data-protection authorities, so they share an institutional accountability theme. However, one concerns preparing a draft budget before the relevant budget year, while the other concerns notifying the Commission of fines and proceedings imposed or initiated under a specific EU provision; the texts do not require incompatible acts, deadlines, or content.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The Autoriteit persoonsgegevens can prepare its annual draft budget and the European Data Protection Supervisor can separately notify the Commission of fines and proceedings. Even if the same or related authority were involved, both duties can be performed cumulatively because they concern different subjects and triggers.

verdict.shared_subject: Retention of communications traffic data and AI-generated logs
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose retention-related duties on potentially overlapping operators, but they concern different categories of records and arise under different conditions. A could require traffic data to be removed or anonymised once no longer needed for transmitting communications, while B requires retention of high-risk AI logs under financial-services law; if the logs contain traffic data, the duties could point in opposite directions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: A applies to traffic data processed and stored by providers of public electronic communications networks or services, whereas B applies to financial institutions retaining automatically generated logs from high-risk AI systems. The texts do not establish that the AI logs are traffic data, that they are no longer needed for transmission, or that B requires retaining data that A requires deleting; the duties can therefore be satisfied cumulatively, with anonymisation or retention of only non-traffic log content where necessary.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A financial institution that is also a public electronic communications provider retains automatically generated high-risk-AI logs containing subscriber traffic data after that data is no longer needed for transmitting communications, because financial-services law requires retaining the logs.
verdict.missing_reference: The missing provisions are the applicable exceptions or priority rules determining whether the financial-services retention duty for AI logs authorises or overrides retention of traffic data that Article 11.5 requires to be removed or anonymised, and whether the logs in fact constitute such traffic data.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of special-category personal data and the resulting GDPR compliance obligations
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits processing special-category personal data unless one of the listed Article 9 exceptions applies, while Provision B mandates appointment of a data protection officer for large-scale processing of such data. One might argue that the mandatory appointment presupposes or facilitates processing that Provision A restricts.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B does not authorise or require the processing of special-category data; it only imposes an organisational obligation when such processing occurs at large scale. The controller can comply with both by ensuring that processing has a valid Article 9 legal basis under Provision A and appointing a data protection officer under Provision B.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of personal data, including special-category personal data, and the data subject’s access request
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A removes the prohibition on processing special-category personal data only in listed circumstances, while Provision B requires the controller to provide the data subject with a copy of the personal data being processed. If the requested copy contains special-category data and none of A’s listed conditions applies, providing it could appear to require disclosure of data whose processing is prohibited.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A concerns whether processing special-category data is permitted; Provision B concerns the data subject’s access right to data that is being processed. The provisions can be satisfied cumulatively: the controller must provide a copy where the access right applies, while ensuring that any special-category processing and disclosure is covered by an applicable legal basis or exception. Provision B also expressly preserves the rights and freedoms of others.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A controller is processing a person’s health data, the person requests a copy of all personal data under Article 15, and the requested copy would disclose that health data to the person, but the facts do not establish explicit consent, vital interests, a qualifying non-profit activity, prior public disclosure, or a legal-claim/judicial-purpose exception under Provision A.
verdict.decisive_exception: The text does not establish whether the Article 15 access obligation, or disclosure of the special-category data in response to that obligation, is itself covered by an applicable exception to the special-category processing prohibition in Article 22/Article 9(2). verdict.shared_subject: Electronic communications information and data-subject access rights
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A extends certain electronic-communications requirements to information stored on or accessed from a terminal device even when the mechanism is not an electronic communications network. Provision B separately requires informing a data subject about Article 46 safeguards when personal data are transferred to a third country or international organisation; one might argue that device-level storage or access could involve such data and create overlapping compliance obligations.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties with different triggers and purposes. A concerns the applicability of requirements for storing information on, or accessing information from, a terminal device; B grants an individual information right specifically when personal data are transferred to a third country or international organisation. Nothing in A permits, prohibits, or substitutes for the disclosure required by B.

verdict.shared_subject: Access to an information-society service and confidentiality of conformity-assessment information
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern conduct involving information-society services or information handled in a regulated digital context. One might argue that access to a public-law entity’s service could require consent, while the other requires confidentiality of information obtained during conformity assessments, potentially limiting disclosure or use of that information.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A prohibits conditioning user access on consent under the referenced consent rule; provision B imposes confidentiality duties only on notified bodies and their personnel concerning information obtained during conformity-assessment activities, subject to legal-disclosure exceptions. They regulate different actors, conduct, and triggers, and compliance with both is straightforward.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern digital services or ICT operations, but Provision A regulates whether access to a public-law entity’s information-society service may depend on user consent, while Provision B requires financial entities to maintain outage-related activity registers. No concrete obligation in B makes service access conditional on consent, and no conflict follows from the shared digital-law context.

Provision B requires financial entities to keep accessible registers when continuity or response-and-recovery plans are activated; an entity can maintain those registers without making user access conditional on consent.

verdict.shared_subject: National competent authorities’ handling of incident-related information
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires CSIRTs or competent authorities to provide information about significant incidents, cyber threats and near-incidents to authorities competent under Directive (EU) 2022/2557. Provision B requires national competent authorities, when performing their tasks, to comply with Article 78 confidentiality obligations; disclosure of the information in A could therefore be constrained if Article 78 prohibits or limits that disclosure.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different aspects of the authorities’ work: A requires specified information to be supplied to the competent authorities under Directive 2022/2557, while B requires national competent authorities to observe confidentiality obligations. The information can be transmitted through confidential channels and handled in accordance with Article 78, so the texts shown do not require incompatible conduct.

verdict.decisive_exception: Whether Article 78 permits disclosure or onward sharing of the incident, cyber-threat and near-incident information required by Article 23.

verdict.evidence_span_b: Bij de uitvoering van hun taken voldoen de nationale bevoegde autoriteiten aan de in artikel 78 vastgelegde vertrouwelijkheidsverplichtingen.

verdict.shared_subject: Information about security incidents involving personal data in electronic public services
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires covered bodies and organisations to provide the Minister with information needed to prevent or end breaches of secure and reliable access. Provision B removes the notification requirement where appropriate technical measures make the affected personal data unintelligible to unauthorised persons; one might argue that supplying information about such an incident could undermine the protective treatment or disclose information that need not be notified to the data subject.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different recipients and serve different purposes: A concerns information supplied to the Minister for access-security measures, while B concerns notification by a provider to the affected person under the personal-data-breach regime. B exempts only the notification described in its second paragraph; it does not prohibit regulatory or security information-sharing under A, and A does not require notifying the affected person.

No concrete incompatibility, competing benchmark, or conflicting permission is stated.

The provisions have different addressees, triggers, and subject matter, so satisfying one does not obstruct satisfying the other.

verdict.evidence_span_b: Conformiteitsbeoordelingsinstanties dienen een verzoek om aanmelding in bij de aanmeldende autoriteit van de lidstaat waar zij zijn gevestigd.

verdict.shared_subject: Entities covered by BWBR0052872
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose obligations on covered entities, but they regulate different matters: Article 24 extends governance rules to managing partners of a limited partnership, while Article 44 requires changes to previously supplied register information to be reported. Nothing in either text makes compliance with one prevent compliance with the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: A covered limited partnership can apply the Article 24 governance rules to its managing partners and separately report any changes to its Article 44 registration information within two weeks. The provisions have different subjects, triggers, and addressees, and can be complied with cumulatively.

verdict.shared_subject: Protection and notification of personal data affected by security incidents
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires an entity to adopt broad cybersecurity measures, including encryption where appropriate, while Provision B makes notification unnecessary when the data are encrypted or otherwise unintelligible to unauthorised persons. One might argue that A's security duty could lead an entity to rely on encryption and thereby avoid B's notification duty, creating uncertainty about whether security compliance substitutes for notification.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose cumulative, compatible requirements. A requires risk-based cybersecurity measures, including encryption only 'when appropriate'; B separately defines when notification is not required, based on the AP's assessment that appropriate technical protective measures make the data unintelligible to unauthorised persons. Compliance with A does not itself establish B's specific notification exception, so the entity can satisfy both by implementing suitable security and notifying unless B's conditions are met.
verdict.decisive_exception: The notification exception in Provision B depends on the Autoriteit persoonsgegevens judging the technical measures appropriate and the data encrypted or otherwise unintelligible to anyone without access rights; Provision A does not deem its cybersecurity measures sufficient for that exception.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing and rectification of special-category personal data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits processing special-category personal data unless one of its listed exceptions applies. Provision B gives the data subject an immediate right to rectify inaccurate personal data, which can include special-category data; complying with that right may require processing or modifying such data where no Article 22 exception is available.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B does not itself require unlawful processing: rectification can be carried out only insofar as processing is legally permitted, and Provision A expressly contains exceptions that may cover particular processing contexts. The texts therefore do not establish that the rectification right overrides the special-category processing prohibition.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A controller holds inaccurate health data about an individual. The individual requests rectification under Article 16, but correcting and storing the amended health data would constitute processing of special-category data and none of the Article 22 exceptions shown applies. The controller must then confront the individual rectification right while lacking an established basis under Provision A for the necessary processing.
verdict.decisive_exception: It is not established whether the Article 16 rectification processing is covered by an applicable Article 9(2) exception, or whether another provision supplies a legal basis that satisfies the special-category-data prohibition. In particular, Article 22's listed exceptions do not expressly mention rectification.

verdict.shared_subject: GDPR-related decisions and prior consultation by a supervisory authority
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern GDPR procedures and impose time limits on written administrative action. A superficial comparison might suggest that the general deadline incorporated by Article 34 could differ from Article 36’s maximum eight-week period, potentially creating uncertainty about which deadline governs a supervisory authority’s written response.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 34 concerns a written decision on a data subject’s request under GDPR Articles 15–22, whereas Article 36 concerns written advice following prior consultation by a controller. They regulate different procedures, actors and triggers, and Article 34 expressly applies the deadlines in GDPR Article 12(3), so nothing in the texts requires the same act to comply with both deadlines.

verdict.shared_subject: Enforcement powers for violations by entities providing domain-name registration services
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions authorize an administrative enforcement measure for violations, so the same conduct might attract both a coercive order and a fine. However, neither provision prohibits the other measure, and they concern different legal violations and competent authorities.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A permits a competent authority to impose a periodic penalty payment for violations of specified domain-name provisions, while Provision B permits the Dutch Data Protection Authority to impose a fine for specified GDPR violations. An entity can comply with both underlying regimes, and the provisions can operate cumulatively without requiring incompatible conduct.

verdict.shared_subject: Recognition of an ontsluitende dienst or machtigingsdienst and exemption from obligations under BWBR0052872
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: The provisions could appear related if the same organisation is both an essential or important entity under BWBR0052872 and a service provider seeking recognition under BWBR0048156. In that situation, an exemption from obligations under articles 25–30 might seem to remove requirements relevant to the recognition decision, while article 11 requires compliance with the applicable recognition rules.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 32 concerns a discretionary exemption from specified obligations under articles 25–30, for entities or activities within listed public-interest domains. Article 11 independently requires recognition when the service satisfies the rules applicable to that service; nothing in either text says that the exemption grants recognition, prevents recognition, or substitutes for the recognition requirements. The provisions can therefore be complied with cumulatively, and they may apply to different actors or activities.

verdict.shared_subject: Access and acceptance of identification means for electronic public services requiring a substantial or high assurance level
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A requires access to be granted only when the identification means meets at least the assurance level required for the service. B requires public authorities to accept all admitted identification means, plus the listed electronic declarations and EU-notified schemes, without expressly repeating A’s minimum-assurance condition; if one accepted means fell below the required level, B could appear to require acceptance where A requires refusal.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be read cumulatively: B identifies the categories that must be accepted, while A independently limits access to means meeting the service’s required assurance level. The listed means in B can therefore be accepted only insofar as they satisfy A, and B’s wording does not expressly deem acceptance sufficient to override the assurance requirement.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of special-category personal data by a CSIRT
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits and limits a CSIRT's processing of special-category data where necessary for specified statutory tasks. Provision B states that processing special-category data is prohibited unless one of its listed Article 9(2) exceptions applies; the text shown does not establish that necessity for CSIRT tasks under A is itself one of those exceptions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can operate cumulatively: a CSIRT may process such data only when necessary for its specified tasks under A and only when an exception under B applies. If the processing also has a qualifying basis such as explicit consent, vital interests, public disclosure, or legal claims, both provisions are satisfied.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A CSIRT processes health data incidentally obtained during a cyber-incident investigation because that processing is necessary for one of its Article 16 tasks under A, but the affected person has not consented, the data were not manifestly made public, no vital-interest or legal-claim situation applies, and none of B's other listed exceptions is established. The CSIRT is permitted to process the data under A's task-necessity condition but remains subject to B's prohibition unless an applicable Article 9(2) exception exists.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the necessity of processing for the CSIRT's Article 16 tasks under A qualifies as one of the Article 9(2) exceptions incorporated by B, or whether another listed exception in B applies. The provisions shown do not establish that legal basis.

verdict.shared_subject: Information-handling duties involving cybersecurity vulnerability reports and notified conformity-assessment bodies
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the coordinator to follow up vulnerability reports and safeguard the reporter’s anonymity, while Provision B requires a notifying authority to provide the Commission with all relevant information about a notified body on request. If a vulnerability report concerned information relevant to a notified body’s competence, disclosure to the Commission might appear to risk revealing the reporter’s identity.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different actors and concern different subject matters: A concerns a coordinator handling voluntary vulnerability reports, whereas B concerns a notifying authority supplying information about a notified body’s competence. Nothing in B requires disclosure of a reporter’s identity, and the duties can be performed cumulatively by anonymising or otherwise protecting irrelevant personal information.

verdict.shared_subject: Access to public-sector information-society services and data-subject information rights
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern interactions between a user/data subject and a public-sector service, but they regulate different matters. One prohibits conditioning access on consent for terminal-equipment storage or access, while the other grants information about safeguards when personal data are transferred to a third country or international organisation; no concrete incompatibility follows.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A removes consent as a condition of access in a specified public-sector service context, whereas provision B requires notice of appropriate safeguards for an international transfer. A service provider can comply with both by not conditioning access on consent and, where a relevant transfer occurs, informing the data subject about the Article 46 safeguards.

verdict.shared_subject: Reporting or forwarding serious/significant ICT and cybersecurity incidents to competent authorities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern incident notifications and the involvement of competent authorities, so an incident involving a financial-market entity might appear to fall under both reporting frameworks. However, provision A is a transitional deeming and forwarding rule for notifications under the Dutch Wbni, while provision B preserves an ESMA/host-state-authority responsibility for a central securities depository under specified cross-border conditions; neither text requires incompatible conduct.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be cumulatively satisfied: a qualifying pre-existing Wbni notification may be treated as an early warning and forwarded by the Dutch Minister, while the competent authority may separately transmit incident details to the relevant host-state authority under provision B. They concern different legal mechanisms, actors, triggers, and institutional responsibilities, with no conflicting deadline, content, or prohibition.

verdict.shared_subject: The administrator’s disclosure of numbers and data and exemptions under the same statutory scheme
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 11.10 restricts disclosures by the administrator to two specified purposes: emergency assistance or combating misuse of a public-services emergency number. Article 11.12 allows an exemption to be granted subject to limitations and conditions, which could appear to permit a disclosure outside those purposes.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 11.12 merely establishes competence to grant an exemption and attach conditions; it does not state that an exemption overrides the substantive purposes in Article 11.10. The provisions can therefore operate cumulatively: any disclosure must remain within Article 11.10 unless an applicable exemption provision expressly creates an exception.
verdict.missing_reference: The provision governing the legal effect and scope of an exemption under Article 11.12 would be needed to determine whether it can override Article 11.10’s disclosure restriction.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the exemption is legally capable of authorising disclosures outside the two purposes listed in Article 11.10 is not established by the text shown.

verdict.shared_subject: ICT incidents involving personal data and security measures
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A removes the notification duty when personal data affected by a breach are encrypted or otherwise unintelligible to unauthorised persons. Provision B nevertheless requires financial entities to register all ICT-related incidents and significant cyberthreats and to document their underlying causes, so an incident covered by B may still require internal recording even when A removes external notification.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different matters: A concerns whether a provider must notify affected individuals after a personal-data breach, while B concerns a financial entity’s internal incident-management and recording processes. A financial entity can comply with both by recording the incident under B while relying on A only to avoid the notification required by the referenced provision.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern regulatory oversight in the digital sector, so an entity involved in ICT services and AI could encounter both regimes. However, Article 57 governs a competent authority’s notification to an oversight forum, while Article 31 governs procedures of notified bodies; neither imposes an incompatible duty on the same actor or regulates the same underlying obligation.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different actors and address different matters: Article 57 requires a competent authority to notify an oversight forum when exercising specified supervisory powers, whereas Article 31 requires notified bodies to maintain procedures that account for provider and AI-system characteristics. Both duties can be performed simultaneously without one preventing compliance with the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Internal allocation of tasks within a committee or membership body
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions require an internal allocation of tasks, but they address different bodies and decision-makers: Provision A requires the members to establish a division of tasks and involve extraordinary members as far as possible, while Provision B requires the Committee's rules of procedure to establish the division between the chair and vice-chairs. No incompatibility follows from performing both allocations.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can readily be satisfied cumulatively: the members can allocate tasks while involving extraordinary members, and the Committee can separately specify the chair's and vice-chairs' tasks in its rules of procedure. They concern different institutional arrangements and do not prescribe conflicting task assignments, deadlines, or contents.

verdict.shared_subject: The scope of obligations concerning electronic business and organisational identification means and services under BWBR0048156.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions carve out situations from rules concerning business and organisational means, so they could appear to overlap if a private-system party operating only at level 1 also provides services to a non-Dutch-established service provider through the central portal. However, the texts do not impose incompatible commands: Article 15 excludes specified central-portal activities from the acceptance duty, while Article 24 excludes a different category of parties from its transitional provision.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 15 concerns the duty to accept the means and declarations referred to in Article 15(2), with exceptions for specified central-portal access and services to non-Dutch-established service providers. Article 24 simply states that its transitional provision does not apply to parties conducting exclusively level-1 activities; both exclusions can operate simultaneously without requiring an actor to accept and refuse the same means.

verdict.shared_subject: The handling and onward transmission of significant-incident reports by authorities and central contact points
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern information derived from incident reports involving essential entities, and both contemplate onward communication to another authority or contact point. One could therefore initially suspect overlapping transmission channels or duties for the same report.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A requires the competent authority to provide information about a reported significant incident to the authority under the Critical Entities Resilience Act. Provision B requires the central contact point, upon request, to forward reports received under Article 23(1) to central contact points in other Member States. These are different recipients, actors, and triggers, and both duties can be performed cumulatively without incompatible content, timing, or prohibition.

verdict.shared_subject: Dutch electronic communications regulation, but the provisions address different subjects
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions appear in the same statutory chapter and concern regulatory control over communications services: Article 11.9 imposes detailed obligations concerning caller identification, while Article 11.12 allows conditions and restrictions to be attached to an exemption. One might argue that an exemption under Article 11.12 could alter how the Article 11.9 obligations apply.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 11.9 requires providers offering number identification to provide specified blocking and refusal options. Article 11.12 merely states that an exemption may be granted subject to limitations and conditions; it neither grants an exemption here nor says that an exemption overrides Article 11.9. The provisions can therefore operate cumulatively without any stated incompatibility.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulation of electronic communications and related data handling
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A imposes a concrete maximum retention period for personal data processed by the CSIRT. Provision B authorises further rules and requirements concerning measures imposed on providers, so later rules could potentially affect how providers handle communications-related systems or data. However, B does not itself require retention, prohibit deletion, or establish a conflicting period.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: A requires the CSIRT to delete the specified personal data no later than 12 months after first processing, while B merely grants competence to adopt further rules concerning specified measures and requirements for public electronic-communications providers. The competence in B can be exercised consistently with A, and nothing in B displaces or contradicts A’s deletion duty.

verdict.shared_subject: The exercise of data-subject rights under Chapter III of the GDPR in journalistic, academic, artistic, or literary processing
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 43 excludes the Act from applying to exclusively journalistic, academic, artistic, or literary processing, while Article 5 regulates who exercises Chapter III data-subject rights, including through a legal representative. If Article 5 were applicable to such processing, it could require representative involvement; however, Article 43 expressly preserves Articles 1–5, so its exclusion does not remove Article 5.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions expressly operate together: Article 43's exception excludes the Act generally but expressly leaves Articles 1–5 applicable. Article 5 therefore continues to govern the exercise of the relevant rights, including by legal representatives, even for processing within Article 43's stated purposes; there is no incompatible command or prohibition.

verdict.shared_subject: Security-related regulation and the adoption of a general administrative measure
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern security-related regulation, but they operate on different legal objects: Provision A delays submitting a draft general administrative measure for four weeks, while Provision B authorises the Minister to impose security measures on communications providers within a specified period. One might argue that the procedural waiting period could delay security obligations that the Minister needs to impose promptly.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A is a procedural prohibition governing when a proposal for an administrative measure under Article 21(5) may be submitted to Parliament; it does not prohibit or delay the Minister's separate competence under Provision B to impose measures on providers. Provision B merely permits imposing obligations within a specified period, so both can be complied with without any incompatible command or deadline.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern information held by public authorities or service-related administrators, so one might initially ask whether information supplied for the national register could also be recorded under the telecommunications provision. However, neither text prohibits the other’s activity or imposes incompatible handling requirements.

verdict.shared_subject: Protection and security of personal data in ICT systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A removes the notification duty when the provider has taken appropriate technical measures making the data unintelligible to unauthorised persons. Provision B requires financial entities to maintain high standards of confidentiality and integrity and to implement ICT-security measures. One might argue that A permits non-notification after encryption while B requires security measures that could imply incident handling or disclosure, but B does not itself require notification or prohibit reliance on A’s exception.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose complementary duties. A concerns whether a personal-data breach must be notified to the affected person, with an exception for appropriately protected data; B concerns the design and operation of ICT-security policies and controls, including confidentiality, integrity, and protection against unauthorised access. A financial entity can satisfy B’s security duties while applying A’s notification exception where its technical measures make the breached data unintelligible.

verdict.shared_subject: Procedural duties of courts and supervisory authorities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions describe procedural obligations involving responses to requests, so one might initially suspect that the court’s handling of a request could overlap with the supervisory authority’s duty to report results or explain a refusal. However, the texts assign the duties to different actors and regulate different proceedings.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A requires a court to grant a request when justified and, where necessary, hear interested parties before deciding. Provision B requires the requested supervisory authority to inform another supervisory authority of results or progress and to give reasons for a refusal; these duties can operate independently without requiring incompatible conduct.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of special-category personal data by trust-service providers
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits processing of special-category personal data in several cases without requiring the specific consent condition stated in provision B, such as where the data were manifestly made public or processing is necessary for legal claims. Provision B, however, requires trust-service providers to process only data obtained from the data subject or with that person’s explicit consent, unless its separate exception applies.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be read cumulatively: even where A removes the prohibition under Article 9(2), B independently limits the source and necessity of personal data processed by trust-service providers. The apparent conflict depends on whether A’s exceptions, or B’s paragraph 3 exception, displace B’s source/consent requirement; that relationship is not established by the provisions shown.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A trust-service provider processes a person’s special-category personal data because the data were manifestly made public by that person, relying on provision A, but obtains the data from a public source rather than directly from the person and without the person’s explicit consent. A permits the processing prohibition not to apply, while B appears to forbid the provider from processing data unless obtained from the person or with explicit consent, and the shown text does not establish an exception covering this situation.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether provision A’s Article 9(2) exceptions, or another applicable legal provision, also overrides provision B’s independent requirement that the data be obtained from the data subject or with explicit consent; paragraph 3 of B mentions fraud detection and processing required by law, but does not expressly resolve the Article 9(2) cases in A.

Preparing documentation does not replace consultation, and consultation does not replace documentation; both can be performed before deployment.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A creates exceptions to the duty to accept only the identification means and declarations referred to in Article 15(2), including for certain non-Dutch-established service providers using the central portal. Provision B extends requirements from another regime to information storage or access achieved by means other than an electronic communications network, so an activity might appear to fall under both regimes and require different treatment.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different matters and have different triggers. Provision A concerns acceptance of recognised business and organisational identification means for specified electronic public services and expressly removes that duty in two central-portal situations; Provision B merely extends unspecified requirements to certain technically equivalent activities and does not state that any identification means must be accepted or rejected.

verdict.shared_subject: A high-risk AI system involving personal-data transfers to a third country or international organisation
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision B requires the high-risk AI provider and relevant third parties to specify information, technical access and assistance sufficient to enable compliance with the AI Act. If providing that assistance entails transferring personal data to a third country or international organisation, Article 44 permits no transfer unless the GDPR Chapter V conditions are met, potentially limiting how the contractual assistance can be delivered.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 25 does not require any particular transfer of personal data, and its required assistance can be designed and supplied without such a transfer or through a GDPR-compliant transfer mechanism. Article 44 therefore operates as an additional condition on any transfer, not as a prohibition on the contractual cooperation required by Article 25.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a provider of a public electronic communications service to maintain an overview of all personal-data breaches. Provision B excludes NIS2 provisions, including supervision and enforcement, where equivalent sector-specific EU requirements apply, which could create an apparent question whether the NIS2 regime displaces other incident-related obligations.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B does not prohibit maintaining a personal-data-breach overview; it only limits the application of relevant NIS2 provisions to entities covered by equivalent sector-specific EU legislation. Provision A is a separate obligation concerning all personal-data breaches, and nothing in the shown text says that the NIS2 exclusion repeals, overrides, or excuses compliance with it.

verdict.shared_subject: Data protection governance involving a temporary committee or advisory body and a data protection officer
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits a committee or advisory body to process special-category and criminal-offence personal data when its conditions are met. Provision B requires the controller or processor to protect the data protection officer’s independence, but it does not itself regulate or prohibit that processing, so no incompatible command is apparent.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative rules: A establishes a narrowly conditioned exception to a processing prohibition for a committee or advisory body, while B governs the DPO’s institutional independence and reporting line. An organisation can satisfy both by meeting A’s safeguards and ensuring that its DPO receives no instructions concerning the performance of DPO tasks.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits processing special-category personal data unless one of its listed Article 9(2) exceptions applies. Provision B requires the controller to assess compatibility of further processing and expressly directs attention to whether special categories are processed, which could appear to support or permit such further processing without itself establishing an Article 9 exception.

Provision A's exceptions and the GDPR's separate Article 9 requirements remain applicable cumulatively; considering the sensitive nature of the data under B does not displace A's prohibition.

verdict.shared_subject: A high-risk AI system involving personal-data processing and its provider/controller
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions may apply to the same high-risk AI system, but they impose different compliance obligations: GDPR Article 35 requires the controller to conduct a data-protection impact assessment before processing, while the AI Act provision concerns the notified body's identification number on CE marking and related advertising. The obligations do not prescribe incompatible conduct or benchmarks.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The obligations are cumulative and concern different matters: the controller can complete the required impact assessment before processing while the provider or notified body applies the CE-marking identification-number requirements. Nothing in either text exempts, substitutes for, or prohibits compliance with the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulatory requests for security-audit or related information from regulated ICT/electronic-communications providers
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits the Minister to impose a security-control obligation on providers of public electronic communications networks or services, including delivery of the results. Provision B permits or requires the lead overseer to obtain broad information, expressly including ICT-security-audit reports, from critical ICT third-party providers; if the same entity and audit are covered, the provisions could create overlapping supervisory demands, but neither text makes compliance with one incompatible with the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose cumulatively satisfiable duties or powers: an entity can undergo the independent security control and provide its results to the Minister while also supplying relevant audit reports and other information to the lead overseer. They concern different authorities, regulated categories, and supervisory functions, and no provision prohibits duplicate disclosure or makes one request satisfy the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Use of an identification means in electronic public services and AI-based identification
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can concern an organisation using an identification system for a natural person. Provision A requires acceptance of an authorised identification means in specified electronic services, while Provision B prohibits the responsible deployer from taking measures or decisions based on the system's identification unless at least two natural persons separately verify and confirm it.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose cumulative duties rather than incompatible commands: the public body or designated organisation can accept the authorised identification means while ensuring that any resulting measure or decision is based on the identification only after the required human verification. They also have different triggers and scopes, since Article 7 applies only where the Ministerial regulation so provides and the required assurance level applies, whereas Article 14 applies to specified high-risk AI systems under Annex III, point 1(a).

verdict.shared_subject: Regulatory treatment of cybersecurity incidents and related oversight
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the Minister or designated authority to conduct analyses and technical research concerning specified threats and incidents, while excluding investigations into the persons or organisations responsible for them. Provision B allocates competence among data-protection supervisory authorities to handle complaints or infringements, potentially concerning the same incident or organisation, but it does not prohibit the technical research described in A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different functions: A concerns assistance-related technical analysis of network and information-system threats and incidents, expressly excluding attribution investigations; B concerns which supervisory authority is competent to handle a GDPR complaint or infringement. The same incident can be technically analysed under A while a competent supervisory authority separately handles any GDPR matter under B.

verdict.shared_subject: Entities that may be subject to cybersecurity governance rules and organisations involved in reliable electronic services
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A extends the application of governance rules to each partner of a general partnership when the essential or important entity has that legal form. Provision B requires ministerial rules governing how recognised services use designated attributes for reliable electronic access. One might argue that both regulate organisational responsibilities in digital services, but neither prescribes conduct that would prevent compliance with the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A concerns the personal scope of governance obligations for partners of a general partnership classified as an essential or important entity. Provision B concerns future ministerial rules for recognised services' use of designated attributes to ensure reliable electronic services; the duties have different subjects, triggers, and purposes and can be complied with cumulatively.
