verdict.shared_subject: Notification of significant cybersecurity incidents by essential or important entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 30 imposes a direct notification duty on the entity, while Article 4 can make the Directive’s relevant provisions, including supervision and enforcement, inapplicable where equivalent sector-specific requirements exist. If Article 4 were read as displacing Article 30 even though the sector-specific regime does not itself impose the same recipient-notification duty, the entity could face uncertainty about whether Article 30 still applies.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 4 is a coordination rule, not an unconditional prohibition: it removes the Directive’s provisions only where sector-specific Union law requires equivalent cybersecurity risk-management or significant-incident-reporting obligations. Article 30 can therefore apply normally where no such sector-specific regime exists or where its requirements are not equivalent; and the supplied paragraph 2 gives criteria for equivalence rather than creating an irreconcilable command.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit stelt in voorkomend geval onverwijld de ontvangers van haar diensten in kennis van significante incidenten die een nadelige invloed kunnen hebben op de verlening van die diensten.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Indien sectorspecifieke rechtshandelingen van de Unie voorschrijven dat essentiële of belangrijke entiteiten risicobeheersmaatregelen op het gebied van cyberbeveiliging moeten nemen of significante incidenten moeten melden, en indien deze eisen ten minste gelijkwaardig zijn aan de in deze richtlijn vastgestelde verplichtingen, zijn de relevante bepalingen van deze richtlijn, met inbegrip van de in hoofdstuk VII bedoelde toezichts- en handhavingsbepalingen, niet van toepassing op dergelijke entiteiten.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: The provisions concern different functions: one governs how a CSIRT processes voluntary cybersecurity reports, while the other governs the organisation of notifying authorities deciding on conformity-assessment-body notifications. No actor, decision, duty, or resource is shared in a way that creates an incompatibility.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Both provisions can be fully complied with independently. A CSIRT may process voluntary reports under Article 36 and prioritise mandatory reports, while notifying authorities ensure that competent, independent persons decide on conformity-assessment-body notifications; neither rule limits or alters the other.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Het CSIRT verwerkt de vrijwillige meldingen, bedoeld in het eerste lid, overeenkomstig de in artikel 36 omschreven procedure.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Aanmeldende autoriteiten worden zodanig georganiseerd dat besluiten in verband met de aanmelding van conformiteitsbeoordelingsinstanties worden genomen door bekwame personen die niet de beoordeling van die instanties hebben verricht.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing personal data concerning criminal convictions and offences in the context of post-remote biometric identification
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A restricts processing of criminal-offence data unless it is under public-authority supervision or authorised by Union or Member State law with appropriate safeguards. Provision B requires or regulates such processing by a high-risk AI operator, including prior authorisation in many cases, but the text shown does not itself establish that every use permitted or required by B satisfies A’s supervision or safeguards conditions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B expressly preserves the application of other data-protection rules and requires judicial or administrative authorisation for the relevant uses. Thus, an operator can comply with both by using the system only under the supervision or legal authorisation required by A and by meeting B’s additional safeguards; B does not expressly permit processing outside A’s conditions.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A law-enforcement authority uses a high-risk post-remote biometric-identification system to search for a person suspected of a specific offence, obtains the judicial or administrative authorisation required by Provision B, and processes data concerning the suspected offence. The text of B does not establish that this authorisation necessarily constitutes the public-authority supervision or appropriate-rights-and-freedoms safeguards required by Provision A, leaving the relationship between the two conditions unresolved.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the judicial or administrative authorisation and safeguards required under Provision B constitute the supervision or Union/Member State-law authorisation with appropriate safeguards required by Provision A; Provision B itself does not establish that equivalence.
verdict.evidence_span_a: mogen op grond van artikel 6, lid 1, alleen worden verwerkt onder toezicht van de overheid of indien de verwerking is toegestaan bij Unierechtelijke of lidstaatrechtelijke bepalingen die passende waarborgen voor de rechten en vrijheden van de betrokkenen bieden
verdict.evidence_span_b: Deze alinea doet geen afbreuk aan artikel 9 van Verordening (EU) 2016/679 en artikel 10 van Richtlijn (EU) 2016/680 voor de verwerking van biometrische gegevens.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulation of entities and rules concerning measures
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires measures under article 21 to receive approval from the governing body of an essential or important entity. Provision B authorises further rules by governmental decree concerning article 11a, but it does not itself prescribe a conflicting approval requirement or prohibit governance approval.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions operate at different normative levels: A imposes an internal governance approval obligation, while B merely grants competence to make further rules under article 11a. Any future rules made under B could coexist with A unless they expressly imposed an incompatible requirement, which the text shown does not do.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De maatregelen, bedoeld in artikel 21, behoeven de goedkeuring van het bestuur van de essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Bij of krachtens algemene maatregel van bestuur kunnen nadere regels worden gesteld ten aanzien van het bepaalde in dit artikel.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of special-category and criminal-offence personal data by a commission or advisory body
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits a commission or advisory body to process special-category or criminal-offence data when its stated safeguards and conditions are met. Provision B may require the controller or processor to appoint a data-protection officer for large-scale processing of those same categories, but that appointment duty does not prohibit or negate the processing permission.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different matters: A establishes a narrowly conditioned exception to a processing prohibition, while B imposes an organisational governance duty when processing is large-scale or otherwise falls within Article 37(1). A commission can comply with A and, if B applies, also appoint a data-protection officer; satisfying B does not replace A’s necessity, consent-impossibility, or safeguards requirements.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of personal data and supervisory access powers
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires authorised persons to obtain an explicit special mandate from the Dutch Data Protection Authority before exercising the power to enter a dwelling without the occupant’s consent. Provision B prohibits collecting or processing the relevant personal data for other purposes without the data subject’s explicit consent, which could appear to constrain data obtained or used during that supervisory activity.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different conduct: A concerns the authority and mandate required to exercise an entry power, while B concerns the purposes for which specified personal data may be collected or processed. Moreover, the supplied context for B expressly provides exceptions where processing is necessary for fraud investigation or otherwise required by law, so lawful supervisory processing need not conflict with B.
verdict.decisive_exception: None is needed for the better-supported classification. Although the context mentions an exception for processing required by or under the law, Provision A itself does not regulate processing of the data covered by Provision B.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De in het eerste lid bedoelde personen behoeven voor de uitoefening van de in het tweede lid omschreven bevoegdheid de uitdrukkelijke en bijzondere volmacht van de Autoriteit persoonsgegevens, onverminderd het bepaalde in artikel 2 van de Algemene wet op het binnentreden.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De in het eerste lid bedoelde persoonsgegevens worden niet voor andere doeleinden verzameld of verwerkt, tenzij de betrokkene daarvoor zijn uitdrukkelijke toestemming heeft gegeven.

verdict.shared_subject: A competent authority adopting an enforcement decision and a supervisory authority adopting a draft decision subject to the GDPR consistency procedure
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions regulate timing by a competent authority, and B prohibits adopting the draft decision during the specified period. If A's enforcement decision were also a draft decision of the kind covered by Article 64(1), A's power to determine an end date could appear to permit or require action during B's standstill period.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: A concerns the conditions under which a Dutch competent authority may determine an end date for an entity to end a NIS2-related infringement; it does not require adoption within any particular period. B concerns only a supervisory authority's draft decision falling within the specific Article 64(1) categories and prohibits its adoption during the Article 64(3) period. The provisions therefore address different decision types and can both be obeyed.
verdict.decisive_exception: Not applicable: the shown provisions do not establish that the Article 76 decision is an Article 64(1) draft decision or that their timing rules apply to the same decision.

verdict.shared_subject: Confidentiality and disclosure of information in telecommunications security audits and AI conformity-assessment activities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can involve information obtained during an externally performed compliance or security assessment, and Provision A requires an operator to provide audit results to the Minister. If a notified body covered by Provision B performed the audit or held the results, its confidentiality duties might appear to restrict disclosure to the Minister unless disclosure is legally required or falls within the stated exception.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A concerns a Minister's power to impose a security-control and reporting obligation on providers of public electronic communications networks or services. Provision B concerns notified bodies and their personnel during conformity-assessment activities under the AI Regulation; it expressly permits disclosure where legally required and to the notifying authorities, and it does not prohibit the provider from complying with a separate reporting obligation.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Onze Minister kan een aanbieder van openbare elektronische communicatienetwerken of openbare elektronische communicatiediensten de verplichting opleggen om binnen een bepaalde termijn een beveiligingscontrole te laten uitvoeren door een gekwalificeerde onafhankelijke deskundige en om de resultaten van dat onderzoek binnen een bij het besluit gestelde redelijke termijn aan Onze Minister te verstrekken.

verdict.shared_subject: Delegated rulemaking concerning incident criteria or further rules
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions authorize rules to be made by or under a general administrative measure, so they could potentially concern overlapping delegated regulation. However, neither provision requires, permits, or prohibits conduct in a way that makes compliance with the other impossible; they merely confer rulemaking competence in different statutory contexts.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A authorizes criteria for determining when an incident is significant under article 25(2), potentially differentiated by sector or entity type. Provision B authorizes further rules concerning article 11a.3, and both delegations can be exercised cumulatively without contradiction because each remains tied to its own article and subject matter.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Bij of krachtens algemene maatregel van bestuur kunnen de criteria worden vastgesteld op basis waarvan wordt bepaald of sprake is van een significant incident als bedoeld in het tweede lid, waarbij onderscheid kan worden gemaakt tussen sectoren, subsectoren, soorten entiteiten en entiteiten.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Bij of krachtens algemene maatregel van bestuur kunnen nadere regels worden gesteld ten aanzien van het bepaalde in dit artikel.

verdict.shared_subject: AI models/systems released under a free and open-source licence
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions address free/open-source AI technology, but Article 25 excludes certain third-party providers from its contractual-assistance obligation, while Article 54 states that the obligation concerning authorised representatives does not apply to qualifying free/open-source general-purpose AI model providers unless the models present systemic risks. One might argue that the provisions create uncertainty about whether open-source actors are exempt from obligations when their models are integrated into high-risk systems or present systemic risks.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different obligations, actors, and triggers. Article 25 concerns written contractual assistance for providers of high-risk AI systems and certain third parties supplying tools, services, components, or processes; Article 54 concerns the obligation of authorised representatives for providers of general-purpose AI models, with its own open-source and systemic-risk conditions. The exemptions can operate cumulatively without requiring either provision to override the other.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Dit lid is niet van toepassing op derden die andere instrumenten, diensten, processen of onderdelen dan AI-modellen voor algemene doeleinden onder een vrije en opensource licentie toegankelijk maken voor het publiek.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De in dit artikel genoemde verplichting geldt niet voor aanbieders van AI-modellen die worden vrijgegeven in het kader van een vrije en opensource licentie die de raadpleging, het gebruik, de wijziging en distributie van het model mogelijk maakt en waarvan de parameters, met inbegrip van de wegingen, de informatie over de modelarchitectuur en de informatie over het gebruik van het model, openbaar worden gemaakt, tenzij de AI-modellen voor algemene doeleinden systeemrisico’s vertonen.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions are obligations in the same instrument, but they regulate entirely different matters: provision A concerns documentation accompanying an application for recognition, while provision B concerns parliamentary scrutiny and commencement of a governmental decree. No actor would face incompatible commands from the texts.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: An applicant or recognised-holder can provide the required accredited certification statement under provision A, while the government separately follows provision B's parliamentary-submission and commencement procedure for an implementing decree. Compliance with one does not prevent compliance with the other.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Bij de aanvraag voor een erkenning wordt een verklaring gevoegd van een geaccrediteerde certificerende instelling, waaraan het vermoeden kan worden ontleend dat is voldaan aan de eisen die gelden voor de betreffende houder van de erkenning of dat middel.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Een krachtens artikel 5, zesde lid, vastgestelde algemene maatregel van bestuur wordt aan beide Kamers der Staten-Generaal overgelegd.

verdict.shared_subject: Bestuurlijke vertegenwoordiging en dienstverlening aan natuurlijke personen
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Beide bepalingen raken aan natuurlijke personen die namens een rechtspersoon of onderneming handelen. Men zou kunnen aanvoeren dat governanceverplichtingen voor bestuurders van essentiële of belangrijke entiteiten botsen met de verplichting van bestuursorganen en aangewezen organisaties om erkende bedrijfs- en organisatiemiddelen te accepteren.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: De bepalingen leggen verplichtingen op aan verschillende actoren en regelen verschillende onderwerpen: art. 24 breidt bepaalde governancevoorschriften uit tot natuurlijke personen die namens een rechtspersoon bestuurder zijn van een essentiële of belangrijke entiteit, terwijl art. 7 een acceptatieplicht voor dienstverleners bevat. Niets in art. 24 verbiedt het gebruik of de acceptatie van zulke middelen, en niets in art. 7 ontslaat bestuurders van governanceverplichtingen.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Indien een rechtspersoon het bestuur of een lid van het bestuur van een essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit is, is het bepaalde bij of krachtens het tweede tot en met zesde lid van overeenkomstige toepassing op de natuurlijke persoon of natuurlijke personen die namens die rechtspersoon zitting heeft of hebben in het bestuur van de essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit.
verdict.evidence_span_b: In afwijking van het in het eerste en tweede lid bepaalde, accepteren bestuursorganen, aangewezen organisaties en rechterlijke instanties bij hun dienstverlening aan een natuurlijk persoon alle erkende bedrijfs- en organisatiemiddelen, indien en voor zover dat middel wordt gebruikt in de toegang van een door die natuurlijke persoon gemachtigde houder die met dat middel handelt namens een onderneming of rechtspersoon.

verdict.shared_subject: Audits and inspections of third-party ICT-service providers involving personal-data transfers to third countries or international organisations
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision B requires financial entities to exercise access, inspection and audit rights against third-party ICT providers, potentially including providers or audit arrangements involving third-country or international-organisation transfers. Provision A prohibits such transfers unless the GDPR Chapter V conditions are satisfied, so an audit arrangement could require access or disclosure of personal data abroad without an established Chapter V basis.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B regulates how financial entities plan and conduct audits; it does not require transferring personal data to a third country or international organisation, nor does it authorise such transfers. The entity can comply with both by conducting audits using compliant safeguards, anonymised or non-personal data, or by ensuring that any transfer satisfies Provision A.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Persoonsgegevens die worden verwerkt of die zijn bestemd om na doorgifte aan een derde land of een internationale organisatie te worden verwerkt, mogen slechts worden doorgegeven indien, onverminderd de overige bepalingen van deze verordening, de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke en de verwerker aan de in dit hoofdstuk neergelegde voorwaarden hebben voldaan
verdict.evidence_span_b: Bij het uitoefenen van toegangs-, inspectie- en auditrechten ten aanzien van de derde aanbieder van ICT-diensten bepalen financiële entiteiten op basis van een risicogebaseerde benadering vooraf de frequentie van de audits en inspecties alsook de te controleren gebieden

verdict.shared_subject: Cybersecurity monitoring, incident information, and assistance involving electronic-service systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern information and cybersecurity-related activity involving digital systems or electronic services. One could argue that CSIRT monitoring, forensic analysis, scanning, and incident assistance may involve information that the Minister must disclose to authorities or designated organisations, creating a possible overlap in handling or sharing information.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different actors and do not prescribe incompatible treatment of the same information. Provision A assigns operational monitoring, analysis, warnings, assistance, and scanning tasks to the CSIRT, while provision B requires the Minister to provide data and information about breaches only insofar as necessary for specified recipients' lawful tasks or services; the CSIRT can perform A while the Minister separately complies with B's necessity limitation.
verdict.evidence_span_a: het verzamelen en analyseren van forensische gegevens en het zorgen voor dynamische risico- en incidentenanalyse en situationeel bewustzijn met betrekking tot cyberbeveiliging;
verdict.evidence_span_b: Onze Minister verstrekt gegevens en inlichtingen aan bestuursorganen en aangewezen organisaties, aan de ingevolge artikel 9, tweede of derde lid, toegelaten houder van een erkenning of aan een ingevolge artikel 11 erkende middelenuitgever of dienst over de inbreuk op de veilige en betrouwbare toegang tot elektronische dienstverlening voor zover dit noodzakelijk is voor een goede uitoefening van hun taken of te verlenen diensten in het kader van deze wet.

verdict.shared_subject: De bevoegdheden van de Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP)
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Men zou kunnen aanvoeren dat artikel 13 de AP uitzondert van bepaalde bevoegdheden uit de Kaderwet zelfstandige bestuursorganen, terwijl artikel 8 haar juist handhavingsbevoegdheden toekent. Dat is echter geen concrete botsing: artikel 8 ziet op specifieke sanctiebevoegdheden onder de dataverordening, niet op de in artikel 13 uitgesloten bevoegdheden.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: De bepalingen regelen verschillende bevoegdheden en verschillende wettelijke grondslagen. verdict.shared_subject: Risk assessment and testing of high-risk AI systems and personal-data processing
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose ex ante risk-related obligations on overlapping AI activities, but they require different things: GDPR Article 35 requires a data-protection impact assessment where processing is likely to create a high risk to individuals’ rights and freedoms, while the AI Act provision requires testing against predefined assessment metrics and probabilistic thresholds. This could create uncertainty about whether the AI Act’s testing process is sufficient for the GDPR assessment obligation, or whether a separate DPIA is required.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The obligations address different compliance objects and can be performed cumulatively: the AI Act testing concerns the performance and risk management of a high-risk AI system, whereas Article 35 concerns the impact of intended personal-data processing on data-protection rights. Testing the system does not purport to replace a DPIA, and conducting both obligations is feasible without contradiction.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Wanneer een soort verwerking, in het bijzonder een verwerking waarbij nieuwe technologieën worden gebruikt, gelet op de aard, de omvang, de context en de doeleinden daarvan waarschijnlijk een hoog risico inhoudt voor de rechten en vrijheden van natuurlijke personen voert de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke vóór de verwerking een beoordeling uit van het effect van de beoogde verwerkingsactiviteiten op de bescherming van persoonsgegevens.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Het testen van AI-systemen met een hoog risico vindt, zoals passend, in de loop van het ontwikkelingsproces plaats en in ieder geval voordat het systeem in de handel wordt gebracht of in gebruik wordt gesteld. Er wordt getest aan de hand van vooraf vastgestelde beoordelingsmaatstaven en probabilistische drempels die passend zijn voor het beoogde doel van het AI-systeem met een hoog risico.

verdict.shared_subject: Designation of officials responsible for supervision and enforcement
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions assign supervisory competence to designated officials, and their wording could appear to overlap where the same activity or regulated entity falls within both statutory regimes. In that situation, the designating authority differs: the competent authority under A versus the relevant Minister under B.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions concern different statutory duties and scopes: A covers compliance with its own law and specified NIS2 implementing or delegated acts, while B covers specified provisions concerning national-government bodies and designated organisations. Each can operate as an independent competence rule, with no text stating that one designation excludes or displaces the other.

The only possible overlap is that information supplied by importers might relate to ICT risks or financial-market effects, but neither provision makes the duties mutually exclusive or sets incompatible handling requirements.

The importer can provide understandable technical documentation on request while the ESAs separately prepare and submit their confidential five-year report.

verdict.shared_subject: The Autoriteit Consument en Markt (ACM) and its implementation of EU data-law obligations
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the ACM, when recording measures, to take the European Commission’s comments and recommendations into account as far as possible. Provision B requires the ACM to implement Article 10(6) of the Data Act, but neither text states what Article 10(6) requires or whether it conflicts with those Commission comments and recommendations.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, potentially cumulative duties: A concerns how the ACM records measures and its consideration of Commission input, while B concerns implementation of an external provision of the Data Act. The texts contain no incompatible command, prohibition, deadline, or indication that implementing Article 10(6) prevents the ACM from taking the Commission’s comments into account.
verdict.missing_reference: Article 10(6) of Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 (the Data Act), including any applicable European Commission comments or recommendations, is needed to determine whether implementation could conflict with the duty in Article 11.8a.

verdict.evidence_span_b: De Autoriteit Consument en Markt geeft uitvoering aan artikel 10, zesde lid, van de dataverordening.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing or accessing information relating to a user or data subject
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can concern an online identifier or other information stored on or accessed from a user's device. One requires information and consent before such access, while the other gives the data subject a right to be informed about safeguards when personal data are transferred to a third country or international organisation; this could appear to create overlapping information duties.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative requirements rather than incompatible commands. Provision A regulates the conditions for storing or accessing information on a user's device, whereas provision B concerns a data subject's separate right to information about appropriate safeguards for an international transfer; complying with A does not remove or obstruct B, and B does not authorise access contrary to A.

verdict.shared_subject: Information provision to the Minister under the Dutch electronic-services regime and the GDPR record-of-processing exemption for small organisations
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions may concern an organisation handling personal data while participating in electronic public services. One could argue that supplying data and information to the Minister may require maintaining or disclosing processing information even where the GDPR provision removes the Article 30 register obligation for a small organisation.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 19 requires specified actors to provide information needed by the Minister to prevent or end breaches of secure and reliable access; it does not require an Article 30 record or prohibit other documentation. Article 30 merely limits when the register-of-processing-activities obligation applies, so an organisation can comply with both by providing the information requested or volunteered under Article 19 without treating that as an Article 30 register.

verdict.shared_subject: The costs of a security assessment or scan
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions address security assessments and allocate their costs differently: provision A places the cost on the competent authority, while provision B allows the Minister to impose an independent safety inspection whose costs are borne by the provider. If the same assessment were both a beveiligingsscan under A and the imposed veiligheidscontrole under B, the cost allocation could appear incompatible.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions do not establish that they govern the same assessment. Provision A concerns the competent authority bearing the costs of a defined beveiligingsscan, whereas provision B concerns an optional ministerial power to impose a safety inspection on a specified provider, with provider-funded costs. They can therefore operate cumulatively or in separate situations, and the provider can avoid the optional B obligation unless the Minister imposes it.

verdict.shared_subject: Record-keeping and detection duties of organisations/financial entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A small organisation may be exempt from the GDPR records-of-processing obligation unless one of the listed exceptions applies, while DORA requires financial entities to maintain and test mechanisms for detecting anomalous activities. If those detection mechanisms involve processing personal data, one might initially suspect that the GDPR provision removes a documentation duty relevant to DORA oversight.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties with no incompatible command: Article 30 concerns whether certain organisations must keep a GDPR register of processing activities, whereas Article 10 requires financial entities to have and regularly test ICT-detection mechanisms. DORA does not require the GDPR register, and the GDPR exemption does not prohibit detection mechanisms or their testing; an entity can comply with both, including by separately documenting processing if another rule requires it.

verdict.shared_subject: A high-risk AI system involving personal-data processing and its importer/controller obligations
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can apply to the same AI system, but they impose different obligations on different actors: the GDPR controller must conduct a data-protection impact assessment before processing where the processing likely creates a high risk, while the AI Act importer must verify conformity documentation before placing a high-risk AI system on the market. The strongest possible tension argument is that market-entry verification under the AI Act might be treated as sufficient despite the separate GDPR assessment duty, but neither text says that one substitutes for the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The obligations are cumulative and address different compliance questions and actors. A controller can perform the required impact assessment before processing, while an importer separately verifies conformity assessment, technical documentation, CE marking, declaration, instructions, and authorised representation before placing the system on the market; satisfying one does not purport to satisfy or override the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of personal data by providers of trust services, including processing for direct marketing
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits processing where the data were obtained from the data subject or with explicit consent and the processing is required for providing the trust service. Provision B prohibits continued processing for direct-marketing purposes once the data subject objects, so a provider might have a basis under A yet still be required to stop that particular purpose under B.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose cumulative, purpose-specific requirements rather than contradictory commands: A limits the source and necessity of processing for the trust service, while B independently requires cessation of direct-marketing processing after an objection. A provider can comply with both by not using the data for direct marketing after the objection; A does not require such marketing.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Verleners van vertrouwensdiensten verwerken alleen persoonsgegevens die van de betrokkene zelf of met diens uitdrukkelijke toestemming zijn verkregen, en voor zover de verwerking van deze persoonsgegevens voor het verlenen van de vertrouwensdienst is vereist.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Wanneer de betrokkene bezwaar maakt tegen verwerking ten behoeve van direct marketing, worden de persoonsgegevens niet meer voor deze doeleinden verwerkt.

verdict.shared_subject: Technical and organisational continuity/security measures for regulated entities or providers
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern technical or organisational measures and continuity/security, so an entity that is also a provider could be subject to requirements under both regimes. However, Provision A merely authorises further rules and possible requirements by general administrative order, while Provision B permits a ministerial obligation when a continuity plan is insufficient; no incompatible measure, deadline, or prohibition is stated.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can readily be complied with cumulatively: any generally applicable measures or requirements made under Provision A can coexist with a case-specific ministerial order under Provision B. Provision B's order is directed at improving an insufficient continuity plan and does not forbid compliance with, or impose content incompatible with, Provision A.

verdict.shared_subject: Information duties concerning the transfer of health-care records and international transfers of personal data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern informing a data subject about a transfer, so one might initially suspect that the general notice under provision A could substitute for the more specific information about Article 46 safeguards required by provision B. However, A concerns a transfer of health records between specified health-care actors under the referenced Dutch provision, while B concerns disclosure of appropriate safeguards when personal data are transferred to a third country or international organisation; the texts do not establish that these are the same transfer or that A replaces B.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties can be performed cumulatively: where a health-record transfer also qualifies as a transfer to a third country or international organisation, the person can receive the general notice and rights information required by A and, separately, information about the Article 46 safeguards required by B. If the health-care transfer is not an international transfer, B is simply not triggered.

verdict.shared_subject: ICT risk-management audits involving personal-data transfers to third countries or international organisations
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A restricts transfers of personal data to third countries or international organisations unless the GDPR Chapter V conditions are met. Provision B requires certain non-micro financial entities to conduct proportionate internal ICT-risk audits, which could in practice involve transferring audit data or auditor access to a third country; that creates a possible compliance issue only if the audit arrangement entails a transfer not otherwise authorised under A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative duties: A governs the lawfulness of international transfers of personal data, while B governs the existence, independence, expertise and proportionality of ICT-risk audits. A financial entity can conduct the required audit while ensuring that any personal-data transfer satisfies Chapter V, for example by limiting the data, using an authorised transfer mechanism, or keeping the audit within the EU. Nothing in B requires an unlawful transfer or deems audit compliance sufficient for transfer compliance.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: The provisions both regulate information-related conduct, so one might initially suspect that a confidentiality duty could constrain communications involving network-endpoint or user-identification information. However, Provision A regulates misleading information supplied to a called user through a telecommunications facility, while Provision B regulates confidentiality by notified conformity-assessment bodies and their personnel; neither provision requires or forbids conduct covered by the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A prohibits using a network-facility identifier to provide the called user with incorrect information about the network endpoint or individual user. Provision B requires notified bodies to keep information obtained during conformity-assessment activities confidential, subject to legal-disclosure exceptions. An actor can comply with both: any applicable information must be kept confidential under B, and any information communicated to a called user under A must not be incorrect.

verdict.shared_subject: High-risk processing or AI systems and the resulting compliance procedures
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions use a high-risk trigger and impose a procedure before or in connection with deployment: GDPR Article 36 requires prior consultation with a supervisory authority where a DPIA identifies unmitigated high risk, while the AI Act requires providers of certain high-risk AI systems to use an internal-control conformity-assessment procedure. One might argue that the provider could treat the internal procedure as sufficient instead of consulting the authority, or that the two procedures create competing compliance routes.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative duties on different actors and are triggered by different criteria. Article 36 concerns a controller's proposed personal-data processing and requires prior supervisory-authority consultation when the DPIA shows high risk without mitigating measures; Article 43 concerns providers of AI systems classified as high-risk under Annex III points 2–8 and requires a conformity-assessment procedure based on internal control. Nothing in either text says that one procedure substitutes for or overrides the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing sensitive and criminal-offence-related personal data by a committee or advisory body, and the data subject’s exercise of GDPR rights
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits an otherwise prohibited processing of special-category and criminal-offence-related data when its listed conditions are met. Provision B requires the controller to facilitate the data subject’s rights under Articles 15–22 and, in the Article 11(2) situation, forbids refusal unless identification is impossible; exercising those rights may require handling or disclosing the same sensitive data. This creates a possible interaction between a permission to process sensitive data and an obligation concerning data-subject rights, but the texts do not themselves establish that the rights obligation requires processing prohibited by A or that A overrides it.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: A is a narrowly conditioned exception to the processing prohibition for a committee or advisory body, while B is a general obligation to facilitate data-subject rights. The controller can comply with both by processing only within A’s conditions and facilitating applicable rights subject to the GDPR’s own rules and exceptions; neither provision says that the permission in A displaces B or that B requires processing outside A’s legal basis.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A committee lawfully processes criminal-conviction data under A to perform a task of overriding public interest, and the data subject invokes an Article 15–22 right requiring the controller to handle or provide information about that data. The controller must determine whether responding involves processing covered by A and whether A’s conditions constitute a sufficient legal basis for that rights-related processing; the shown provisions do not resolve that relationship.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the GDPR provisions governing the particular Article 15–22 right, including any applicable restriction or exception and the legal basis for processing necessary to respond, cover the requested handling of the special-category or criminal-offence-related data. Provision A establishes an exception for the committee’s processing purpose, but the text shown does not establish that it also covers every processing operation required to facilitate the data subject’s rights.

verdict.shared_subject: A high-risk AI system involving personal-data processing
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose an assessment-related obligation on potentially overlapping high-risk systems, but they require different assessments by different actors for different legal purposes: a GDPR data-protection impact assessment by the controller and an AI Act conformity assessment by the provider. The strongest possible tension is that an actor might mistakenly treat one assessment as replacing the other, but neither text says that it does.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The obligations are cumulative and can readily be performed independently: the controller conducts a DPIA before processing where the processing is likely to create a high risk to natural persons’ rights and freedoms, while the provider follows the applicable AI-system conformity-assessment procedure. They concern different duties, actors, triggers, and subject matter, and nothing in either provision exempts compliance with the other.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions appear in the same instrument, but they regulate entirely different matters: Article 5 concerns consent by a legal representative for services to protected persons, while Article 21b concerns suspending publication of an administrative decision during interim-relief proceedings. No actor is required by one provision to do something that the other prohibits or makes impossible.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can operate simultaneously without interaction. A service provider can comply with Article 5's scope rule, while the relevant authority separately suspends publication under Article 21b when an interim-relief request is made.

verdict.shared_subject: Information and communications-network services
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions may concern an entity operating communications or network-related services, but Article 47 requires supplying registration information to a central contact point, while Article 11.10a regulates misleading information about network-termination points or users. One might argue that information supplied under Article 47 could include identifying network information and therefore raise a concern under the prohibition.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different subject matter: Article 47 requires specified entity and IP-range information to be provided to the central contact point, whereas Article 11.10a prohibits using a number-provision facility to give a called user incorrect information about a network termination point or individual user. An entity can provide the required registration information accurately while complying fully with the prohibition; neither provision requires the misleading conduct prohibited by the other.
